item.title: [a16z] Why AI’s Next Breakthroughs Could Come from Outside the Big Labs
item.dc:creator: a16z
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

三个让人意外的观察

1. 「节奏（pacing）」这个词本身就是一次语言学上的溃败

大家都在争论要不要放慢AI，但真正被劫持的是词汇表。这场辩论中所有的关键词——pause、swarm、rogue、pacing、x-risk——都是反AI阵营发明的。当你被迫用对方的词来为自己辩护时，你已经输了一半。

这里有个跨领域的隐藏映射：AI实验室现在的处境，几乎精确复刻了2005年金融衍生品行业的公关困境。当时华尔街也试图用"金融创新"这样温和的词来对冲"toxic assets"（有毒资产）的负面叙事，结果2008年一到，整个词云被反对派彻底占领。任何试图在中间地带发明新词的努力都会被解读为"话术"。Anthropic的"pacing"提议正在重演这条路径——一个模糊到无法被证伪、也无法被支持的词，注定同时得罪两边。

真正令人意外的洞察：Dario不给灭绝概率一个具体数字，看似是谨慎，实际上是博弈论上的最优选择——因为一旦给出数字，二分搜索就开始了。"更高还是更低？"这个问题会一直逼近直到答案变得荒谬。不可证伪 = 不可攻击 = 不可承诺 = 不可监管。这就是为什么"non-zero"这个词在这个语境里如此危险。

2. AI监管的真正范式，藏在1980年代的一份计算机犯罪法案里

对话中最深的一层，其实是Steven讲GTE Telemail入侵案的段落——1983年发生的黑客事件，花了两年半才促成1986年的《计算机欺诈与滥用法》，而且法案是围绕具体事实模式写的，不是围绕假想威胁写的。

这里有一个跨领域的惊人平行：FAA的诞生也是这个模式——莱特兄弟1903年首飞，直到1920年代才有飞行执照要求，1938年才有真正的适航监管。35年的实证数据积累，才换来一部有效的法律。

而AI现在的处境是倒过来的：我们在没有事实模式的情况下试图立法。这不是"预防原则"的胜利，这是监管本身的认知论危机——立法者第一次要基于一个假想的未来来约束一个还没有明确损害记录的技术。

跨领域连接：这和当代物理学的困境同构。弦理论几十年拿不出可证伪的预测，导致理论物理学陷入停滞。当你的领域开始基于"不可证伪的灾难场景"来做重大决策时，你其实已经离开了工程学的范畴，进入了神学。

3. Jab Chef模型的意义，被所有人低估了——它是一次编程范式的时间旅行

Steven提到"1960-70年代的计算机科学几乎全部是概率编程"这个点，被埋在对话末尾，但这是整期节目最颠覆性的洞察。

大语言模型这几年一直在做一件极其别扭的事情：把一个概率性文本生成器硬塞进确定性程序的if-else框架里。而Jab Chef模型说：别再让LLM生成文本了，让它在预设选项里选一个，并返回概率分布。

这看似只是效率优化，实际上意味着：软件的本质正在从"确定性执行"回归到"概率性模拟"。1970年前，所有计算机程序本质上都在做随机模拟——导弹轨迹要考虑风向的随机分布，排队模型要考虑到达时间的泊松分布。然后会计软件出现了，我们花50年"驯化"计算机去做确定性的事情。

最出人意料的一跳：这意味着未来五年的最热门的CS研究方向，会是从1965年被遗忘的教科书里挖出来的。概率编程、模拟退火、蒙特卡洛方法——这些在深度学习时代被视为"过时"的东西，会突然变成AI应用层的核心基础设施。

更深层的跨领域联系：这与生物学的"演化发育生物学（evo-devo）"革命异曲同工——现代生物学的一个大发现是，动物身体形态的巨大差异，其实用的是同一套非常古老的基因工具箱，只是调用方式不同。AI应用层正在经历同样的时刻：创新不再来自训练更大的模型，而来自重新组合早已被遗忘的计算原语。

这也是为什么a16z这期节目用"AI's Next Breakthroughs Could Come from Outside the Big Labs"作为标题——平台层的创新已经饱和，创新的重心正在向应用层迁移，而应用层的武器库，反而是从计算机科学的考古现场里挖出来的。

一个额外的、他们没说破的暗线

整场对话有一个没有被明说但反复浮现的隐藏结构：安全社区（security community）和X-risk社区之间的和解，正在成为AI治理最重要的隐性进展。

Noam Brown关于"CPU发热作为侧信道通信"的评论，被Steven描述为"两个部落第一次能在同一个语言层上对话"——一边是从1980年代的Tempest攻击和CRT像素采样中走过来的老派安全工程师，一边是从科幻小说和贝叶斯认识论中走过来的X-risk理论家。他们过去互相看不起，但突然发现agent swarm的攻击面就是老派侧信道攻击的乘以10000倍。

这是一个非常"啊哈"的时刻：AI安全的真正未来，不是新的哲学，而是把冷战时期的计算机安全思维重新激活——那些为核武器实验室设计的多层安全（MLS）、Tempest防护、covert channel理论，这些学术论文躺在图书馆里40年无人问津，因为没人愿意为易用性付这个代价。现在AI来了，AI本身就是那个"愿意付易用性代价的用户"——操作系统研究可能迎来一次文艺复兴。

📝 转录文本

Why AI's Next Breakthroughs Could Come from Outside the Big Labs

a16z Podcast · 精选摘录

开场：几个关键论断

"If you regulate AI too early, you actually don't solve anything. You still just kind of had the same risk ultimately."

"You will the thing into being, but you haven't figured out how to control it."

"The problem we have now is this rift between the labs and the security community that keeps coming to two conclusions. Sloppy — and you're not complete in what you're telling us happened."

"An employee is like 10% chance of species extinction. Agent swarms completely flip that. These are just roaming drones but like times 10,000, and they will easily mistake a good task for a bad one."

"So now we need a whole layer internally that just is tracking way more about what authentications are being done, what APIs are being done."

"The US about 15 years ago stopped leading in tech antitrust. The problem is that Europe is going to lead with that because they have nothing to lose."

"This could change the nature of software fundamentally. The center of innovation has just moved. This is the signal that —"

一、开场与回归

Host: Guys, welcome back to the podcast.

Guest A: Happy to be here.

Guest B: Thank you.

Host: Your beard. Didn't think we'd ever do this again. This is — I can't believe it. This is great.

Guest A: I mean, Martine's just building these like hundred billion dollar companies. Too busy for this podcast. So —

Host: At least taking credit for, as VCs do.

Guest A: Exactly.

二、Pacing the Frontier：Dario 的贴文与"节奏"之争

Host: Um, we have a lot to discuss today, but first look, Aaron, why don't we start with you? Pacing the frontier. How have you reacted and reflected on what's happened there and just the discourse that's followed?

Aaron: Oh boy. I think we should start with Martine on this one. He — he you were fighting lots of good ground wars.

Um, I I maybe I'll say one thing that we probably all agree with, and then we can figure out where we maybe fracture off.

共识：前沿实验室应当以最安全的方式建设

I think we would agree that any AI lab right now at the frontier should be building — you know, in the safest way possible — with the highest degree of governance and security, and, you know, kind of whatever your definition of alignment is. Like this is an incredibly important area of research. It's incredibly important area for the diffusion of AI.

Like you're not going to have AI diffusion without extremely high-quality products that can be trusted by enterprises and that aren't kind of constantly hacking systems.

对 Dario 那篇贴文的具体评价

So when at least I read the Dario post, I actually didn't disagree with almost anything. Because it was all about how do you have better security of these systems, sandboxing, better testing.

There's going to be some debates around the embedded nature of the testers and — do you agree with who those are and does the industry all align on that? But I think actually all of the major points were probably salient and appropriate.

真正的问题：这份文本会被拿去做什么？

Then the only question is: does this get sort of used or leveraged to do things that maybe we don't agree with? Which would be like a slowdown of AI dramatically because of regulatory controls that would sort of not make it easy to compete with the frontier labs.

Or do politicians kind of end up sort of taking the message and running with it, and maybe even worse outcomes happen — like it's used to ban data centers far faster, and whatnot?

So the actual substance of the topic is actually incredibly important and very important for AI advancement in general. And then the question is what do you do about it, especially what do you do about it from a regulatory standpoint. And that's probably where the industry is going to land on very different points in the continuum.

But Martin was putting up a good fight on: let's make sure that we don't use this for regulatory capture — which I also agree with, but I think the ideas in the pacing conversation are important.

Um, you know, again, like it's a little bit of a funny concept because maybe it's not even pacing as much as just like good hygiene and good engineering. And so with good engineering, obviously there is a slight slowdown, but it's a slowdown that obviously allows acceleration of your diffusion — because you wouldn't be able to have any of the AI be diffused if nobody would trust using it.

So the post is very reasonable, but the atmospherics are not right.

三、"氛围"错了：X-risk 与 Pacing 之间的裂缝

Aaron: Like — so an employee is like "this is going to kill, whatever, 10% chance of species extinction," and then Dario says —

Martin: I agree with him more than I disagree with him, right? Like —

Aaron: On TV, on TV the same day that he landed these things. And so in some way you can't have these conversations in isolation. Because if he's going to agree in species extinction, this post that he has looks like this milktoast capitulation that's totally not adequate for the task at hand.

And so I think the atmospherics are totally broken. And a lot of my comments were on the atmospherics.

"Pacing" 这个词本身就是错的

And then I have this quibble, but it really bothers me because I'm impeded — which is:

I think "pacing" is the wrong way to describe this.

For one, yes, it is orthogonal to security. Right? So like you can very slowly build a nuclear weapon and that doesn't make anybody feel better that it's slow versus fast. So that's one.

The second one — it just feels like a capitulation to the pause folks without actually addressing it. So you're saying, "Well, we're not going to pause. We're going to pace to make them happy, but we'll also somehow make the regulators happy." And I think it makes them both unhappy.

Because the pause people are like, "Well, that's not a pause. That's just pacing." And then the regulators are, "You're still doing the thing."

实验室在两个极端之间找不到中间地带

And so I just feel — my sense of what's happening is: the labs are actually trying to do the right thing, and I applaud them for that. I think this is a pragmatic proposal and I applaud them for that.

I think the messaging is wrong because they're trying to split the difference between an internal kind of fringe faction — which are doomers, pause — and then the regulators on the other side. And the problem is they're making both of them unhappy.

And I think what they have to do is: they need to come out, they need to address the x-risk question directly. Like they need to say, "No, we don't think this stuff we're going to do is going to cause extinction." And then I think this becomes very sensible.

四、恐惧与从业：那个"既害怕又要造"的研究员画像

Host: And what would you do — just to play the other side for one second — what do you do? Do you make room for the one possible Venn diagram, which is the lab researcher that is both simultaneously super scared but also works on advancing the state of AI because they believe that it's so important to get right that they want to pursue that?

And obviously the language is right now very problematic, but that person does exist and that is a real kind of person in our industry — which is like, "We have to be at the forefront of AI. I'm also very scared of it, and so that's why I'm working on this."

Martin：如果真的相信有生存风险，答案是国有化

Martin: So let me address this directly. I used to work for Lawrence Livermore National Labs on a weapons program — nuclear weapons. I know what it's like to work on things that have access —

Aaron: You were the first pacer.

Martin: We were part of the first pacers.

So if a constituency within the labs — that are the most knowledgeable people — believe the stuff has existential risk, the answer is to nationalize it and actually put controls that we know that work.

Right now, if they don't actually believe that — and in the private conversations I have, the most sensible people don't — it's a small fraction that do. This is an HR problem.

Right? So to me, an HR problem is a company problem. Like if they are worried that they can't recruit people, or they can't retain people, which it seems to me a lot of this is just that concern. It's almost more of this kind of researcher currency, if that's the case.

I think that is the wrong reason to cause a national-level lockdown on a very promising technology.

So listen — I think the post, again, I think the post is actually very sensible. I think there are real concerns around security. We've had many compute epochs that have real security concerns. I don't think you can reconcile discussions on X-risk with the proposal that was put out. You just can't reconcile those two things. And that has always been my primary —

Host: Right. Right. Okay. Unleash. Okay. Holding it back.

五、Steven 加入战场：pacing 的逻辑漏洞

Steven: So, okay. The first thing is — you can't have — is there a schedule that they've published that says when all this stuff, whatever bad stuff is going to happen, is? They haven't. So you can't pace it because nobody knows when it was supposed to finish in the first place.

It also just seems disingenuous. It's completely — This is like when the press reports on Apple's latest iPhone is late.

Aaron: The phone from — what — nobody knows exists that they haven't told anybody about.

Martin: Yeah. My Apple car was very late.

Steven: Yeah. Like I don't understand. In order for something to be slower, you need to know the rate at which it was moving in the first place. So it's all just utter nonsense and you can't escape that.

更根本的问题：其实根本没在放慢

And then, by the way, this is another problem — that again, from my little quibble on PR: nobody believes it anyway, right? And so if that's the thing, the pacing — right? Which part are they going to pace? That they're going to pace — they've been at a dead run. They've raised more money than ever before. They've grown faster than ever before. There's no indication that they're pacing.

Aaron: So if this is what you're going to hang your — I see, I see, yeah. Well, the internal issue obviously is that the models that everybody has internally far exceed what anybody else has access to. So it's really just the pacing of external releases. But again, back to your point — pacing versus what? Right? Like, we don't know if the one that scares everybody also doesn't, you know, work for a legal brief. Like, it might actually screw all that stuff up because it's — so who knows, right? So there's that.

Steven: And that's — it's just disingenuous to claim that you're pacing.

第二重问题：为什么要请政府来管你？

Second, why do they have to announce all of this and ask the government to tell them to pace? Like that's the part that starts to go, "Well, this is really spooky." If you are the most afraid of how everything is going to go because of your product, just stop. Don't do it.

Like — this is the — I worked at a missile factory in college and we had nuclear missiles and I walked the floor —

Aaron: What's with you guys and missiles? I don't — I'm just here with software.

六、冷战往事：从核导弹车间到"pacing"这个中间地带

Steven: You were one of two people in college when we were — which was either you were protesting to keep them off campus or building them. So that was your choice.

And like, we had nuns from the Catholic Church show up and pour blood all over on missiles. And I'm busy just wheeling PCs around on carts saying "here's the secure PC," and I'm like scared to die. I have no idea what's going on. And I'm like, it's a nuclear missile. And then you find out that that's what stopped the Cold War. Like that literally — it was a Pershing missile and that was what did it.

"Pacing" 是一个模糊到不成词的词

And so — you said something I think is super interesting, which is: pacing is this sort of fuzzy nonword between like going and not going. Yeah. And the problem is — you're exactly right — like there's — no one is going to be happy with the middle road.

一个体育观察：这些人并不理解政府是怎么运作的

And so one of the things that people — I think it's almost fun for me to watch as a sport — they think that all these people saying to the government "do this, don't do this," they think they're going to get what they want. And it's a complete 100% misunderstanding of how government works.

Which is — you, when you talk to the government, they actually know how these things work. And they know they're just listening to you and they're listening to everyone. And no one is going to get what they want, because they know in order to do anything in our system, it's a compromise.

And so everything — that all the inputs — can make it into the government. The output never makes everyone happy, right? 100% of the time it either doesn't go far enough or it goes way, way too far.

And so you can't take the view that you're going to talk to the government and talk your way into the solution you want. So the bottom line is: if they're asking for pacing, they're going to get the wrong velocity.

Aaron: Well, my favorite thing is — what was it, David Sacks was like — I think it was David Sacks, but someone from the government said, "Uh, you're asking us to regulate you." No. Facebook. The answer was no.

Host: Well, but the thing that —

Aaron: Probably just Trump, I think, but —

七、监管的雪球一旦滚起来就停不下来

Host: The thing that they know now — that you just know from experience — is: once the wheels start on regulating, you can't slow that one down. And now it's become an election issue for every party in every jurisdiction, up and down the whole government stack. So there's now this whole basket of regulatory approaches.

Aaron: Well, the next election will 100% be a referendum on AI. Like, it has to happen. That 2028 is the AI election. And you could basically run on — the problem is, it's not obvious who would run on the pro-AI story because it's going to be too nebulous to tell that story.

So then it's just basically varying degrees of how much do you regulate it, or at least try and avoid the topic.

Yeah. But it is too bad that we as a country are in a spot where the pro-AI case is just like — it sounds too — it's just like takes too many words. It's way too nuanced. It's defensive.

Martin: Yeah, it's defensive.

Steven: It's defensive and we own none of the vocabulary. Right? So the whole debate is "pause." It's "swarms." It's "rogue." Every word has been chosen by the people who don't want to do AI.

Aaron: Yeah. And so it means the first thing you have to do is invent new words and say that their words are wrong — which takes so many words. So we got to be like "union jobs" and "cancer" and like — there needs to be another word cloud that emerges.

八、X-risk 的立场问题：为什么实验室不明确否认？

Martin: What I don't understand is why the labs have not taken a position on X-risk. Like, short of that, I don't think this goes in any direction other than heavy-handed regulation.

Yeah — well, it would just be negligent of the government to be like, "There's a 10% chance of species extinction. The CEO of the top company says he agrees with it." Like, how can a government not do — have you had a regulation?

Host: Well, but what — but who — but what would anybody, really knowing this ecosystem though, I don't know that you would be able to pin anybody down on that, other than something —

Martin: No — I would say Dario said it on —

Host: No, but I'm saying you're not going to pin anybody down on a lower — Well, in fact, he does the worst thing about it, which is he agrees with people who claim that they believe that there's an X percentage of extinction happening, but he specifically goes out of his way to say, "I'm not going to put a percentage on it."

Which I just think is the weirdest —

关于"边际风险"的清晰化提议

Aaron: To be fair — no, nobody could be fair. To be fair, that's like it's not 100% disingenuous or whatever. Like, he probably doesn't specifically agree that it's 10%. Or maybe he does and it's just too scary if he were to say —

Steven: Let's just play binary search. I mean, is it more or is it less?

Aaron: But the whole thing is a made-up concept that we just created. Like, nobody can — you can't quantify any of this.

Martin: Well, but that's sort of Martin's point.

Aaron: Well, but you just had an official position, though. So the only official position you could possibly get would be the PR version of this — that would be the only thing that would be intellectually honest, which is: "There are real risks with AI. There's incredibly positive benefits as well. We are working to mitigate the risks so they are as reduced as humanly possible."

Martin: I don't think that's — I don't think that's true.

Listen, so — we've been through multiple epochs of technology. We've been through compute. We've been through the internet. We've been through the web. We've been through social networking. We had a discussion about the risks without talking about X-risk.

Right? So for example, one thing you can say is: "We do not think the marginal risk for species extinction is different than it is."

Host: But what if they do think it is higher?

Martin: Well, then we should — okay, okay, yeah. Like I think the answer is they do think it's more than just the internet.

One of two options: you believe that we're going to go extinct and we shut it all down — like, shut it down — or they believe that this is just a chance that we got —

冷战时期的核战争概率与"非零"陷阱

Aaron: Dario thinks less — but these Cold Warriors, no one — like the Pentagon — you know, they ran a lot of simulations on the chances for nuclear war. Great movie War Games about the whole thing. But the thing was, it was nonzero.

Host: Can they say — can they say non-zero, then? Is that allowed?

Aaron: I think as soon as you think it's non-zero —

Steven: The problem is if you say non-zero, that could be like, you know, the guy thinks 93%.

Martin: But let's — wait, so just so we're all having a clean conversation, let's talk about marginal risk here. We're not talking about absolute risk. Right? Okay.

Aaron: It's just that I think once you say it's non-zero, the only answer of catastrophic — the only answer is you have to nationalize it.

Martin: Yes. And so what the labs in general that have that view are trying to thread is: they want it to be nonzero as a license to do a certain set of things, without the burden of just becoming a national —

九、被"事实上国有化"的行业：从核武器到银行到 KYC

Host: Well, do you have — I actually don't know all of the precedents, you hopefully do — but like, there must be some things that are non-zero, uh, let's say X-risks, that are not particularly nationalized, but the regulatory environment around them is so heavy that it might as well be nationalized because of the KYC requirements on — like, like — I'm sure like to develop anthrax, you have to go to a particular kind of lab.

Martin: Well, BSL-4 labs are — but they're nationalized. They are national.

Host: Okay. But ethics tends to be nationalized. Yes. Like normal human safety, not so much. Right? Like industry oversight that over the time becomes federal regulation.

Martin: Right. 一个奇怪的 Stanford 往事

Like I even remember — there's at Stanford during our PhD, I remember the oscilloscope was kind of janky. I'm like, "What's going on with this oscilloscope? Like it's a little slow." And I was measuring the network traffic and it was like more network traffic than you would expect.

And I'm like, "Why is there network?" I didn't know the thing had a TCP stack. Somebody had broken in — because it's an old version of Windows CE — and was running a porn server, you know. And so like —

Aaron: I noted that.

Martin: For the record, nothing —

Aaron: It used to be — It used to be the case that any time you turned over a stone, somebody had broken into something and was — like, it wasn't this worst-case malicious whatever. And actually, very rarely, even though the capability was there.

And so if we could just somehow tone down the rhetoric and put it in context — and these are still computer systems, and yes there's very serious stuff, and people have definitely died because networks have gone down, there's been real issues — but like — and then can we just quibble about GDPR? That would be amazing.

But the problem is: that's not the discussion. It's not about GDPR and prompts. It's about species extinction and philosophy.

Steven: And philosophy and irrefutable things. And it's just — it's very soon —

二十三、汽车、飞机、药品：所有安全监管都是花40年演化出来的

Steven: I think that's such a great point. And I think you hear people now talk about "we regulate airplanes, and we regulate cars," and you forget — well, the first cars were at the turn of the century. And "Unsafe at Any Speed" was in the mid-1960s.

Aaron: Totally.

Steven: And people had been doing — selling pharmaceuticals in the gold rush — and thalidomide, you know, 50 or 75 years later, and not even in the US. And then there was the FDA.

And the first pilots were flying — obviously at the beginning of the 20th century. And it wasn't until the 1920s that you had to get a license to be a pilot. And you literally showed up with your own plane and you got a certificate — if you had — it was like getting — it was literally no different than driver's ed is today.

And then it was 20 more years until they had anything to do with airworthiness and looking at your plane. But it was — it is minimal. And then it wasn't until way after World War I that they got involved in what you think of as the modern FAA.

And so you're looking at 40 years of innovation.

Aaron: And they were not moving slow. I mean, if you've ever seen that video in black and white of all the different planes that crashed and everything — that was 20 years after the Wright Brothers.

Steven: And is incredibly effective. And it's the safest form of transportation.

Aaron: And so I do think that this process — It's also the slowest, most difficult form of innovation. And so if you start the FAA — if you had started the FAA in 1910, you never — you never — Well, I was listening to a Nick Bostrom podcast just a couple days ago. It was interesting.

Steven: And but no — but he actually makes his point: if you regulate AI too early, you actually basically don't solve anything, and you still just kind of had the same risk ultimately. But you don't understand the system. Then you will the thing into being, but you haven't figured out how to control it.

二十四、AI 到底是什么，我们还在搞清楚

Aaron: Well, we have to figure out what it actually is. Like — there are new things coming out all the time, and casting AI completely differently than we thought of just six or nine months ago.

And I think that like all the innovation that's going to happen at the application layer is going to cause things to move in and out of the models in different ways.

Like we — you know, we thought up until last week, I think, that text prompts and text coming back was going to be the best way to interact with —

Host: I know — then Jeff —

Aaron: And then Jeb Chef —

Jab Chef 与传统软件的耦合问题

Host: So good too. And then — so talk about that, because I think — why you find it so remarkable.

Martin: Yeah. Well, okay. So, the way I think about it is — so, okay — so LLMs were kind of text-in, text-out, right? They generate text, and they came from chat, right? It was to communicate with a human.

And we've spent the last few years trying to take this thing that spits out text and cram it into a traditional program. Right? But traditional programs don't really speak text, right?

And so then you end up doing this janky thing where you're like — in the prompt you're like, "Here's the schema" — here's the schema, but the thing is generating text and it kind of ignores it. And it's just been super janky.

Jab Chef 的核心洞察：不是生成文本，而是从选项中选

And so what Jeff basically said is: "Listen, generating the text is a very expensive thing, but it's also kind of more complicated than you need. So why don't we — we'll read text, and we'll have all of that kind of knowledge to read the text, but then rather than generating text — which is very expensive — we will just, if you give us a set of options, we'll choose the best option."

We can do that incredibly — we can do it incredibly fast, incredibly cheaply, but also we can do it with much more accuracy because we can train just for this.

And so for all of the use cases that are not talking to a chatbot but are actually trying to put it in traditional software — this is a great fit.

And so this has probably been the fastest adoption of an AI model since ChatGPT. It's just been remarkable, because we're all primed for this.

二十五、自然语言从来不是最有效的接口

Steven: I just want to pile on this one, because I can't tell you how much I love seeing this exact form of innovation. Because what it does is: it does the thing that's bugged me from the very beginning — which is there's been no user study ever that shows interacting with the computer using full natural language is efficient.

It's literally always the least efficient way, and it's very simple. And it's just like — ask yourself, how many people are really really good at asking questions? And immediately that's like less than half the people can ask a good question in a meeting.

And then, how often do you look at the answer and get really frustrated before it's finished, but you have to pay all this money to watch the seven paragraphs come out and then apologize that it's only a little —

概率编程回归：1960-70 年代的计算机科学又活过来了

And so that's one — like having a different model. And then the other, of course, is my favorite — which is the output of it is designed for probabilistic programming.

And so instead of saying "is this a customer service question, then route to customer service, otherwise route to general help desk" or whatever — it's like "well, this is 80% customer service."

And that's exactly simulation. And it turns out there's like 50 years of computer science research in literally probabilistic if-statements.

And so suddenly the coolest place to be in computer science is going to be in probabilistic programming — which was all of computer science in the 1960s and 70s.

So it was basically — because all of computers started with doing math, and it was all simulation. So it was like, "Let's launch the missile and hit that target, but it's windy — but wind isn't constant. So let's model the wind and decide where to put the thrusters in order to do the arc."

And so most programming through, like, say 1970 before it got to accounting was probably — and then we ruined everything.

No — but accounting, there's no probability in accounting, right? But most programming was basically this modeling kind of thing. And so most programming language design was trying to figure out how to put probability into if-statements or into while-loops. Like "do this until something happens maybe most of the time."

一个1960年代教科书的复活

And like — so my first CS class, like the very second assignment or so, was a simulation about like waiting online at a store. And I didn't know it at the time — I actually looked all this up when I was reading about Jeb — which was like the whole thing was: my professor was — like, he wrote the book called The Theory of Simulation in like 1960. And I just didn't know that, because it was kind of died by the 80s because it was all replaced by hyper.

那份未来的幻灯片

And so this notion of probabilistic — and that slide deck you shared about the future — what's different about language models and stuff that you said — was super good.

Aaron: Oh, HALPER Flags.

Steven: One phenomenal — Thomas. Great. But the part that I felt was missing was that, oh wait, this is not all new. Like all of computer science was this probabilistic stuff.

And so it's going to be very interesting to dust off all of that work — because it's exactly what's going on. Like it's not an "if" statement. Now it's "if X%," not "if always." And so the way that Jeb worked is: you basically — it's a custom programming language, almost — which is "here's the prompt, come back with a percentage." And then you put that in the if statement.

大模型终于能被塞进传统软件

Martin: But the consequential thing is: like, finally we have a way to integrate these language models into a traditional software.

And I think it's kind of funny, because you ask the question — like, why haven't the labs done this, right? And it's kind of like a — not an indictment, but a reflection on how they think. Like they're trying to create beings, and beings speak. If you're trying to create God, God speaks in natural languages or whatever.

Where this is really about something that's for traditional software — which is kind of not the direction that they've been taken.

But one of the reasons the uptick has been so dramatic is because a lot of us software people have been trying to integrate these models into software. It just hasn't —

So even before you get to the probabilistic — if I want a language model to drive an if-statement — like it's really hard today. With this model, it makes it much, much, much easier.

And then, of course, this could change the nature of software fundamentally, to make it more stochastic over —

二十六、创新中心已经转移到模型之外

Aaron: Well, I think — but I absolutely — and I think that what's so cool is that it is happening outside the models. Because that's what I think is just going to happen, which is: the center of innovation has just moved.

And now people need to — like, it turns out that the —

Host: I mean, outside of the lab, the big —

Aaron: The platform providers 100% — you know, basically reach a critical — a point of critical mass where the innovation stops happening at the platform layer.

"Sherlocking" 与平台注定的宿命

And then, you know — Apple — there's this famous expression in the Apple community called "Sherlocking" — where Apple looks around, and the things from the outside world become features, and people complain. And it's a real — but that's sort of how the innovation works, because once you're a platform, you're overwhelmed. No matter how many people you add, you're overwhelmed with just keeping the thing running, and compatibility and stuff like that.

And so I think that this is the signal that now people have figured out that there's innovation to be done — to the model, but outside the model.

Host: That's awesome.

Martin: Yeah. Yeah.

Host: Guys, thanks for coming. This is great.

Aaron/Martin: Okay. Great.

## 三个让人意外的观察
### 1. 「节奏（pacing）」这个词本身就是一次语言学上的溃败
大家都在争论要不要放慢AI，但真正被劫持的是**词汇表**。这场辩论中所有的关键词——pause、swarm、rogue、pacing、x-risk——都是**反AI阵营发明的**。当你被迫用对方的词来为自己辩护时，你已经输了一半。
这里有个跨领域的隐藏映射：**AI实验室现在的处境，几乎精确复刻了2005年金融衍生品行业的公关困境**。当时华尔街也试图用"金融创新"这样温和的词来对冲"toxic assets"（有毒资产）的负面叙事，结果2008年一到，整个词云被反对派彻底占领。任何试图在中间地带发明新词的努力都会被解读为"话术"。Anthropic的"pacing"提议正在重演这条路径——一个模糊到无法被证伪、也无法被支持的词，注定同时得罪两边。
**真正令人意外的洞察**：Dario不给灭绝概率一个具体数字，看似是谨慎，实际上是**博弈论上的最优选择**——因为一旦给出数字，二分搜索就开始了。"更高还是更低？"这个问题会一直逼近直到答案变得荒谬。**不可证伪 = 不可攻击 =

item.title: [邦妮區塊鏈 Bonnie Blockchain] 知名投資人：籌碼已完成換手，比特幣即將重演暴漲戲碼！British HODL【邦妮區塊鏈】
item.dc:creator: 邦妮區塊鏈 Bonnie Blockchain
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的观察：Bitcoin 的原教旨主义者正在成为 Bitcoin 最大的威胁向量

整段访谈里最刺耳的一句话不是价格预测，而是这句："the community and it turns out that that's a real threat vector and nobody was evaluating it"（社区本身就是威胁向量，而没人在评估它）。

这里有一个惊人的悖论：BlackRock ETF 持有者的 HODL 率，远远高于那些天天喊 "not your keys not your coins" 的自托管信徒。$500 亿流入 IBIT，资产跌 50%，净赎回仅 2–3%——这个数字连 BlackRock 自己都没见过。冷钱包信徒被"验证不信任"的口号骗光了终身积蓄，而那些"腐败的华尔街西装"却在真正意义上"HODL"。

这是一种制度理性对情感忠诚的胜利。原教旨的 Bitcoiner 拥有"信仰"，但机构拥有"配置纪律"——后者不需要爱一个资产才能长期持有它。

二、跨领域连接：这和早期基督教、日本三代目、Amway 的结构完全同构

British HODL 讲的三件事，其实是同一个跨领域母题在不同时代的再现：

  1. Affinity scam 结构（宗教-社区诈骗）：冷钱包事件不是技术故障，是"社区信任传染链"崩溃。同样的模式发生在摩门教庞氏、伊斯兰互助基金骗局、以及硅谷 FTX 圈——当所有人互相背书时，实际上没有一个人在做独立验证。ChatGPT 4.0 就能测出漏洞，却因为大家忙着卖钱包没人做——这是社会学上的 pluralistic ignorance（多元无知）经典案例。

  2. 家族传承的三代困境：他讲的亚洲家族企业、房地产传到孙辈就卖掉——这是日语里的"三代目が身上を潰す"（三代目败家）现象。所有传统资产都有"运维摩擦"：房子要换灯泡、公司要管员工。Bitcoin 是人类史上第一个"零运维成本的跨代资产"——这才是他真正的洞见，而不是价格。这对亚洲家族资本的意义，比对美国散户大得多。

  3. 早期教会范式：Bitcoin 现在正在经历早期基督教从"地下反抗运动"变成"罗马国教"的过程。原教旨派（Peter Schiff 级 Bitcoiner）就是当年反对君士坦丁妥协的孟他努派——他们的"纯洁性"最终会威胁到运动本身的延续。

三、最被忽视的宏观信号：AI 集中交易吸走了本该属于 Bitcoin 的流动性周期

主流分析都在看 Bitcoin 是否见顶。British HODL 提出的角度更根本：过去两年根本没有发生流动性周期，只有一个畸形的 AI 集中交易。S&P 500 和 Nasdaq 里 45% 的市值是 AI 交易——这不是牛市，这是单一叙事对全市场流动性的虹吸。

由此衍生的隐藏推论极其锋利：

  • "你不能在反 AI 的立场上赢中期选举"——这是他对 AI 见顶时点的政治经济判断，而不是技术判断。政客的选举周期成了资产轮动的隐形节拍器。
  • 财政部从 $40 亿 buyback 威胁到 5 天内 $1 万亿——这不是量化宽松，这是"财政部化的 QE"（Treasury-ized QE），Fed 已经不是主导者。市场分析师还在盯着 FOMC，真正的液压泵已经转移到了 Yellen/Bessent 的办公室。
  • 2013 双顶类比：如果他对，那么现在不是熊市尾声，而是"第一顶后 → 流动性回归 → 第二顶暴涨" 的中间态。这个类比若成立，$340k 目标反而是保守的。

四、藏在最后一句里的哲学：这是一次 IQ 测试

"Keep waiting. It's an IQ test and you failed."——这句话如此傲慢，但它揭示了一个残酷的行为金融学定律：在稀缺资产上，"等更低"本质上是一种否认稀缺性的行为。如果你真的相信 Bitcoin 是绝对稀缺的，就不会等；如果你在等，说明你潜意识里不相信自己的论点。

"Waiting for lower price" 是一种自我背叛的信念披露。这在心理学上叫 revealed preference——你的行动比你的语言更真实。

📝 转录文本

知名投資人 British HODL：籌碼已完成換手，比特幣即將重演暴漲戲碼

开场：2013 年剧本即将重演

British HODL： This Bitcoin cycle is going to be like 2013. We had the top in 2013. What happened was the liquidity conditions eased in 2013 and it went through the roof like a rocket ship. That's what's about to happen right now. Right now, we are stepping into it.

I'm excited. We've had the longest period of an M2 break and an M2 lack of correlation and we're about to mean revert — in the middle of the institutions taking 2 million coins. So, what's going to happen to the multiplier this time round in a bull market?

I got this stat from BlackRock. Insane. They brought in $50 billion into IBIT. The asset went down 50%. They had like two or three % net redemptions. They have never seen anything like that. That's the HODL rate of a Bitcoin ETF hodler. It's in the hands of price-insensitive people.

A lot of people think that this $126K was a top for Bitcoin, right, for this cycle. I disagree with that. Everything tells me we're about to see something. And my price target, by the way, has always stayed consistent even through this whole thing.

You're going to see all of these IPOs flush through. All of that liquidity is going to be dumped onto retail. They're going to make out like bandits. You can't run a midterms being pro-AI. That's going to rotate. I think that somewhere between Q4 of this year and Q2 of next year, you're going to top out on the speculation cycle.

This wonderful thing that we have called Bitcoin — that's protecting the futures of people with absolute scarcity for the first time in human history — the circular economy, whatever… Great. Have your fun. It's fantastic. I don't care. You're idiots. This is a mentally unequipped point. We're now entering the mentally unequipped level of Bitcoiner.

一、Cold Card 事件：自托管的「911 时刻」

主持人： You're an investor, very popular YouTuber. Offline, we were talking about the Cold Card incident.

British HODL： Massive incident. I just got off a panel and someone called it the "9/11 for self-custody."

主持人： And what changed after this incident for you?

British HODL： I think what people realized is that — as I've been calling them — the Bitcoiners have been pitching this idea of "verify, don't trust; don't trust, verify," right? And I think what people realized was that even though the people that held their Cold Card and lost their entire net worth and their life savings and their children's inheritance by following every single step that the Bitcoiners told them to do…

I think they realized that ultimately they were trusting something. And nobody was verifying. It was the "cool wallet" to promote. So everyone kept talking about it and everyone was just LARPing. It was the affinity scam of self-custody — and I think a lot of people woke up to that.

主持人： Are you able to explain to the viewers what exactly happened? I don't want to cause chaos and now they're like, "Oh, self-custody is a bad thing." But what exactly happened in that particular incident?

British HODL： Yeah. So self-custody is not broken, right? If self-custody was to ever break, then Bitcoin itself would break. What broke here was the trust that this particular wallet was generating entropy in a secure way. That was a complete lie and a complete LARP. And this could have been tested since ChatGPT 4.0. Nobody was putting their own code through it. They were too busy selling their wallets instead of maintaining security.

And I don't know any other Bitcoin company that I can trust anymore. I need absolute verification, because people are in different positions obviously with the amount that they're protecting. And this is one of those moments where we've now crossed the Rubicon on trust. You have to decide who you're trusting — because you're always trusting someone.

From my perspective, I'm rather trusting a $14 trillion asset manager with hundreds of millions of dollars of insurance — you know, 17 spare nerds sitting somewhere making sure that my custody of my assets are safe, incentivized to do so because they're earning fees — not a company that's incentivized to sell me a hardware wallet.

主持人： Which is who?

British HODL： Anyone. Anyone selling a hardware wallet has to be verified at this point, right?

My message has always been over the last three or four years: assign a probability to America and the financial system and everything collapsing. Put that into a multi-sig self-custody — which is I think the benchmark at this point. The rest of it, split it between IBIT and FBTC.

主持人： Why specifically those two?

British HODL： Well, you got BlackRock on one side — they're custodying with Coinbase — and you've got Fidelity on the other side, and they're custodying with Fidelity. So you got complete spread of risk on the custody side, and I just think that's the best solution that we have so far.

二、"自己的责任" vs. 「机构 HODL 优于 Bitcoiner」

主持人： Supposedly if you hold Bitcoin, you have the responsibility of holding it, verifying it. You can't lose it and blame other people.

British HODL： Absolutely. That's a very valid point. And I think people became awake to that. But that's not what's been going on — which is why these institutional products… when you had FTX and all this other stuff…

But now, one of the crazy parts: I was doing a panel with a very prominent Bitcoiner and he tried to compare Alex Mashinsky to Larry Fink. And I was like, "We're now entering the mentally unequipped level of Bitcoiner." Because — and again this is my POV — this is a mentally unequipped point. Larry Fink and BlackRock compared to Alex Mashinsky and Celsius? We're talking about two different hemispheres of the universe here, right?

And again, this is how an asset is maturing. This wonderful thing that we have called Bitcoin, that's protecting the futures of people with absolute scarcity for the first time in human history — we have to protect it.

I'm not here for a joke. I'm not here for people that listen to me, or myself or my family, to buy this asset once in a lifetime and then they lose it because they're part of some community that's telling them to be religious about something. I want you to hold it forever. And part of that threat vector is the community — and it turns out that that's a real threat vector, and nobody was evaluating it.

Then you've got other things now: the fact that you can do lending on IBIT or any of the ETFs; the fact that you can have jurisdictional arbitrage. A lot of people talk about sovereignty — LARPing again, because they're not willing to give up their citizenships. If you're not willing to hedge your citizenship and you're talking about "I want to put my money into a cold wallet," listen — I'll tell you this: if the British government or the US government has an issue, they're going to find you, right? So you got to be smart about this.

But here's what I'll say from my experience for the people I speak to: there's zero serious money that's thinking about self-custody since the ETFs came out. So no, this is not even a question. It's just a Bitcoiner topic. In the real world, no one's talking about this. It's all ETFs, it's all trust structures, it's all lending, it's all smart solutions.

主持人： Even the Bitcoiners that go on these shows and pitch self-custody — you think they're also doing that if they have enough money?

British HODL： Yeah. So the question you got to ask yourself is: do you want to listen to someone that's broke about money, or do you want to listen to someone that has money talk about what they're doing with their money?

三、Bitcoin 的真正效用：不是「花掉」，而是「永远持有」

主持人： See, there is a disconnection here. A lot of Bitcoiners love Bitcoin because you can send it to your family right away, or once you have internet you have access — all these little things. With ETFs, IBIT, you can't do that.

British HODL： But I can send credit anywhere. Yes.

And the benefit — so here's the crazy part. You're telling me if you're a Bitcoiner, and imagine there's a Bitcoiner over here — you're telling me the advantage for you is to buy the scarcest asset humanity has ever seen, and then sell it? I think you're an idiot.

Like, your whole argument is "I want sovereignty so that I can spend my assets, or I can send it to my kids so they can spend it." What I want to do is: I want that Bitcoin that I've accumulated, worked hard and accumulated, put my value into — to stay belonging to my last name and my kids and their kids and their kids and their kids and their kids forever.

And I want to borrow against that. I want to generate liquidity against that. I want to use these tools so that my kids have an advantage over every other kid. That's what I want. That's what every wealthy family has ever generated.

A big point when I speak to people with businesses — legacy businesses, family businesses. This is very common by the way here in Asia — businesses that have been built and sustained for 50, 60 years. And then the kids finally inherit it and they don't want anything to do with the business, because the world has moved on. So then what do they do? They sell that business. Now it's happening with real estate — kids are now going, "I don't want to deal with this property portfolio. I'd much prefer equity, so I want to sell."

The beautiful thing about Bitcoin is it's completely frictionless. It's the first asset that you can just hold forever, because there's no friction attached to it. You don't have to run a business. You don't have to worry about real estate. You don't have to change the toilets. You don't have to replace the light bulbs. You can just hold it frictionless for eternity.

And I want the people that I'm surrounded by to hold our Bitcoin forever. I'm not LARPing about spending your Bitcoin. It's irrelevant to me. The circular economy, whatever — great, have your fun. It's fantastic, I don't care. I want my people to hold their Bitcoin forever for the benefit of their kids and their kids' kids' kids' kids forever, because we have an asset that you can actually do that with now, with zero drag. That's what I care about.

四、告别黄金：从 Peter Schiff 到 Bitcoin 的觉醒

主持人： We met at a Peter Schiff dinner.

British HODL： Oh god.

主持人： In Dubai.

British HODL： That was entertaining for me.

主持人： Yeah, that was very interesting. And you yourself — you were in gold.

British HODL： Yeah. Back in the day.

主持人： Could you tell the story for people that might not be familiar with your journey?

British HODL： Yeah. So listen, I started my first business working when I was 16 years old, and then eventually found my way to gold. I thought it was the scarce asset, etc. I thought Bitcoin was a complete scam. And then in 2020 I woke up to the fact that I've understood Bitcoin completely wrong. I was evaluating it like an equity when I should have looked at it as a commodity. It was completely wrong, my thinking.

Anyway, so March/April of 2020 I discovered Bitcoin. I had a gold education business as well. By November — November 2020 — I was zero gold and silver. I sold it.

主持人： Why?

British HODL： Because Bitcoin was better. Bitcoin is the far superior asset. So I shut down the business and I told all my clients, "Go buy the Bitcoin. It's better for the use case that we're buying gold for. It's a better asset. Bitcoin's better."

So I shut off this business — he was doing almost a million dollars a year at the time. And that's my journey into Bitcoin.

When I listen to someone like Peter Schiff — I know Peter, I know all of his friends, we know the same people — I just think he's missing the fundamental point.

The crazy thing is: you get a lot of Bitcoiners that say "I'm going to own Bitcoin and gold because I'm going to diversify." That's not diversification. They solve the same purpose. You diversify across different needs. If you want gold, then you look at the best asset for that need — and that's Bitcoin. It's absolutely finitely scarce.

I had a lot of my gold and silver friends — personalities you would know if I said them. They called me and said, "This is stupid, because you're buying up Bitcoin. It's not real, it's this, that, and the other." I said, "Look, tell me exactly how many grams of gold came out of the earth yesterday, and I'll move 50% of my net worth back in." I'm still waiting.

五、投资组合结构：三桶理论 与 130% 比特币敞口

主持人： So your portfolio is 100% Bitcoin?

British HODL： No, it's like 130% Bitcoin exposure.

主持人： So you don't believe in diversifying your portfolio at all then?

British HODL： That's not true. Bitcoin to me is money, right? I look at my portfolio in three buckets:

  1. A savings bucket
  2. A growth bucket
  3. An income bucket

It's the simplest way to look at it.

  • A savings bucket to me is: what's the baseline hurdle rate? It's just basic value storage. That's Bitcoin.
  • The growth bucket is: what can I grow above Bitcoin, and in a risk-adjusted way, because I don't want to take too much risk.
  • The income bucket is the smallest part for me, and that's just basically to stack up cash flow coming in.

So that's the way I look at it. I'm interested in other things. I love biotech right now. The future of biotech is exciting for me. The future of AI — but I think AI right now is an over-bloated trade. I think we are going to see a capital market rotation in that. And when that happens, I look forward to buying up all the AI stuff I'm interested in that's on my watch list. But I don't think, as of this moment, it's the right time for me to do that.

六、宏观时点判断：流动性周期、PMI 与 2013 类比

主持人： When will that happen?

British HODL： A lot of people think this $126K was a top for Bitcoin, right, for this cycle. I disagree with that. We have not had a liquidity cycle. We have not had a confidence cycle. We've not had any cycle. The only thing that's been going on is a concentrated trade into AI.

You're going to see all of these IPOs flush through. All of that liquidity is going to be dumped onto retail. They're going to make out like bandits. It's going to be amazing for the people that were in the private equity of these AI companies.

You can't run a midterms being pro-AI. It's not going to happen. That's going to rotate. Not that anything's wrong with AI — I think it's a revolutionary technology. I want to buy an AI position. I'm probably going to do that at the bottom of the next liquidity cycle.

I think that somewhere between Q4 of this year and Q2 of next year, you're going to top out on the speculation cycle. And then it's going to be questions to see how long it takes to go down on the liquidity cycle. We'll see.

They just went from $4 billion of buybacks to a trillion in 5 [days]. The threat of a trillion in 5 days — that's not normal. We're in a whole different regime here.

主持人： What does that mean?

British HODL： It means that what the Treasury is threatening you with is: "I don't care what you think about the bond market. I'm going to drive the price down."

主持人： And what does that mean for the everyday investor?

British HODL： I don't know what it means for the everyday investor, because most of them make stupid decisions. But for the person who's paying attention — what that means is: we are entering a PMI cycle increase. It's finally above 50. It's been below that for 4 years now. We're finally entering a liquidity cycle.

So I believe this Bitcoin cycle is going to be like 2013. We had the top in 2013 and everyone thought "okay, this is done at like $200-something." Then it collapsed. I was like, "It's over." Then what happened? Nothing happened with Bitcoin — what happened was the liquidity conditions eased in 2013 and it went through the roof like a rocket ship.

And I think that's what's about to happen right now. Right now we are stepping into it. PMI cycle expansion, liquidity expansion. So what I'm planning personally is how I'm going to hedge if I'm right.

七、如何对冲：Dubai、期权、MSTY / WTR 工具箱

主持人： How are you hedging then?

British HODL： I'm looking at everything. I'm looking at put options in the market that are now available. I'm looking at potentially selling. Luckily, I live in Dubai — in the UAE we have zero tax. So there's a lot of things going on right now. You got the in-kind conversions that a lot of people are doing now to avoid the taxation in the US.

There's just a lot of tools now to hedge your position. You don't have to sit there throughout this whole thing. You just have to be smart about how you're looking at the market. And Raoul's done a great job educating on this — but you got to understand how liquidity works in order to make these decisions.

Most people are trying to make these decisions after they see the evidence. You can't do that. You got to be able to go: "Okay, so what happens if the government goes negative on AI, not permanently, before the midterms?" My trades, my Trading View — Trading View.

主持人： What are some metrics or signs that you're looking at other than the buyback for liquidity?

British HODL： That's the one right now. I don't even think interest rates need to come down too much for liquidity to start pumping. I think the liquidity is going to come through the Treasury. I think everyone's looking at 2008 going "oh, it's going to be the Fed — they'll backstop anything that collapses" — but we don't need a collapse here to drive liquidity.

So looking at that, I'm looking at the confidence numbers. Raoul's done the best work on this, best data on this. The liquidity — the PMI cycle topping out — will symbolize a massive top in speculation, interest and speculation. So that's what I'm looking at.

When that happens, I'll place some hedge positions. Whether it's — even in my income bucket, I use a tool like MSTY, for example, which is a yield-harvesting product on MSTR's volatility. They have a flip product for the bear market called WTR. So whenever I see that happen, I'll just sell my MSTY and get into WTR and generate income on the way down.

All these tools are available now. And this is the sophistication of this market. I think a lot of Bitcoiners are just not paying attention to any of this. This is the development that's going on. It's crazy.

八、会场观察：西装们来了，Bitcoiner 走了

We're here in this conference, and just around the corner is the Bitcoin for Corporations, literally in the same conference hall. Everyone's hanging out in this main one, but the real money is around the other corner.

By the way, I'm extremely bullish now on Bitcoin conferences. Since 2021 I haven't been. 2026, I'm extremely bullish.

主持人： Reason?

British HODL： Because the Bitcoiners are out of here. The suits are here. The money's here. This is what I said in 2021 — I said, look, this market needs to mature. The maturation is why I'm here. The real money's here. If you are someone with real money and real investments, you need to start coming to these conferences now. 2021 till now — it's been a waste of time.

Now, man, being here, shaking hands, asking the right questions — yeah. If you're rolling around here talking to the LARPers, that's different. But if you're around here talking to where the real money's going, understanding the cash flows, where the capital's moving — the alpha's here.

主持人： What else can you tell us about what the really rich people are talking about?

British HODL： Zero conversation on self-custody. Zero. They want to know: how do I buy Bitcoin in the best way possible? What percentage exposure do I need? Which banks are involved? What are the institutional rails coming into Bitcoin? How does lending work? These are the serious conversations that are going on.

九、BlackRock 的 1–2% 建议 与 机构级 HODL 率

主持人： Larry Fink, BlackRock came out with a report that says 1 to 2%. Do you believe that?

British HODL： Do I think it should be more? Yes. Because I understand what Bitcoin is. But if you're talking about a diversified portfolio that doesn't know anything about Bitcoin — and by the way, $14 trillion of AUM — I don't mind 1 or 2% flooding into Bitcoin, especially with the price reflexivity that we're going to have.

This is the crazy part. They're saying 1 or 2% after we've spent 2 years rotating 2 million coins from the Bitcoiners to institutional hands. These guys don't let go. These guys hold. They HODL. They actually HODL. And you know why they HODL? They HODL because they're allocating 2%, 3%, 4%, whatever. So if that asset drops — by the way, I got this stat from BlackRock, insane — they brought in $50 billion into IBIT, the asset went down 50%, they had like 2 or 3% net redemptions. They have never seen anything like that. That's the HODL rate of a Bitcoin ETF HODLer.

When I was saying this three years ago, people used to attack me. I used to say, "These institutions are better HODLers than the Bitcoiners." And it's now proven. They're not selling this because they've already got the kids educated. They've already got the three or four homes. They've already taken the holidays. This is an exposure play for them and they're only allocating 2 to 5 to 10%, whatever it is. So when it drops 50%, they don't care.

So they HODL and they understand the long-term game that's being played here. That's what serious capital cares about.

十、Bitcoin Treasury 公司：MSTR / Strive vs. 「带业务的假 DAT」

主持人： Talking about long-term game, what is your thought on Bitcoin Treasury companies right now?

British HODL： I think there's a few really good ones and I think there's a lot of really bad ones.

I'm personally not interested in companies that have — you know, there's been a lot during a bear market — always a conversation of "I want a Bitcoin treasury company that has a real business attached to it with cash." I'm not interested in any of that. That's the wrong way of looking at the purpose of that business.

If you want a cash-flow business and you want a value business, go buy McDonald's. Go buy some of these value businesses.

I want pure undiluted returns. I want pure alpha. And that's MSTR to me in the US. That's what Strive is trying to do right now, and they're doing an amazing job at it. So I'm not interested in companies that have got the drag of a real business behind them.

I bought MSTR — as I told you — like the very first trading day after they announced a Bitcoin strategy in 2020. What I want is a company like MSTR that goes up $2 if Bitcoin goes up $1. And also — this is where most people can't handle it — I want it to go down $2 if Bitcoin goes down a dollar, because that's how you get that volatility. And I want volatility.

If MSTR ever matches the volatility of Bitcoin from a risk-adjusted basis, I want to hold the Bitcoin. I want it to be more.

The problem when you add in these businesses that have got the drag of a real business is that it might look good on the downside — because they got the cash flows buffering that — but on the upside I now got to value what the risk of that real business is as I'm investing in the DAT. I don't want that. I don't want the hassle. I want the pure-play speculative platform on Bitcoin, and that to me so far seems to be MSTR and Strive.

主持人： What do you think about all these people attacking Sailor when the market is down?

British HODL： They're idiots. These people don't understand. Firstly, I've seen Michael Saylor go through the last cycle, which was his first cycle. If you think Michael Saylor is sitting here stressed at this point — with tens of billions of dollars of assets, tens of billions of dollars of runway and liquidity, creating a product that has never been created before…

By the way, Stretch (STRC) has the most liquidity for a preferred in the entire American markets. These are phenomenal products. All they're pissed off about is the price.

For all of those people, "number go up" — which is what they LARP and say they don't care about — "number go up" is going to fix everything for them, because as that goes up, the flywheel kicks in. As soon as STRC goes above 100, they start printing Bitcoin.

So yeah, they've got to raise some cash — because guess what? Turns out that institutions don't like a 50-vol asset trying to pay me dividends. They wanted cash. MSTR learned that. They pivoted. Fundstrat / Lee said that as well. They pivoted. But these are all learning things, because it's the first time this has ever happened. So everyone's learning now. And that's okay — we got to ride through it. That's the benefit of the returns you get, because if you want the explosive returns, you got to deal with the downside. If you don't want that, go buy a real cash-flow business with a fake Bitcoin treasury.

十一、目标价 $340,000：均值回归的暴力

主持人： You're not stressed at all during the down market?

British HODL： I'm excited. You know what we've had? We've had the longest period of an M2 break and an M2 lack of correlation, and we're about to mean-revert. That's my thinking. We're about to mean-revert back to correlation.

And now — this is so — we've broken this correlation in the middle of the institutions taking 2 million coins. So what's going to happen to the multiplier this time round in a bull market, when all these retail have given up their Bitcoin? They're not price [sensitive]. It's in the hands of price-insensitive people.

So what happens now? We're about to violently mean-revert here. At least that's my thinking. Maybe I'll be wrong, but everything tells me we're about to see something.

And my price target, by the way, has always stayed consistent even through this whole thing: $340,000, plus or minus 15%, somewhere between the last halving and the next halving. And I think that's going to come Q4 this year to Q2 next year.

主持人： What has to happen for you to say that prediction is wrong?

British HODL： We don't make a new all-time high by the next halving; liquidity tops out; PMI tops out; all of these things happen and Bitcoin just sits at somewhere between here and $100K or $126K — if it doesn't make any [new high], I'll be completely wrong.

And by the way, if I am completely wrong, then I might need to re-evaluate the extent to which Bitcoin plays a part in my portfolio. Nobody wants to sit through a 50% drawdown for an 11% CAGR. Bitcoin has to perform.

So I'm very transparent about that — but I think it will perform. I don't think we've had a speculative cycle. I think we've seen a concentrated trade into AI, and the broad market didn't start going up until really right now. 45% of the S&P 500 and the NASDAQ are all AI trades. Korea found that out. What happens when that starts to unwind?

So yeah, I believe the trade's going to broaden out now. The market's going to do really well, until the PMI number tops out and then the liquidity starts turning.

十二、结尾：一场 IQ 测试

主持人： I think my last question is for somebody that — while they're still holding cash, they're waiting for Bitcoin to crash even lower. What should I do now?

British HODL： Keep waiting. I don't care anymore. Okay.

主持人： So, no, just —

British HODL： It's an IQ test, and you failed.

主持人： It's okay. Wow. Refreshing. That's a great ending. Thank you.

British HODL： Pleasure.

item.description:
## 一、最反直觉的观察：Bitcoin 的原教旨主义者正在成为 Bitcoin 最大的威胁向量
整段访谈里最刺耳的一句话不是价格预测，而是这句：**"the community and it turns out that that's a real threat vector and nobody was evaluating it"**（社区本身就是威胁向量，而没人在评估它）。
这里有一个惊人的悖论：**BlackRock ETF 持有者的 HODL 率，远远高于那些天天喊 "not your keys not your coins" 的自托管信徒**。$500 亿流入 IBIT，资产跌 50%，净赎回仅 2–3%——这个数字连 BlackRock 自己都没见过。冷钱包信徒被"验证不信任"的口号骗光了终身积蓄，而那些"腐败的华尔街西装"却在真正意义上"HODL"。
这是一种**制度理性对情感忠诚的胜利**。原教旨的 Bitcoiner 拥有"信仰"，但机构拥有"配置纪律"——后者不需要爱一个资产才能长期持有它。
## 二、跨领域连接：这和早期基督教、日本三代目、Amway

item.title: [Business of Sport] Manchester United Accounts Reviewed
item.dc:creator: Business of Sport
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个反直觉的核心悖论：品牌是「衰败的赞助人」

大多数人看到"677M英镑创纪录营收 vs. 43M英镑运营亏损"，会本能地叹息"要是能在球场上争气该多好"。但这里藏着一个残酷的反转——曼联的品牌力，恰恰是这场慢性财务失血能够持续20年的原因。

如果这是一家汽车工厂，Glazer结构早在第五年就会崩塌，被债权人重组、被市场淘汰、被工会掀翻。可品牌像一层"生物膜"，把一个已经失去造血功能的核心包裹起来，让它体面地衰老。换言之，品牌不是解药，而是麻醉剂——它推迟了必要的休克疗法。这也解释了为什么Toys R Us（同样是KKR杠杆收购模式）能被杀死，而曼联不能：Toys R Us没有部落信仰。球迷的情感忠诚在会计报表上不体现，但它就是那颗让Glazer敢于反复加杠杆的"甜蜜果实"。

跨领域连接：这是私募股权的"僵尸模型"，被误植入了不会分红的生态位

私募基金的LBO（杠杆收购）逻辑成立的前提是——被收购公司有稳定的现金利润流，用来还贷。这是KKR、黑石、TPG的教科书打法：买下一家现金牛，装满债务，用它自己的利润养债，最后卖掉赚溢价。

但足球俱乐部这个"物种"从生物学上就不适合LBO：它的商业目的不是创造利润，而是把利润再投资到球员和薪资，去维持竞技表现，进而维持品牌。这形成一个悖论——凡是产生利润的足球俱乐部，往往是竞技上不思进取的俱乐部（比如某些法甲、意甲中游）。当Glazer把一个"利润再投资生态位"的公司硬塞进"利润偿债"的模型里，它必然演化出下面这个畸形结构：

新体育场必须由独立SPV融资。这一步很少被解读，但它其实是基础设施领域"特许经营权抵押"的翻版——像收费公路、高铁、机场私有化那样，把未来现金流碎片化、抵押给外部资本。表面上是"缓解母公司债务"，实质是把俱乐部的未来收益永久性殖民。当Arsenal、Tottenham把体育场当作"收益杠杆"时，曼联的新体育场从设计之初就注定是"收益漏斗"——大部分增量流向陌生股东。

最反直觉的一点：Ratcliffe目前"缓慢、克制、不像曼联"的操作，恰恰是唯一正确解

球迷的愤怒直觉是"我们是全球营收第一的俱乐部，为什么不像利物浦、皇马那样疯狂签人？"——但从财务力学看，任何激进操作都会瞬间放大77M的利息支出，把体系推向真正的悬崖。Ratcliffe面对的不是"如何让曼联再次伟大"，而是"如何让曼联不被自己的品牌重量压垮"。

这里出现一个跨领域连接，来自化工背景的Ratcliffe（INEOS的老本行）——化工过程优化的核心思维是"稳态先于产能"：一个反应器如果压力和温度没有先稳住，加大投料只会让它爆炸。他现在做的"清理结构、稳定运营、慢速换血"，恰恰是化工工程师的本能反应。但足球世界的"反应时间常数"由合同周期和文化更替决定，不是他熟悉的分子扩散速率。他真正低估的，不是债务profile，而是"人"的转化率——球员、教练、招募网络的更换，无法像蒸馏塔加装填料一样立竿见影。

一个更冷的观察：Glazer此刻应该卖，但他们大概率不会——因为持有一个"每年亏钱但估值飙升"的资产，是全世界最好的私人对冲头寸。真正推动他们出售的不会是财务压力，而是遗产焦虑：当第二代Glazer继承者开始考虑自己的传记怎么写时，出售才会发生。而这可能还要等5-10年。

📝 转录文本

破题：账目刚刚发布

Should we take a look at a story that's literally broken half an hour before we came on air, which is well worth us discussing based on conversations we had a few months ago on Manchester United and their financial position — because their accounts have just been released for the 25/26 season. There's some interesting numbers to pull from there. Record revenues, Charlie — 677 million despite not being in football.

Yeah, good achievement.

品牌韧性 vs. 运营亏损

We've spoken before about Manchester United and the power of the brand, and their ability to perform as a business regardless of how they're doing on the pitch. And that of course has enabled them over the last — what, now I'm trying about 14, 13, 14 years since Fergie's left — to maintain a certain level of operation, should we say, at least of the spending capacity.

But most importantly, the overall loss increased 10 million from last year to £43 million. That's the operating loss. They've then increased their debt for a refinancing operation from 471 million to 577 million. So that's an increase of 100 million of debt, right?

利息滚雪球：单年70M，累计超10亿

And the problem with that is, it's ramping up the amount of interest they're having to pay. So they were paying in this year — and bear in mind that this number is going to be higher because the next number will reflect the increase in the refinancing, which this one will not do — 77 million pounds in interest payments.

Right. So you've got your 43 million pound operating loss, but then you have to chuck on top of that the 77 million…

  1. Yeah. Sorry, 70. Is it 70?
  2. Yeah.

70 million interest payments. So you're talking about, you know, 115-odd million combined operating loss and interest payments on the debt. And that's just a hell of a lot, right? That's just a hell of a lot for a business turning over 650 million quid.

Well, it takes their total payments on interest since the Glazers took over to over a billion. That's over a billion.

那10亿本可以变成一座球场

I mean, you can totally understand why Man United supporters are so furious about that original deal, right? Because that 1 billion is pretty much the money required to pay the equity on a massive new stadium.

Yeah.

Right. So in other words, United in theory should during this time have been able to build themselves a massive new stadium with very little debt off the back end of it, right? And they should be heading into the situation which Arsenal and Spurs and co are in — of having a stadium situation fully developed and settled, and all this type of stuff.

Well, the Spurs stadium cost less than that total interest payment. Yeah. Which is quite incredible. Sorry, sorry, sorry. You mean cost less than than the total what? Interest paid. Oh, the total interest paid over the entire Glazer… So, exactly. That money could have been put towards building a piece of infrastructure that would not just improve but secure the base finances of that club for many many years, plus the opportunities that it provides alongside it.

新球场的困境：只能靠SPV，未来收益必被稀释

The flip side is that they can't take any more debt to build the stadium — because to do that would increase that interest payment to numbers that would be completely unfeasible for a functioning business, even if you're valued at 5 billion.

And so what they're having to do — they're having to create a separate entity. They're having to raise separate capital into it, which will mean that the opportunities to make money from that stadium in future will all be distributed amongst multiple shareholders and stakeholders rather than all going back into the club. So all of this impacts the earning capabilities of the club, which as we know in football really, what does that mean? It impacts the spending capabilities of this football club.

俱乐部的"紧口袋"：一年注入180M

And as you said, if you're a fan looking at this, it just continues to be something that's frustrating. Now the message that came out of the club when these accounts were released wasn't one of "we've had a record year" — it was very much "well, we forecast 740, 750 next year because we're in Europe, we will still be operating on a tight leash."

Well, I'm not surprised that they're operating on a tight leash. Because if you combine the operating loss and the interest payments, that's 115 million. But then they've also spent 65 million acquiring land for their new stadium. Right? So the total amount you're talking about — you're talking about 180 million that the owners have had to put in to finance the operating loss, the interest payments, and the acquisition of land for the new stadium.

So vast amounts of money are having to be tipped into this club, right? And something has to give. And the thing that has to give is that they're not able to be as free spending in the transfer and wages market as their supporters would like. And when you see other clubs going out and spending vast amounts of money on players, and you know that on a revenue perspective you're the biggest club and you're not able to do that — that is obviously very frustrating for United fans.

无解的原罪：只有全盘换手，才能把债务换成股权

And it all is wound into and goes back to the original deal, as everyone knows. But ultimately it is what it is. That deal happened and there's no way around it — until there is a total takeout of the entire club by an entity that can afford to effectively replace that debt with equity, effectively.

Yeah.

You know, I don't know what people think about how long that might take for the Glazers finally to decide "we're off." I've always thought that they wouldn't stick around to build a new stadium — that's a big long-term gamble with, as you say, having to bring in lots of external money and all this type of stuff. It sort of feels to me like now's the moment to take the rest of the money off the table. Current valuations for big Premier League clubs are high. They will do unbelievably well out of their investment as a whole.

Obviously they aren't in a position to enjoy being owners of Man United from a purely lifestyle perspective because of their reputation with the fan base. So from where I'm standing, this would be a great time for them to sell out, but I'm not sure we're particularly seeing any signs that that's happening.

与"正常企业"的关键分野：足球俱乐部没有利润可用来还债

Well, as you said — you know, I think you said to me before we came on air — if you have five, 600 million in debt and you're a six billion value company, it's not the end of the world if you're a normal business.

But the problem is with football clubs — they don't make profits. So if you think about a normal business that a private equity firm acquires in a leverage buyout situation, effectively the interest payments get paid out of the profits.

Mhm.

The problem we have here is there aren't any profits, right? So effectively the interest payments either have to be met by loading up more debt on the club — which is what's happened, get the debt going from 470 to 577, right — and/or the owners have to put more money in. So there aren't any good options. It's all bad options.

Ratcliffe 在想什么

What do you think Ratcliffe's thinking? Um, well, that's a great question. What do you think?

The first few years have, I think, been about him — should we say, cleaning it up and structuring it in a way that he thinks this club has been mismanaged and should be run. And I was looking at the start of the season — I was like, this could be the season where you really start to judge the impact that he has had, particularly on the business.

Right, it depends on the motivations that he had when he came in to own this. He was a fan of the club, right? He had wanted to get into English football for a long time. Reportedly he had flirted with Chelsea — to the extent he was the other investor before Clearlake / Boehly got in.

So I'm not completely convinced that he's purely looked at this as a great business investment where he's tried to make the return out of it on an eventual opportunity. I think there's an element of this which is: could he get in there, make some positive changes, and — as you said — be well positioned to get a little bit more of that club, assuming that the Glazers may want to get out in that near future, and the stadium be a major part of it.

Ratcliffe 真正低估的东西

I think the bit that would have bamboozled him is how quickly you can affect the turnaround of a football club that's been headed in the wrong direction for a very long time.

You know, we saw this when we took over Sunderland. To the uneducated looking in from the outside — or even people in it — it's sort of "well, surely it's straightforward: you appoint a technical director, you hire a good manager, and then you sign some good players, right?" And I'm pretty sure, given Jim Ratcliffe's supernatural self-confidence, that this is the bit that he underestimated.

Yeah.

He underestimated how difficult it was going to be to actually tear apart and reconstruct a fully functioning football club.

The likes behind the scenes had issues that far exceeded the obvious business ones.

Absolutely. Cultural issues, technical issues, profound technical issues. I mean, they were so far off the pace when it came to their use of analytics, to the way in which they were looking at their academy. They were miles off the pace, right? And had been for some time. It was like a club that had been molded in Edward Woodward's image — unbelievable, not even up to pace, leading the pace on the commercial side, and then just miles off the pace on the football side.

And I suspect that Jim Ratcliffe significantly underestimated how long that would take. And the result of that of course is that it is still your core business. Football is your core business — and when you play badly, your players become worthless. When you're not in Europe, you have to pay more to players to come there because they know they're not going to be playing in Europe. There are so many impacts that come from being bad at football.

动机拆解与走向

Motivation on the investment — you think was a bit of both?

The belief that he could be the guy to turn it around — legacy, enjoyment. I think we can also make a lot of money. All these things, right? And that's all perfectly legitimate, by the way. Fine.

But I suspect that, as I said, the underestimation was not in terms of "what's the debt profile" — I'm sure he knew very well what the debt profile was. It was more around how quickly we could turn the football side around, which in turn will start generating significant revenue, and then the whole thing will be able to sort of work from there.

Whereas at the moment, it's still a bit of a leaky ship.

一个可能不受欢迎的判断：方向其实是对的

I have to say — I know they've started the season poorly and there's a lot of heat around at the moment — I don't think that they have done a lot of bad things in the last year football-wise. I think Man United fans are going to hate on me for this, right?

I think they are actually headed in the right direction. It's just — of course it takes longer than you would like, and it's going to be multi-window because the profile of their playing squad and the liabilities that they have mean that it just takes a while for those things to work through the system. And some of those liabilities are self-inflicted under Ratcliffe. So it's not just the stuff that he's inherited, it's also stuff that has been put in place during that time.

But do I see the same frenetic, panicky, mad, sort of 30-years-out-of-date style of operating that I see at Spurs?

No.

No. I think mostly it looks reasonably judicious. A bit slower than people would like. But then, when you're paying 70 million a year in interest payments, I'm sorry — it is going to be slower than you would like.

Yeah. Well, when you look at the way they dealt with the transfer window this year, that stands up — because they didn't get to the stage where towards the end they were panicking. They didn't have the people in the door and so they spent loads of money. I mean, they did one deal probably later on in Biba, but I think it was the first time in however many years, I read, they didn't make a signing on deadline day. Whether you agree the players they bought in were the best players is a different discussion — but to your point, there wasn't the rashness that you would have associated with the previous Man United.

双重打击：结构性问题 × 更强的英超

Yeah — the double whammy, Charles, is that Spurs and United are having their own failings exposed at the same time as the Premier League, as we discussed earlier on, has become so strong in depth that you get punished.

Yeah.

Like, if you go back 10, 15 years, Premier League was still quite — you know, obviously more competitive than other leagues etc. — but generally speaking there were still some easier games in the league. I'm looking at it right now going: easy, easy games? If you're a bit off it, like — you are going to get done.

结语：一切都回到最初那笔交易

The problem with it is: the central underpinning tenet of this topic is the immovable fact of the original Glazer deal.

Yeah.

Right. And effectively everything after then is trying to ascertain whoever is running United right now and whoever is managing United right now: are they doing as well as could possibly be expected, given that they have inherited that terrible deal?

Yeah. And look, to anyone interested — we did a deep dive into it on a previous show. I'll put a link in the description and you can go back and have a look, because we talked kind of at length about how that actually came together — interest from the Glazers.

## 一个反直觉的核心悖论：品牌是「衰败的赞助人」
大多数人看到"677M英镑创纪录营收 vs. 43M英镑运营亏损"，会本能地叹息"要是能在球场上争气该多好"。但这里藏着一个残酷的反转——**曼联的品牌力，恰恰是这场慢性财务失血能够持续20年的原因**。
如果这是一家汽车工厂，Glazer结构早在第五年就会崩塌，被债权人重组、被市场淘汰、被工会掀翻。可品牌像一层"生物膜"，把一个已经失去造血功能的核心包裹起来，让它体面地衰老。换言之，品牌不是解药，而是**麻醉剂**——它推迟了必要的休克疗法。这也解释了为什么Toys R Us（同样是KKR杠杆收购模式）能被杀死，而曼联不能：Toys R Us没有部落信仰。球迷的情感忠诚在会计报表上不体现，但它就是那颗让Glazer敢于反复加杠杆的"甜蜜果实"。
## 跨领域连接：这是私募股权的"僵尸模型"，被误植入了不会分红的生态位
私募基金的LBO（杠杆收购）逻辑成立的前提是——**被收购公司有稳定的现金利润流，用来还贷**。这是KKR、黑石、TPG的教科书打法：买下一家现金牛，装满债务，用它自己的利润养债，最后卖掉赚溢价。
