item.title: [Alan Chen加州生活号] 美债收益率继续冲高，美股为何不跌？资金正在抱团AI、半导体和M7 ｜美股圆桌
item.dc:creator: Alan Chen加州生活号
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的观察：这轮上涨其实是一场"资产负债表种姓制度"的胜利

表面上大家在讨论"资金抱团AI、半导体、M7"，但视频里被主持人不经意点破的一个细节才是真正的题眼——Meta、Apple、Microsoft 之所以领涨，是因为它们"不需要借钱"；而 Amazon、Google 虽然也是 M7，却因为"愿意借钱"被隐性降级。

换句话说，当 10 年期美债收益率冲高到让房贷利率突破 7.3% 时，市场并不是在为"AI 叙事"定价，而是在为"现金流免疫力"定价。M7 已经内部分层：

  • 顶层种姓（无息贵族）：Meta、Apple、Microsoft —— 自由现金流足以自融资，利率上升对它们几乎是通缩式利好（因为竞争对手的资本成本被抬高了）。
  • 中层种姓（有息领主）：Amazon、Google —— 仍然发债扩张 AI 基建，利率敏感度上升。
  • 隐形贱民：所有需要外部融资的中小盘 AI 概念股 —— 这也是为什么"AI 涨"但 Russell 2000 死气沉沉。

这是一个跨领域连接：这种结构和 15 世纪威尼斯商人共和国的"贵族名册（Libro d'Oro）"惊人相似——只有被登记进名册的家族才能承接国家专利与低息融资，其他人只能眼睁睁看着财富集中。高利率时代的美股，正在完成一次静默的"金融贵族化"。

二、被忽视的信号：Oracle 数据中心"延期免罚"条款，可能是 AI 资本支出周期的第一道裂缝

嘉宾在最后几分钟一带而过的 Oracle 消息，其实值得单独立一集节目。Oracle 在新墨西哥数据中心的合同里加入了"延期交付免于处罚"条款，市场只把它当成一次普通利空处理掉了。但如果你把这条消息和另外三件事叠加起来看：

  1. 美债收益率冲高 → 数据中心融资成本骤增；
  2. Meta / Apple 现金流为王 → 客户方开始有议价权；
  3. Muse 这类 C 端 AI 应用30 天留存率断崖（视频里明确提到"30 天热度然后归零"）。

你会得到一个非常危险的推论：AI 基建的下游需求（企业 SaaS + C 端订阅）正在被过高估计，而 Oracle 那份合同实际上是在把"客户可能撤单"的风险，用法律语言重新分配给自己。这类似于 2006 年抵押贷款合同里悄悄加入的"提前还款重置条款"——当合同开始为"最坏情况"预留出口时，往往说明卖方比买方更早闻到了味道。

三、跨领域连接：Muse 的"三日热度"暴露的不是产品问题，而是"注意力凯恩斯主义"的终局

视频里主持人对 Muse 的评价非常克制但致命——"3 天、7 天、30 天留存率会归零"。这句话如果放在产品经理语境里，只是一个 UX 问题；但如果放到宏观经济学里看，它揭示了一个更大的结构性真相：

AI 应用正在进入"注意力凯恩斯主义"的流动性陷阱。

凯恩斯当年描述的流动性陷阱是：利率再低，人们也不投资。而今天的 AI 应用面对的是：功能再强，用户也不复用。原因不是产品不好，而是——用户的"心智货币供给"是有限的，当 ChatGPT、Claude、Gemini、Grok、Muse、Perplexity 同时印发"注意力债券"时，边际用户的心智已经通胀到无法为任何单一产品建立忠诚。

这里有个反常识的推论：真正能穿越这轮 AI 泡沫的，不是模型最强的公司，而是那些能"锁住上下文"（context lock-in）的公司——也就是拥有你的邮件、日历、代码库、家庭 IoT 的公司。Apple 和 Microsoft 之所以在这波成为无息贵族，本质原因不是现金流，而是它们控制着用户"最难迁移的那部分上下文"。Meta 想靠 Muse 追上，但社交图谱是"弱上下文"，一次算法调整就能失效——这才是 Meta 需要不断激进投入的深层焦虑。

给你的一个操作层洞见：下次盯 M7 时，别再看"AI 叙事强度"，改看两个更冷门的指标——(1) 自由现金流/资本支出比率的变化率；(2) 用户上下文迁移成本。这两个数字会比任何 K 线都提前告诉你，谁在下一轮加息或降息中会真正胜出。

降息预期与中期选举时点

I don't want to guess. Last time, I thought it wouldn't be a holiday, but it was. This time, it's a holiday. Because there's no solid basis for this. But this year, according to the index, it's expected to be a holiday twice. But I didn't notice it the day before. Oracle 数据中心异常条款：值得深挖

But speaking of debt, I noticed that Oracle has a message in advance. It said that he is in a data center in New Mexico. He wants — If it can't be handed over on time or if there's no problem, it can't be handed over, then it can't be punished and can be pushed back.

On that day, Oracle fell. I think this thing still needs to be dug deeper. It's like, ah, it's falling, the gold is very low, it's falling, it's going to buy the gold back. Because we have to understand why this thing is like this. But I haven't spent time doing this research yet. But I don't think this thing is that simple. Because it's connected to —

That's right. It's worth our research and sharing with our members.

结束语

That's all for today. If you like our content, please let us know in the comments section. If you have any questions or concerns, please let us know. We will try to update you next week or next video.

Thank you, everyone. Have a good weekend and a happy weekend. Have a good weekend and a happy weekend. Bye bye. Bye bye. Thank you, everyone.

## 一、最反直觉的观察：这轮上涨其实是一场"资产负债表种姓制度"的胜利
表面上大家在讨论"资金抱团AI、半导体、M7"，但视频里被主持人不经意点破的一个细节才是真正的题眼——**Meta、Apple、Microsoft 之所以领涨，是因为它们"不需要借钱"；而 Amazon、Google 虽然也是 M7，却因为"愿意借钱"被隐性降级**。
换句话说，当 10 年期美债收益率冲高到让房贷利率突破 7.3% 时，市场并不是在为"AI 叙事"定价，而是在为**"现金流免疫力"**定价。M7 已经内部分层：
- **顶层种姓（无息贵族）**：Meta、Apple、Microsoft —— 自由现金流足以自融资，利率上升对它们几乎是通缩式利好（因为竞争对手的资本成本被抬高了）。 - **中层种姓（有息领主）**：Amazon、Google —— 仍然发债扩张 AI 基建，利率敏感度上升。 - **隐形贱民**：所有需要外部融资的中小盘 AI 概念股 —— 这也是为什么"AI 涨"但 Russell 2000 死气沉沉。
**这是一个跨领域连接**：这种结构和 15 世纪威尼斯商人共和国

item.title: [All-In Podcast] Anthropic IPO at Risk, Meta’s Muse Pop, Token Prices Fall, Open Source Gains Share, Alignment Fails
item.dc:creator: All-In Podcast
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

三个反直觉的系统性观察

观察一：Anthropic 正在患一种"公司层面的解离性身份障碍"——但这不是意外，而是估值结构决定的必然

大多数评论者把 Anthropic 的"精神分裂"（一边发布 Claude 5.5 推进前沿，一边写《为前沿踩刹车》；一边警告生物风险即将灭绝人类，一边在旧金山开湿实验室）解读为管理层的伪善或糊涂。但更深的系统性真相是：这是"实验室"与"公司"两种叙事在同一个法人实体中同时被货币化的直接后果。

"实验室"叙事融的是恐惧溢价——世界越危险，前沿玩家的护城河越深、监管俘获越可行、超级投票权越合理。"公司"叙事融的是增长溢价——收入曲线越陡、企业客户越集中、IPO 估值越高。当同一位 CEO 必须同时向两类完全对立的资本市场"报价"时，他不是在撒谎，而是在做双币种套利。分裂不是 bug，是精心设计的价格发现机制。

这也解释了一个看似怪异的时机学：为什么"末日论"总在竞品发布前后集中爆发？因为末日论是竞争性护城河的期权——不用行权，只需持有。

观察二：Vercel 那张 12 周从 80/20 闭源翻转到 80/20 开源的图表，本质上是"李嘉图比较优势"在 token 经济里的第一次显现

播客里所有人都把这张图当作"开源冲击闭源"的故事来讲，但真正的系统性洞见在别处：这是一次经济学意义上的"要素分工"觉醒。

当 Chamath 说"你必须给模型套上 harness 才能让它工作"时，他实际上描述了 token 经济的三层生产函数：原始智能（模型）× 具身化（harness）× 场景适配（垂直任务）。过去 18 个月，闭源公司试图在三层都收租，这就像英国工业革命时想同时垄断棉花、纺纱和成衣。而 12 周的翻转说明市场刚刚意识到：原始智能已经变成大宗商品，护城河永远在最靠近用户痛点的那一层。

跨领域连接：这和 1990 年代 Intel Inside 战略在今天完全反着走。Intel 当年成功地把 CPU 从"零部件"重新定价为"品牌"；而 Anthropic/OpenAI 现在正被市场从"品牌"重新定价为"零部件"。同样是 x86 时代的教训，向下兼容反了方向。

观察三：一个真正让人意外的联系——反 AI 联盟的深层驱动，不是恐惧，而是"慈善基金会（DAF）经济学"

Chamath 顺口提到但没展开的一句话可能是全场最锋利的洞察：Anthropic 要求员工把股票预捐进 DAF（捐赠者建议基金）。这背后是一个几乎没人在公开讨论的系统性事实：美国左翼精英已经把慈善基金会体系变成了政治权力的延时通道。

如果你把 Anthropic/OpenAI 的员工财富流做长期建模：未来 5-10 年，仅这两家公司大概率会产生 1-2 万亿美元的员工净资产，其中相当比例会流入 DAF 结构。而 DAF 的独特之处在于：捐赠人在缴纳时立即获得税收减免，但资金派发不受时间限制——这意味着这些钱在派发前，实质上是一个巨大的政治军火库。

跨领域连接：这和 19 世纪末洛克菲勒基金会、卡内基基金会的形成路径几乎完全同构。当年的"强盗资本家"用基金会洗白垄断资本，塑造了整个 20 世纪美国的教育、公共卫生和外交政策议程（例如"绿色革命"、公共图书馆运动）。今天的 AI 前沿实验室不是在建模型，而是在建下一个洛克菲勒基金会。

真正令人啊哈的一点在于："AI 灭世论"的政治功能，不是阻止 AI，而是延迟 AI 财富的社会扩散，让财富尽可能集中到少数几家"合规"公司里，从而尽可能多地流入 DAF 通道。 从这个角度看，Bernie Sanders 的禁令法案和 Anthropic 的自我警告不是对立，而是共谋——两者都在为同一个财富虹吸结构提供合法性外壳。

一个更深的系统性预测

如果上述三条同时成立，那么下一个 12 个月最值得押注的非共识预测是：

Meta 的 Muse 会成为一个"意识形态破坏者"，其影响远超商业本身。 因为 Zuckerberg 是唯一一个既有 AI 前沿能力、又主动选择"开源+消费者普惠"路径的玩家。当十亿普通人开始每天使用免费的、有实际用处的 AI 助手时，"AI 会消灭我们"的叙事会像"电视会让孩子变傻"一样迅速崩塌——不是被反驳，而是被日常使用消解。到那一天，Anthropic 精心构建的恐惧溢价会一夜之间归零，而这才是真正的 IPO 风险因素——不写在 S-1 里的那种。

📝 转录文本

开场：All-In 峰会回顾

All right everybody, welcome back to episode 290 of the number one podcast in the world. It's the all-in podcast. With me again, it's the core 4. David Freedberg is here. Chimoth Poly Hapatia and David Saxs calling in. I am your host, Jason Calakanis, and we have a full docket today.

I'd be remiss though if I didn't ask everybody for their fondest memories of the fifth annual All-In Summit produced by Mr. David Friedberg.

David, do you have any thoughts? How do you rate your performance as executive producer of the All-In Summit?

You know what we didn't do? What we forgot to do at the end of day two? We didn't give a big shout out to our production team, to Kimber, to Lisa, to Nick. I think we— No, Jason. Okay. I thought we should have brought him out, but I just want to give a big shout out.

Bring him out for the standing—

The team backstage absolutely crushed it as always this year. And then I had a great time. Actually, you know, my favorite part is going to Universal Studios. You just get to have a good time. It's great. Just great.

I am reliving my childhood. Shabbath with no trauma.

By the way, shout out to our friends at Dongi. I got one of those coffee machines that we had at the event. I put it in my kitchen.

You know what I got? I don't know if you guys saw, but there was a water machine in the VIP area.

Well,

that is a zero plastic water machine. It goes through super filtration.

No microplastics in the water. I have one now in our office. Thank you very much to them. I appreciate it.

Amazing company.

川普致电与 Jensen 演讲

Sax, do you have a favorite moment from the show?

Well, I think the highlight of the show, the thing that we'll remember for a long time was the president calling in during Jensen's talk. And I think Jensen's overall the content and demeanor really helped calm down this national panic over AI. It felt like we were the center of this national conversation. And I think it happened very organically.

You remember there's basically been this SCOP for the last few weeks leading into the summit to convince everyone that humanity was going to go extinct unless we did exactly what the Democrats want and stop all AI development. And then you know we had first Satcha came out and kind of calmed everyone down and then JSON did the same thing and the president called in and did what he did best which is sees total control of the narrative that I'm sure these doomer groups have been carefully planning for weeks and kind of thwarted that whole operation.

Nerds enough. Get back to work. You have a super intelligent Trump — intelligence is now the term. We're going to call it Trump intelligence going forward. But I think you make a good point.

A lot of people wanted to know, Freeberg, if this was planned. Was the President Trump calling planned, Freeberg? Take us behind the scenes.

Basically, Jensen was connecting with him right backstage and said, "Hey, call me back." And then he called him while he was on stage. There was some texting going on.

Yeah, it was completely spontaneous.

It was spontaneous. Yes. It was not like a planned thing where Jensen was like, "Hey, let's do a whole thing." And so that was pretty amazing to have this conversation that Jensen was waiting for from the president to happen live and clearly this was the topic desour in DC as well as in the news and the media and it was amazing to see it all happen on stage with us.

And yeah, just to be clear, I thought it was a bit and I was like well put him on speakerphone, and Jensen says to me "how do you do that" and I just handed him — I always keep an extra mic there in case somebody's mic goes out — just put them on speaker phone put the microphone and President Trump, the funniest president in history, funniest politician history.

Did you notice, Sachs, that he drops a oneliner through a speaker phone perfectly?

Perfectly. Jensen makes the greatest chips. Everybody tries to reverse engineer them. Impossible. Impossible. But he can't figure out how to press the speakerphone button. Okay.

I was just like, how does he do it? How does he do it? It just drops the perfect line.

"实验室" vs "公司"：成年人回归房间

But Shimoth, in all seriousness, the nerds were losing their mind last week and the adults came, daddy came, Elon came, Jensen came, all the adults in the room came and they just said, "Listen, if you have software that's defective and not ready to put in the world, maybe don't put it in the world and make it a little bit, you know, as you like to say, less brittle." So your thoughts on where we are in this national discussion which went from slow down to maybe just release non-brittle resilient software.

Well, I think that there was this classification that happened last week between up-and-coming organizations that want to call themselves labs, but are in fact companies that have P&Ls and shareholders and have to abide by the same rules that everybody else does. And then the sophisticated companies that have lived in scrutiny for many decades and have learned the hard way the process of making things robust and the cost of making things not robust.

So what do I mean? On the one side you saw — in many ways it's like curious times creates curious bedfellows right — you have the cohort is Satya, Jensen, Sachs, Zach, Elon, the president, Lena Khan. We have product liability language.

Strange fellows indeed.

We have this product liability perspective in the United States. It's meant to prevent companies from doing things that they're not supposed to do, especially if they know that those things could be harmful. And on the other side, it's folks making the thing that were being, I think, a little naive and basically saying, "We're not a company. We're a lab. Protect us."

And I think the mature response is, "You should have internal controls and you should robustly test things." And what Zuck said earlier and what Elon has said in the past is we're just under a lot of scrutiny. And so when things aren't perfect, we just slow things down.

Elon has done that with FSD. You said this, Jason. He could have been at FSD 3 or 4 years ago, but he has publicly stated, "We can't afford it because every accident that Tesla incurs is magnified a 1000x than what any other company would incur, and so we just have to go slower."

Zach last week said, "We were about to roll out Muse, which looks like one of the most successful product launches in recent memory, has huge implications actually, which we should talk about, and he had to slow roll it." He and Alexander who I was talking to last night had to slow roll it for a couple of months to get it perfect.

So it's all within your control. It's just what do you choose to do? And I think that was the most interesting observation. We have to stop calling these companies labs. They're companies and we have to be judged on the same standards including product liability.

个体责任 vs 全球治理

Yeah. And there was a lot of coverage of this moment, Sachs. Interestingly, some of the fake news media were like on a popular podcast and then they play the clip, but they're just afraid to say the name of the podcast. Pretty hilarious.

I think Jimoth is getting us into the first topic here already, which is whether we're going to have individual responsibility as our northstar or some sort of collective action. And the thing that always works the best is individual responsibility. Whether it's at the level of individuals or companies, the relevant decision to make in every case is should we ship this product? Not can we get the whole world to agree.

And the problem with talking about these collectivized approaches is that they defray accountability away from the actual decision maker. And I think people sort of feel this. You know, like this week you had Daario and Sam go to the United Nations and say we need some sort of global AI governance. And it kind of reminds me of like the billionaires who fly to Davos in their private jets and then rail against climate change. You know, there's something fundamentally sort of unrealistic and kind of out of touch about it.

Hypocritical.

Hypocritical. And it's like, guys, look, what we need is for you guys to make smart decisions about what to release. If a product is unsafe, which is to say it's unreliable or behaves unpredictably, then don't release it. And stop looking to some sort of global governance as the answer. Because if you guys don't get this decision right, it's not going to matter what the United Nations does. And by the time the United Nations agrees on anything, we're going to be much further along in this whole journey.

So, there's something just very weird about the way that the principal actors in this keep talking because it really feels like they're trying to push off the responsibility.

阴谋论：Section 230 for AI？

Well, there's a theory going around here and I think it is worth us discussing here that the Frontier Labs are covertly—

Companies. They're companies.

They're companies. Yes. Let me just finish the—

No, no, no, but you made a really good point that I want to make sure we just don't miss. Okay. They are corporations.

Yes. Yes. And when you call them labs, they sound like nonprofit entities, and it's not true.

Okay.

So, the corporations making these products are looking for President Trump to specifically give them what the internet companies had with section 230, which is shield them from liability. And that there is a consideration inside the Trump administration, the 47th administration, that maybe there could be some leverage put on these companies that they would give 10% of their equity to the sovereign wealth front of the United States, etc., and then that would result in them being given some pass when it comes to their liability.

That's an insane thing to do. It's like giving some plane company that gives 10% of their equity to the US government the ability to not be responsible for their planes falling out of the sky.

But what is your thought on that conspiracy theory? I'm sure you've heard it, Sachs, that they're looking for—

You're making it sound like this is the idea of the Trump administration. That's not true.

No, not the Trump administration. This is what the Frontier Lab/Corporations are pitching to them and that there might be — the rumor is there might be some people who are open to that in the administration. Again, this is all a back channel.

Here's what we know is that in the past week, you had virtually every Trump administration official come out and say some version of what I just said, which is first and foremost, the AI companies have to take responsibility for their own products and that we will not wave product liability. I think Speaker Johnson said it, the congressional said it, Besson said it in the most recent interview.

Everybody said if your game is to get a waiver of product liability or antitrust liability, if you're trying to form a cartel, if you're trying to collude, forget about it. We're not going to do it. So, I think they completely threw cold water on that whole idea.

And remember what President Trump said is he just tweeted today, we have the DOJ. That's a guardrail. The administration is a guardrail. The administrative state, civil lawsuits, criminal lawsuits, all these things are there as potential liability to make sure that you make the right risk-reward tradeoff. And again, at the end of the day, if those guys release an unsafe product, it's not going to matter what the United Nations agrees on. So, we need them to internalize the responsibility.

Are they — Listen, come on. Be candid with me. You got the inside goods here. Are they trying to lobby for that? Are they — do you think they are lobbying to get this protection? Yes or no? Come on.

Well, I have heard — this is not like first-person experience. They have not asked me like, "Hey, we want product liability waiver," but I have heard from people in Washington that they have been seeking something like that.

It's hard to pin down, right?

Yeah.

Freeberg 论 Frankenstein

Okay, fair enough. Freeberg, your thoughts here — as we are going to get into the first story here with the token maxing and the prices going down, but I'll give you the final word here on what America should do in terms of dealing with the corporations that are pretending to be labs who cannot take ownership of their own Frankenstein creations, which I think JD Vance, you know, I thought had a spectacular appearance. He was crisp and looked quite presidential, if I was going to describe it. You threw a lot of fast balls—

And he knocked him out of the park. By the way, fast — you know, home run hitters want fast balls. You can't hit a fast ball if it's out of the strike zone. So, I gave him the three hardest questions I could think of and he proceeded to knock all three over the fence.

I think there was JD's excellent. Listen,

I mean, on the Sunday shows, they played the clips of the questions I asked him. Bang, bang, bang.

Freeberg right over the fence. But, you know, he said basically, if you're creating Frankenstein, here's an idea. Stop. And then he added, if you've already kind of let the cat out of the bag, then create anti-Frankenstein. Basically, create the safeguards.

Yeah, it makes total sense. I think Suck gave a good interview on this.

They took their time doing this Muse release this week. They said they wanted to get it right. They wanted to make sure that it was safe, that it didn't give people capabilities to do bad things. That's the responsibility that they took as a corporation. Anyone that's outputting a model should take the same responsibility.

Pretty obvious.

This is an organization that understands it. Having paid a series of fines from Cambridge Analytica to recently—

We have a lot of laws that make it illegal to do a lot of things.

竞争 = 不安全？一个左翼批判的历史反驳

All right, let's move on here.

By the way, can I add one philosophical point to this? So I think that implicit in — let's call it the Daario position — that let's call it the regulated free market that we have, his fundamental contention is that that will lead to a race to the bottom, that competition jeopardizes safety.

It's in all of his blog posts and many other people reflect this idea that competition equals lack of safety and that is implicitly a critique of our economic system. It's basically a left-wing critique of our system and it goes back a long way.

I remember back in the days of the cold war when we really had this duel between two different systems. Do you want the free market system or do you want the communist system? A lot of people made the claim that the capitalist system would do things like jeopardize safety and beauty, that our buildings would always be uglier because the greedy capitalist wouldn't want to spend a dime on beautification or good architecture, things like that.

In fact, it turned out that the Soviet system was the one that produced the cold gray landscapes. Why? Because people want beauty. They want safety. And therefore, if you have a well-functioning market economy, then it gives people what they want. And obviously, the American system won out in that battle.

So, I just fundamentally disagree with the idea that competition means lack of safety. As Zuckerberg and Jensen were saying, there are huge incentives on both the upside and downside to be safe. On the upside, no customer wants a product that is unpredictable and unreliable, that doesn't do what they say. No enterprise wants an agent that's going to leak their data or hack a competitor. And on the downside, as the president made clear, they've got tons of liability, product liability, civil liability, administrative liability, criminal liability.

So, I just firmly disagree with this idea that competition is a bad thing. Competition is a good thing that can be harnessed to get the right result.

Wuhan 的幽灵与"实验室"一词

And just to build on that, Shimoth — our friend Nash from PaloAlto Networks, friend of the pod, he released in the past week or so unit 42. He's building — there's a business opportunity here to build a product to do continuous cyber defense — and also a friend of the pod George Kirch from Crowdstrike. He also released Falcon, his new product to do cyber defense. Chimath, if these guys in the Frontier Labs/Corporations were so concerned about cyber security, why didn't they ever release a cyber security product and PaloAlto Networks and Crowd Strike are on it?

That's probably more in the second topic that we'll talk about, which is as the models essentially cluster in terms of capability, there's no differentiation, and so they'll be forced to move up the stack. But let's wait on that for one second. You have a point here you want to make and then we'll go to the first.

I do. The point I wanted to make is more philosophical and sociological — which is the last time we heard the word "lab" in the social consciousness was during COVID and there was a lab that was responsible for a leak of a virus that then killed 15 million people all around the world and caused $45 trillion of damage. It's the Wuhan lab.

And I think it's important to recognize that there has been zero transparency or culpability around this. And I think part of why people are comfortable calling themselves a lab is because of that fact — that a lot of these young people that work at these places lived through this and saw absolutely no responsibility taken by the lab that caused this leak.

And now we're talking about leaks of different kinds. And we have organizations and corporations that try to fashion themselves as labs as well, but they're not labs. These are corporations. I just want to remind everybody, these are for-profit corporations that have absorbed hundreds of billions of dollars of debt and equity, that have thousands and thousands of shareholders, that have trillions of dollars of market cap. And if I were them, I would not want to call myself a lab at any cost. And I think if you saw the recent speeches that they gave at the United Nations, they're still using that terminology.

Yeah.

They are not labs. These are for-profit corporations that are subject to product liability risk and they should act accordingly.

Yeah. I mean, and we've had a conversation here for a year about this. Like if this stuff is so dangerous, you don't have to release it or you know my proposal like — know your customer, give logs.

Do not compare yourself to the Wuhan lab. It's — well, Shimoth, it's bad PR, but also I do think it's part of their like virtue signaling routine where they just don't want to say that we're companies. We have a for-profit incentive. They always want to say that we're either a research institution or they say things like we're a public benefit corporation, which no one really knows what the hell that means. So, it's this patina — virtue signaling that obscures what's really going on.

It tries to obscure the word corporation, but legally you're not allowed to hide it. I think they should have — uh when they—

We are all running corporations. All-In, all be it very small but mighty, is a corporation. I think we should call—

Is a All-In lab.

This is the All-In lab where we discuss different formulas.

No, we're experimenting with ideas. This is a meme workshop.

Lab. These ideas are getting so dangerous that we don't want any liability for our opinions. Welcome to the All-In lab podcast.

Here we— Topic zero, Freeberg.

Is there a mindset in scientists' minds that you know needs to kind of have a hard stop and then the corporation kind of takes over? Maybe they could put the labs on the side here and then say, "Hey, these are the adults doing the corporation stuff." What are your thoughts here if you were going to architect how anthropic operates in the world? And maybe you could speak to scientists' views of the world versus capitalists and management teams.

I don't have a good answer for you on that.

第一话题：模型价格坠落 + 开源海啸

Okay. Well, you're doing it. You're the answer. Look at—

Let me kick off the first topic. What I wanted to do was just take a step back and look at the insane flurry of model releases happening.

Yes.

过去 10 天的模型发布狂潮

I think the pace of model releases happening on both the open-source side and the premium side, the anthropics, Grok of the world, is unfathomable right now. The list is insane. And just in the last 10 days:

  • September 9th, DeepSeek 4.1 Flash gets released. 20¢ for a million tokens output if they're hosting it. Key Value Cache from V1 of DeepSeek — remember what a big deal DeepSeek was when it came out — the key value cache then was like 390,000 bytes. Now it's 890. Insane drop, insane efficiency improvements.
  • September 20th, Qwen, which is the Alibaba model, comes out version 2.1. It's an open weights model that outperforms Nano Banana 2, which is Google's big breakthrough, insane image generation model. This thing is free, open-source. You can put it on your desktop computer and run it at home to generate images for free. And it's made by Alibaba.
  • September 22nd, Xiaomi put out MIMO. Mimo Pro performs on par with Claude's Opus 5 — which is like this insane model that everyone thought was going to change the world and break the internet — and GPT-5/6 Sol across most benchmarks. It's a 309 billion parameter model. It is entirely open. You can download this model and put it on your server and run your own instance without paying anyone any money except for the cost of running the server.
  • September 17th, this model called Bonsai 2 came out by Prism ML. This is actually a fork of Qwen, which is another one of the Alibaba models. It's a 27 billion parameter model. 98% of the performance of the big Qwen model. It's 5.9 gigs in size and you can run it on a local computer. You can have an Nvidia chip or have a good Mac Studio computer and you can run this insane model on your desktop computer for free.
  • And then the big crazy models, the big closed source models: Anthropic releases Opus 5.5 on September 22nd. OpenAI Astro comes out with Sol and Luna on September 23rd. Grok 4.7 comes out on September 21. Meta Muse comes out on September 22nd.

Any one of these stories would have broken the internet a year ago and they all happened in the last 10 days.

Does it have a specific function?

And so protein discovery is the baseline of all antibody discovery, which is the majority of the therapeutics industry today — is discovering novel proteins that we can use as a therapeutic agent. So that's the sort of work that's going on. It's BSL-1, BSL-2, which means, you know, these are biosafety levels. The lab that they set up, they've publicly talked about the lab.

So, the lab itself is sort of like a low-level research lab where they can make simple proteins and test them in the lab to see if the AI is doing a good job discovering or postulating protein folding or these sorts of theories and to actually run really rapid testing and experimentation cycles to see if these proteins are what they're predicted to be.

Okay. So, they like — 4,000 agents against it and do a Hugging Face with proteins. Yeah.

No, I mean I think what they're really doing is just having experimental proof that what the software is predicting. Remember, go back to AlphaFold. AlphaFold was predicting protein structure, three-dimensional structure of a protein from the DNA sequence that codes for that protein. And so in order to prove that, you had to basically predict what the structure of a protein would be from a DNA sequence, make the protein, and then look at it and see if it actually looks like it's supposed to look like.

And so in the case of some of the other things that they're doing, they're trying to discover function. I want to find an enzyme, which is a type of a protein that degrades a certain molecule that can be used to degrade, for example, you know, a therapeutic target or something in the body that we want to get rid of. And so they'll start to kind of make these predictions in software, but then you need to test them in the lab to say, okay, does that target actually do what it does?

Now, there are literally hundreds of labs like this. These are low-level research labs that are not doing like gain of function research. They're not making viruses. They're not making pathogenic things that can escape. That's why they're BSL-1, BSL-2. They're benchtop labs where automation can help kind of reduce the cost and increase the throughput of the testing of what the software is making predictions around.

And ultimately the objective here I think is for them to get some proof that their software is actually doing what it's predicting and they have an incredible life sciences function. I think at this point I don't have as much insight on where Gemini is at with the new models with Google, but they have the best life sciences models at Anthropic and I think this is the fast track to basically seeing if these models can be used by therapeutic companies, by pharma companies, by government labs to help discover new therapeutics and so on.

I don't think that the world should be scared away from discovery, R&D, research and development into new therapeutic modalities as predicted by AI because we heard the word "wet lab" in Wuhan and everyone's like "okay any lab is bad." We still want to progress the frontier of therapeutics, of human health, of discovery, and this is a really important aspect of Anthropic proving that their models can add value here. I think that's the summary of it.

收尾：赞助商与告别

All right. Thank you so much to our friends at IN. They were the presenting sponsor for this year's All-In seminar — fifth IN's AI cloud lounge. It's packed for all three days. Did a great meet and greet with INE on Sunday and got to take some selfies and met many of you there. Thanks again to INER.

Niagen — did you catch Niogen in the wellness hub for IVs? Tons of great gifts and supplements being given away. Great experience, great product. Great job to our friends at Niogen for doing the lounge again. Nigen is the official NAD partner for the all-in pod. Yes, Niogen BioScience created the NAD category, now has 45 plus clinical studies.

And PayPal, my favorite way to settle up. They had a great lounge on site at the summit where everybody got to hang out and get those beautiful embossed luggage tags, and they hosted the payments and fintech dinner which was a huge hit.

Let me tell you folks, All-In Summit 2027 will sell out again and the applications are open now. Go to allin.com/events and apply for your chance to be in the room where it happens. What are you waiting for folks? Allin.com/events.

All right, there you have it folks. Episode 290, the all-in pod for David, Paulie Hakatia, and your Sultan of Science Freeberg. I am the world's greatest moderator. See you next time. Bye-bye.

Let your winners ride. Rainman David and it said we open sourced it to the fans and they've just gone crazy with it. Queen of Besties are gone. That is my dog taking a notice in your driveway. Oh man, my appetizer will meet me at— We should all just get a room and just have one big huge orgy cuz they're all just useless. It's like this like sexual tension that they just need to release somehow. Your feet.

We need to get merch going. All in. I'm going all in.

item.description:
# 三个反直觉的系统性观察
## 观察一：Anthropic 正在患一种"公司层面的解离性身份障碍"——但这不是意外，而是估值结构决定的必然
大多数评论者把 Anthropic 的"精神分裂"（一边发布 Claude 5.5 推进前沿，一边写《为前沿踩刹车》；一边警告生物风险即将灭绝人类，一边在旧金山开湿实验室）解读为管理层的伪善或糊涂。但更深的系统性真相是：**这是"实验室"与"公司"两种叙事在同一个法人实体中同时被货币化的直接后果**。
"实验室"叙事融的是恐惧溢价——世界越危险，前沿玩家的护城河越深、监管俘获越可行、超级投票权越合理。"公司"叙事融的是增长溢价——收入曲线越陡、企业客户越集中、IPO 估值越高。当同一位 CEO 必须同时向两类完全对立的资本市场"报价"时，他不是在撒谎，而是在做**双币种套利**。分裂不是 bug，是精心设计的价格发现机制。
这也解释了一个看似怪异的时机学：为什么"末日论"总在竞品发布前后集中爆发？因为末日论是竞争性护城河的**期权**——不用行权，只需持有。
## 观察二：Vercel 那张 12 周从 80/20 闭源翻转到 80/2

item.title: [Latent Space] The $10 Trillion Token Economy — Alex Atallah, OpenRouter & Anjney Midha, AMP
item.dc:creator: Latent Space
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽略的历史押韵：Token 经济正在重演支付基础设施的百年史

Anjney 在末尾抛出的类比其实是本集最锋利的洞见——但它比表面听起来更深刻。在线支付从 1980 年代到 2000 年代花了 20 年才从 0 长到 1 万亿美金 GMV，Token 经济只花了 3 年就到了同一起跑线，却被预期在 5 年内冲到 5 万亿、10 年到 10 万亿。

这意味着一件反直觉的事：Stripe 收购 OpenRouter 表面上是一次分发层收购，本质上是一次"新时代 Radar"的资产收购。Stripe 在支付领域真正的护城河从来不是支付通道（Adyen、Braintree 都能做），而是十年积累的欺诈图谱。Alex 说"我们上个月拦截的欺诈金额是上个月的 10 倍"——这个 10 倍不是运营指标，而是 Stripe 未来 Radar-for-Tokens 产品的原始训练数据。OpenRouter 是 Stripe 的下一代欺诈神经网络的数据入口。

二、"人类作为路由器"是一个未被命名的产品原型

节目中一处闪光但一带而过的观察：Anjney 讲到 Mixtral 发布时人们觉得它比 GPT-4"更聪明"，其实只是因为它更快，然后他说——"这是 humans as router 的开始，最后演化成 OpenRouter 的 auto router"。

这句话隐藏着一个跨领域的深层模式：用户体验优化的历史，就是把人类不自觉承担的路由决策逐步吸收到系统底层的历史。 - Google 之前，人是网页目录的路由器（Yahoo 分类） - CDN 之前，人是延迟路由器（选就近服务器） - 推荐系统之前，人是内容路由器（订 RSS） - 现在，人是模型路由器（"我先问 Haiku，不行再上 Opus"）

按这个规律推演，OpenRouter 现在正处于 Google 1998 年的位置——把一个用户被迫手动做的高频决策"自动化并变成一层默认基础设施"。这不是"just a wrapper"能容纳的野心。

三、Discord 是 AI 世代的意外原型工厂——而"社区即数据管道"是被严重低估的产品哲学

大多数人复盘生成式 AI 崛起时会讲 Transformer、Scaling Laws、RLHF。但这一集透露了一条完全被主流叙事遮蔽的支线：Claude、Midjourney、11Labs、早期 Mistral 全都是先以 Discord bot 形式接触用户的。Anjney 在管 Discord 平台时无意间把加密社区留下的基建（大流量、bot 生态、moderation 层）当成了 AI 应用的孵化器。

跨领域连接：这与生物学里的"预适应"（exaptation）惊人相似——羽毛先为保温进化，后来被拿来飞行。加密社区为了处理 NFT 交易高频事件构建的抽象层，恰好被下一波完全不同的负载（AI 推理）复用。这暗示了一个更普遍的规律：真正颠覆性技术的初始基础设施，几乎从不是为它自己建的。

四、意外洞见：Alex 在直播里发生了一次"被 Claude 反向训练"的语言事故

节目中间 Alex 说了句"the shape of open router"，然后立刻自我修正："oh no, I've been overtrained, I've been using Claude way too much, haven't I? Claudish is what people say"。

这可能是整期节目最不经意但最深刻的时刻。它揭示了一个 AI 从业者尚未系统研究的现象：高频使用 LLM 的产品负责人正在被自己的产品反向 fine-tune。当 CEO 的自然语言语料被特定模型的输出风格污染，他关于产品的判断、审美、直觉都会被静默塑形。这对整个 AI 产品生态是一个隐藏的系统性风险——决策者与他们所选模型的"审美共振"会让市场收敛到少数几种"味道"，就像所有 Instagram 网红照片开始看起来一样。

五、Focus 悖论：为什么"看起来最该做的邻接品类"往往是最不该做的

Anjney 反复强调 Anthropic 从第一天就只做 AI 结对编程，Alex 反复强调 OpenRouter 拒绝做 fine-tuning、memory、sandbox。这些"应该做"的邻接品类被系统性放弃。

深层机制不只是资源问题，而是"品牌可寻性"（brand-findability）——当世界需要"最懂 X 的那个人"时，能被检索出来的名字只有一个。这与生物学的生态位窄化同构：物种越专注，越不容易被替代。在 AI 时代，试图变成"AI 界的亚马逊"的通用平台，反而最容易被下一波聚焦型玩家吃掉。Vercel 之于前端、Cursor 之于编辑器、OpenRouter 之于模型路由——都是同一模式。

📝 转录文本

The $10 Trillion Token Economy — Alex Atallah, OpenRouter & Anjney Midha, AMP

冷开场：Token 经济的规模预警

Hey, there's a new type of unit of value that's being streamed across the internet called a token. And over the next 10 years, the entire internet value chain was going to have to deal with the fact that like the more valuable tokens got, the more bad actors were going to go to try to get their hands on those tokens. And anytime you scale something and the payload gets more and more valuable, more bad things people try to get access to that value.

Online payments, you know, is started roughly in the 80s and '90s, right? And grew to over a trillion dollars over the next 10 years, and we needed to build entirely new payment solutions to deal with online fraud. Where we are today is roughly there on tokens, but over the next even five years, we're expecting the token economy to get to like roughly $5 trillion. And over the next 10 years, I'd be shocked if we went to 10 trillion of token flow.

We blocked 10x as much dollar volume last month as the month before, and the types of token fraud are diversifying quite a bit.

主持人插播：订阅呼吁

Before we get into today's episode, I just have a small message for listeners. Thank you. We would not be able to bring you the AI engineering, science, and entertainment content that you so clearly want if you didn't choose to also click in and tune into our content. We've been approached by sponsors on an almost daily basis. But fortunately, enough of you actually subscribe to us to keep all this sustainable without ads, and we want to keep it that way.

But I just have one favor to ask all of you. The single most powerful, completely free thing you can do is to click that subscribe button. It's the only thing I'll ever ask of you, and it means absolutely everything to me and my team that works so hard to bring the Inspace to you each and every week. If you do it, I promise you, we'll never stop working to make the show even better. Now, let's get into it.

开场寒暄：在 Anj 家里录制

Okay, we are here in Anj's house, which is where all great startups in San Francisco start.

— Howdy.

— And congrats on Cursor, Mistral… God knows what else. You got so much stuff going on.

— There's a lot going on. Well, OpenRouter is probably the most, I would say, one I'm excited about recently.

— Yeah. And we have Alex — first time on the pod, but you've been a few times. I appreciate every time you've shown up for the community. Congrats. I just like — what a journey.

Pub/Sub 作为产品原则：OpenRouter 的哲学起点

When I was looking back at your past posts, one of the earliest principles that I saw you write as a sort of product person is pub/sub as a product principle. I wanted you to maybe explain how you think about what should exist in the world.

Alex: Yeah. The pub/sub piece — which was early 2023, I didn't think about it until we we talked like 10 minutes ago — is about how there is like a way of thinking about products as an intersection between subscribing to data and publishing data. And marketplaces are an easy example of this. You have suppliers that are publishing some kind of product to a SKU. And the SKU is kind of like a pub/sub topic that a consumer is subscribing to and just going to consume whenever they want.

And humans consume in a very discreet, ad hoc way. It's not very scalable. All their attention is on the topic when they're buying the thing, and their attention is nowhere else when that happens. Agents and consumers of inference don't act like that. They're consuming continuously and they're changing the SKUs that they consume from all the time.

So OpenRouter is sort of like a blend between a normal API experience and a marketplace where we create model slugs. We have the auto router. We have all kinds of product SKUs that you can subscribe to — and then you can continuously derive value and make decisions based on those consumers.

模型可互换的顿悟时刻：Alpaca

— Yeah, this is something that was more consensus now but not consensus when you guys started — which was that there is such a demand for swapping models and changing things out, and that people would not use the native SDKs. I guess, for each of you, what was your realization moment that this would be it? You've given a talk at EIE about Alpaca as one of your inspiring moments?

Alex: Alpaca — I can rehash the Alpaca moment for a sec. At the very beginning at the end of 2022, OpenAI was the only game in town. There was OpenAI, Cohere, and then a smattering of early attempts at open-weight models.

When Llama came out in January of 2023, it was like, "Wow, really exciting. This is really big. It outperforms GPT-3 on one or two benchmarks." But you can't chat with it. It wasn't actually an engaging model. But it seemed like someone just needed to fix a couple things and do some RLHF on it to get it all the way there.

And Alpaca was the first model that I saw that did that. It only took $600 to do. A team at Stanford generated a bunch of synthetic data, fine-tuned Llama, and made Alpaca — a 7 billion parameter model, or maybe it was 13 billion parameters. And it was so good — like I was just on an airplane using it. In many cases you could not discern a ChatGPT versus an Alpaca result.

And I figured, if it was this easy to make a model — one, we have a whole new way of monetizing data for the first time. You can just take really valuable data and turn it into a service in $600. And that cost will probably go down over time.

— When you say monetizing your data — as what? Eventually will become an MCP endpoint, or as training data for a model?

Alex: Training data for a model. Like an abstract way of saying: hey, I have this data, compress it into a model. It makes sense for me in my product, but I could repackage it in the form of a model and sell it. And so it's just a whole new business model for the economy.

It also provides a way of following what frontier labs are doing — but in a way that a single developer or a small team of developers can roll on their own. Whenever you have an example of that — a breakout app that's doing really well — and then some kind of framework for imitating it with your own flavor, you have an immediate ecosystem that should arise. Because there's a huge gap between the decisions that the single company is making and all of the variations that a wider ecosystem can create themselves.

And so then you need a marketplace to discover all of those services and all of those products. There wasn't any place on the internet that was like a home base for LLMs in terms of seeing how much they were being used and seeing who was using them and why.

— The closest would be Hugging Face.

Alex: Hugging Face was the closest. They just started Hub like a few years ago. Yeah. And Hugging Face also didn't have the closed-source models. And they didn't — you couldn't use the models at the time. And there wasn't data about who was using it. There are a bunch of differences between OpenRouter and Hugging Face — and those differences felt really critical to me, especially when I was just trying to learn about LLMs and why people are choosing all these different little ones that are emerging over time.

13 年前的斯坦福：Alex 和 Anjney 的初遇

— Got it. And Anj, no stranger to wanting more model diversity — at the time, you're a couple years into your Anthropic journey which we covered in a previous podcast as well. What was your introduction to Alex?

Anjney: Well, the introduction was I think 13 years before that. Oh. But the OpenRouter handshake actually happened right over there, if you remember. Which was — Alex and I met, I believe as sophomores now if I remember correctly — meeting for the first time. I think so. Yeah.

So Stanford Review was the libertarian newspaper on campus at Stanford that Peter Thiel had started back in the day. For whatever reason, Alex and I both showed up to one of the meetings. And I remember the editor-in-chief was a mutual friend of ours — Lisa was a really great editor-in-chief.

Part of an editor-in-chief's job is to assign responsibilities to people and make sure the work gets done. I may be misremembering the details, but I remember wanting to — it was kind of surprising to me that at the time there was no dedicated technology section in the newspaper.

— Because it's political, right? Yes.

Anjney: Yeah. But to take us back in time — you may remember this — there was this technology legislation that was being debated called the Net Neutrality Act. And net neutrality is inherently this political concept, right? It's about the regulation of internet broadband access. And so there was a community of us who were kind of technologists but also debating the politics of the technology.

And I thought the Review would be a great place to write about that. I was working on I think a net neutrality article, and I remember proposing, "Well, maybe you should start a technology section." Alex was one of the only people who said, "Yes, that would be cool," and said — I forget whether we ended up writing stuff together, but that's when we first met. It was 2011 or 12, I forget which year it was. It was one of those. It was at Old Union, if I remember correctly. That's where we used to meet.

在 Discord 交集：加密狂潮与内容审核

But along the way, Alex and I have had a chance to hang out often. And probably the time when we had the most professional overlap was when I was running the platform of Discord — and it had become this explosive kind of platform for crypto.

— Yeah. And NFTs in the middle of the pandemic.

Anjney: Which, also, by the way, you were in charge of safety and security as well, right? I was the head of platform, which meant all of the crypto DAO and NFT launch security debugging fell on me — and the phishing, the social engineering attacks, like a ton of DDoS that we were getting hit by. Around that time I started teaching security at Stanford CS53, and Alex was at OpenSea at the time. And I was trying to figure out how we could defend against all these attacks.

At peak — I forget if you remember how much NFT volume was running through Discord — but it was like several billion dollars in NFT volume of GMV running through the platform, and it was all coming from OpenSea. It was these buy/sell/trade — I mean the server, the D&D is Discord — yes. And so that's when I think we had hung out professionally.

GPT-3.5、Clyde 与内容审核：开源模型的必要性

But a year after that, OpenAI gave Discord early access to GPT — sorry, GPT-3. No, it was GPT-3.5 actually. Yeah, GPT-3 which is the RL version of GPT-3. And that's around the time we made a Discord bot with OpenAI for internal deployment. And that's when I realized we would need — since I was part of the deployment team…

— What was the use case there?

Anjney: There were two — and there's actually a post now called "Discord is your place for AI with friends" that somebody sent me recently that I wrote and published in 2023. But there were two use cases.

One was Clyde — a first-party friend inside of Discord that could help you set up your Discord server and talk to you about onboarding and get your friends to hang out more.

And then there was content moderation. One of the realizations we had with content moderation was — it would refuse to moderate. It would just refuse our prompts because the RL, the post-training, was — we were very early in the post-training era — and our prompts would trigger it. Like guardrails.

And we told OpenAI, "Hey guys, we need access to the weights, because if we're going to be doing content moderation at scale — we had 250 million monthly active users — we need more reliability that the model will do what we need it to." And they said, "Well, sorry guys, that's not how this works. We're a closed-source company."

And so that was my first realization that we needed open models, and that enterprises would need more control over capabilities, and then ultimately would need some kind of control plane or management system to orchestrate these open models. But there weren't any good open alternatives until maybe 6 months later when Llama came out. And 6 months after that I led the Series A into Mistral, which was started by Guillaume and the Llama team.

Around that time is when I remember hearing about Alex launching OpenRouter and going, "These worlds are going to collide, and I don't know when it'll make sense to team up." But Alex was so early and could see — I think he was totally right about this ecosystem starting with Llama that then needed an easy layer to manage, especially for — I was approaching it from the enterprise perspective, because as the VP of platform at Discord it was my job to ensure that when we deployed models to like 250 million users they did what we wanted them to. And that was very hard. If you outsourced it to the labs and they controlled the guardrails, and their safety policies forbid the model from responding to your prompts, that was catastrophic.

为什么通用审核端点不够：每个社区自己的规范

— Yeah, but moderation is a thing that they want to support. And obviously beyond that, they would work with you presumably to give you a moderation endpoint, which they offer for free.

Anjney: It was an interesting use case. They did give us a moderation endpoint. However, as you guys know, every Discord server is like a mini deployment of itself.

The use case was: instead of having human moderators that have to interpret the norms of the community, you just give — the public Discord servers have their own rules. Every subreddit, every Discord server public one has its own rules that the users randomly space Discord in. And then humans used to read those norms and then enforce it every day manually, observing each message in these communities. And these communities are like millions of users.

So we had a 5,000-plus person team globally on the Discord content moderation team. These are outsourced contractors who had a really tough job.

And so the idea was: if instead you could give the norms of that server to the LLM, then the LLM would do custom moderation for that server. It's almost like in-context moderation for that server.

And many of those servers' norms just violated OpenAI's rules. It was like — we had our own custom eval. Each server had its own custom eval. But at the time OpenAI's evals — so primitive in our thinking about how to deploy these LLMs — often the post-training prompts were super heavy-handed. It said, "Oh, anything about Harry Potter, anything that has trademarked content — don't respond." And if it was a Harry Potter fan community — this is a real use case — that had a content moderation, the LLM would just refuse.

— Yeah. And that was just not precise enough.

Alex: Another one that we heard was: if someone was trying to write a detective story and there's one chapter with a lot of violence, like maybe someone kills someone — the LLMs would just refuse to help with that part of the story.

And then the user would be like, "Okay, this is not structurally inherent to LLMs. There must be some choice out there so that I can switch to another model when I'm getting a refusal or a bad result from the main one that I have." And that tension also drove me for a marketplace.

VC 早期质疑：Big Model Wins?

— Yeah, I think that is well accepted now. What was it like back then when you were raising or starting this? Did people get it? What were some of the struggles? Basically — I like getting stories out of him about how other VCs don't get it. So, anything you want to talk about now — now that let's call it the early journey of OpenRouter is done — you can obviously talk about some of the early days stuff.

Alex: Well, I was going to say that the biggest objection we got is "big model wins" — which is: all the value…

— Scaling laws.

Alex: Yeah, scaling laws and natural network effects are just going to accrue to one company. It'll be like a Google-style monopoly, just like how Google won the search market by a large large margin. And you'll just be fighting for scraps at the end basically. That was probably the biggest objection we got.

And it is interesting that Google won the search-engine race with such a huge margin. Had there been more interesting benchmarks, or had people seen search engines a little bit more like LLMs — where they're services that you can build companies on top of — that might not have been the case. LLMs don't merely have a user interface. They're also ways of building entirely new businesses.

And a Google-level monopoly would be like the Dutch East India Company times a quadrillion in magnitude — because the whole economy ends up depending on the one monopoly as well. So it didn't seem like it would be a really crazy outcome if that happened. And it's also less likely because the economics of creating good competitors are much more decentralizable.

Anjney 视角：Scaling Laws 是 feature，不是 bug

Anjney: Everything Alex said is true, and I came at it from a completely different perspective, which is: yes, this is why we're here. The scaling laws in my mind were always a feature, not a bug, for why OpenRouter would be very valuable.

Because I was one of the first investors in Anthropic. And it was obvious to me — other researchers in our friends group, and I went to grad school for machine learning, I just had a lot of friends in the ML community — it was very obvious to us that the bitter lesson holds. And so I was like, oh, fantastic, now we have at least two proof points that compute scaling works. It was OpenAI and Anthropic.

研究员心态 vs. 开发者心态：Checkpoint 之后的沉默

But the shared problem I was noticing across all of them was: often, the research teams were fantastic at figuring out how to reason about new capabilities. They think in terms of capabilities — but they're not developer-mindset-oriented. Like what happens after the training is done and the checkpoint comes out.

You'd be shocked how similar the early pre-training teams at OpenAI — sorry, Anthropic, BFL, Mistral — were in their default approach to taking their research out of the lab and scaling their impact. Which was often: "Oh, the checkpoint is done, put it out as an API, done." And then there'd be crickets.

In the case of Claude — the first Claude checkpoint was actually done a year before they released it internally. And then ChatGPT came out and we decided, "Okay, yes, it's a good idea to release a Claude version externally." And they had no plan for how to get developers to actually try it out.

So if you go to the Claude 1 blog post, you'll notice they list three developer examples for users of the API. One is a Discord bot, and the second is Vivian — my wife's startup called Junior Learning — and then there was Notion. Because these are all friends of the Anthropic team. That's how last-minute the planning was around "hey, once the model's done training, how do you get it out to the world?"

There was no distribution platform that understood what developers needed — all the key management, provisioning, simple endpoint management, versioning control — all these things that the scientists and researchers go, "I mean, that's plumbing, I don't do that detail."

And instead, Alex came at it from that perspective. So it was so obvious to me that every single lab I was funding would spend sometimes literally billions of dollars into training, and then a checkpoint would be done and there'd be crickets. Doing early access — cuz they're like, "Oh, that's right, it's hard to use a checkpoint to make anything. You actually need a whole bunch of plumbing around it to make it usable by a developer."

Marketplace 作为中立营销层

Alex: In addition to building a really good developer experience around it, the marketing that we do for different models is totally different and perceived totally differently from the marketing that a model lab does for itself. We are, you know, a neutral layer.

Looking at this market — it's like a big dark room with all the corners completely obscure to users, and users were walking into the room and feeling around and trying to figure out what objects to grab off the tables and build into their companies. It's an insane way of working.

Models are not products where you can just enumerate all their features onto a web page. They're all black boxes, including the open-weight ones. So in addition to developer experience, there's also a very important marketing and product packaging component. And a way of routing and discovering models becomes critical to your go-to-market as a provider or a model lab or a server tool and more in the future.
