I mean, these projects were so different in their goals that it was totally normal to me to be like, "Oh yeah, let's call Alex and see if you'd want to team up on pooling data." Cuz they're so different — we actually don't have that kind of data at all. We didn't have API prompts. We didn't have what developers want to do with the models — which is very different from what researchers inside a model lab want to do before releasing the model.

Does that make sense? And so to this day, I think you see that this difference — even though at a 30,000-foot level you could I guess kind of conclude that Arena and OpenRouter are adjacent — the roadmaps, the missions, and so on at the time at least were in very different directions.

Focus 的复利：为什么专注在 AI 时代仍被低估

— The ideal customer — I totally get that. As a founder, I want to own everything, right? So like, this is clearly the adjacency, then I'm going to explore that. Own everything meaning — like you don't know what to do yet, so you want to make sure you catch PM.

Alex: I think what he said — you want to own the entire infrastructure space, and so you'd kind of expand to whatever demand. Clearly, you know, this is the only one of focus, right?

Yeah. I think that's hard, you know, in reality — because serving multiple customers is [hard]. I still think even in the age of AI, focus is underrated and critical. Not just because you end up with a better product by focusing your humans on it, but also because the world knows what your focus is.

The world can map like, "Oh, I have this issue. Which brand out there is going to help me with that issue? This is the brand that's known for that focus." So if I want real attention on this issue, if this really matters to me, I should go with the brand that cares the most about it.

Anthropic 的编程赌注：从 Day 1 的最高期望客户

Anjney: To underscore Alex's point about how important focus is: in the early days of Anthropic, people think that the early days of Anthropic were super easy because they were the GPT-3 guys who left. But it was actually very competitive. The company was starting $10 billion behind OpenAI, right?

And so to get to the frontier, the big question was: what do we want to be known for? What's the mission? And the mission was AGI pair programming. And so to the exclusion of all kinds of other things that were really shiny at the time — like image models and video models that were getting lots of momentum — the Anthropic team was like, "We just got to focus on coding. That is the core capability that we're focused [on]."

And today you can see the results, right? It's a trillion-dollar company within 5 years. And that focus — the focus on who your highest-expectation customer is, and how you exceed their expectation, because exceeding anyone's expectations is hard and doing it for multiple customers is even more difficult — is part of the reason why OpenRouter succeeded, and Anthropic as well.

— Was the focus on coding that early, though? Or did it come later?

Anjney: Literally from day one, it was: "AI pair programming — responsibly commercialize an AI pair programmer" was the seed memo. That was when I invested. We actually kind of refined that memo a lot. Well, you got to ask Dario and Tom for permission on that. But it's an extraordinary piece of writing that they had put together.

And "responsibly commercializing AI pair programming" was the mission from day one. And I would say there was maybe a couple moments in the company's history where they did experiments to see if little detours made sense — like a general chatbot like Claude.ai when ChatGPT was really taking off — but at the end of the day, especially once they got their significant pre-training compute online, all the main evals at the company for example have always been coding evals, long-horizon agentic programming. I mean, from day one that was always [true].

— When Claude Instant came out and Claude 2 came out, yes — I remember the marketing mostly being focused on prose, like "this model writes better," and long context.

Anjney: Long context.

— This directly affected me, cuz I built something on that.

Anjney: What did you make?

— Uh, "SmallDeveloper," which was my Devon before Devon. Oh yeah, SmallDeveloper.

未走的路：拒绝的产品线

Yes. And so I think there's all that really good like focus — is another thing that is a question that people do want to ask. You could have built any other things, and obviously OpenRouter was working. Were there other ideas that you wanted to pursue that you turned down? You know, just the paths, roads not taken.

Alex: We made a couple prototypes for things that we didn't launch. One was a fine-tuning model as a service — a lot of that, OpenPipe and all those things. But it was in a very consumery form factor where you would give us a YouTube video or two or three, we would then extract all the transcripts from it and try to fine-tune a model to talk like the person in the YouTube video or the people in the videos that you sent. So like a really really easy way of creating a fine-tuned model based on some kind of videos that you like.

— That would be so useful.

Alex: We made it, too. It was like — and nobody used it. We didn't actually test it with that many people, because the model marketplace was our main focus and it was growing and we were building more conviction in it over time.

— Just as a creator, I've been pitched many like — "I have 500 hours of recorded voice of myself, make a 'thing of you,' charge access to it." Works for OnlyFans, doesn't work for us as regular people. I think this is mostly — it's just a glorified RAG bot, whether it's in the weights or outside the weights doesn't really matter. You're just doing RAG on the videos, and people ultimately always just want to find the source video that directly answers it.

Alex: My use case was mostly to practice with — with myself — cuz I often like to see what the way I practice for a job interview, or if I'm hiring a candidate, or public speaking or whatever, is I wish there was a good mini-me that I could critique. Cuz it's kind of hard to pull yourself out. I would never offer it to other people.

— A service like: pick your top five mentors that then talk to them instead of talking [to yourself]. That would be cool too.

Alex: Yeah, that's a Replica. And that was the use case we were aiming at.

— It's like, you want to create an experience like AI Steve Jobs. AI Steve Jobs was the initial use case. That's a common prototype, even though it's not allowed.

为什么 OpenRouter 不做 fine-tuning as a service

You know, talking about adjacencies — fine-tuning as a service as part of the router service is something that I would typically think about as well, right? Why don't you do that? Because if people are running already their inference through you, store everything, log everything, fine-tune to a smaller model that is cheaper, faster, all these things — that's within your control, right? You didn't do that. But other people would have pitched that in the general state of infra startups.

Anjney: I think you were just maybe a little bit early — because today that's an extraordinarily fast-growing segment. Like from Mistral, where they do a lot of enterprise deployments — often fine-tuning is custom models for ASML or whatever.

— But not as a router. They're just like, "I come to you because I like your ML models, I want a custom model," right? It is not "I want to run all my OpenAI prompts, get, store all my results, and then just move off of OpenAI," right? They're not doing that. As a way to export off of dependency on a frontier lab — I have not seen that yet. Which was your decision to do.

Alex: I mean, we decided to lean into our focus and figured that there are — we just saw the ecosystem develop over time. All these inference providers that do want to help companies do that. It makes sense for us to partner with them and to give users lots of choice and to figure out what makes them what gives them competitive advantages. It's a whole new business basically, and there's value in being a neutral marketplace that just kind of works with those companies.

Fusion 的起源：Mixture of Models 的第一次尝试与两年后的重启

— Could you share a little bit — to Sean's point — how you prioritized features? Because you've always done it so elegantly. It just happens and you make all the right decisions, that always have product-market fit from the outside looking in. Consistently you seem to have prioritized a lot of hit features that worked.

Alex: Maybe I have a sample-set bias, or whatever.

— Sean, can you list what you think hit features worked well?

— Like the leaderboards.

Alex: Leaderboard, okay. Yeah, you know, like from day one.

— The feedback. Charting. Okay. But like — he had plugins, and I think there was a whole thing I want to get into about completions versus — Chat Completions versus Completions — and then also, let's call it, the rise of the reasoning models, and how you deal with multimodality, all those things. By Huge one.

Alex: There's one — I think it was in early 2024, very early 2024 — we thought it might be interesting to fuse the results of multiple models together. And we launched a prototype called MoM: Mixture of Models that let you pick a couple models — we'd pick them for you — and then it would fuse the results together at the end. And it would show you all the intermediate results in this big Kanban board–looking product.

— What does the fusion at the end? Another model?

Alex: Another model — the smartest of the three of the set.

— So this is like a council idea. It was a model. It was like a very early LLM council. This is a multi-agent swarm, as they would call it at one of the frontier labs in the early days.

Alex: Yeah. Some of those ideas are going in the right direction, but the devil's in the details. There's a lot of product refinement needed to make them really work. They take your focus away from whatever else you have going on, and there's a lot of community building and learning that you need to do. And the technology might be too early — so there are all kinds of reasons they might go wrong.

And in our case, the technology was a little too early. In other words, the fused result was a little bit worse — sometimes the same as the best model that was being used to fuse — because the best model was so far ahead of options two and three at the time.

Over time, the top three or four LLMs have gotten closer together. Still neurodivergent, but all capable of inserting pretty interesting ideas. Like RL has basically expanded the surface area of creativity for machine learning researchers within each lab, and so they can diversify the reasoning power of different models more effectively. At least that's my theory for why Fusion works better than it used to [in] early 2024.

And so the technology was a little bit too primitive. The form factor was not right. And so we would have had to go through a couple more iterations. And so we decided to just delete all the code.

And then years later — middle of 2026, or early 2026 — we're like, let's bring it back. The research is looking kind of promising for fusion. The models now have two, three, four top frontier models that are all really good. I was frequently trying to consult multiple models to get the best results. And then I ran a little personal experiment where I was like, I'm going to do an architecture plan for a code change. I'm going to give it to all the models. I'm going to fuse the result. And I'm going to ask all the models if the fused result is better than the individual result each model came up with.

And they all said yes — that the fused result was better. And this happened a couple times, and I was like, okay, spot check pretty good. We should benchmark this. And that's how we built Fusion.

— Yeah, and it came on your Fable.

Alex: So you were like, this is Fable-level. Yeah.

OpenRouter 的里程碑：Sonnet 3.5 与代码浪潮

Yeah. Let's start leading up to this year, which we haven't gotten to. Can you mark out the main milestones in the journey? It seems like your promise was routing. You decided the business model very early — you take a cut. What are the major milestones that inflect the growth? You're growing like 9% week on week now — is that the official number?

Alex: In terms of token volume, I think that sounds about right.

— Yeah. So can you mark out the brief history of OpenRouter up to the acquisition, let's call it? We're just talking about — you know, people have your birth moment with the Mistral stuff where people are really competing. You have your State of AI thing where it's very cute — you have 100 trillion tokens, haha — because now you're doing 10 a week.

Alex: We're doing 10 a day.

— 10 a day now? Yeah, more.

Alex: So you do this in 10 days. What are the major points there? I just want to — there's a smooth curve, but you feel the inflections.

A lot of this is kind of oriented around model launches. We had a huge focus on prose all the way up through May of 2024. Because coding was just not there, and no apps were able to build much on top of it. So it was a diversity in models, but not a wide diversity in use cases. Dream Tavern was one of our top apps at the time. The creator of Dream Tavern now runs product at Cognition Devon.

Then in the middle of 2024 we saw Claude Sonnet 3.5 that came out — incredible leap forward in coding. And we saw the dynamics of apps building on top of us change. We saw a huge surge in volume, in users using OpenRouter. And this is when I think people started to look at the money that they were spending and get a little bit like, "Whoa, what's going on? I might need to think about more cost-efficient but equivalent models."

And shortly after that Sonnet 3.5, Mixtral 8x7B came out. And everyone was like, "What?! This is the model. Like the open-weights community delivered." And so it was really good timing.

— Basically all of Anj's co's are just helping you out.

Alex: It takes an ecosystem to grow an OpenRouter, you know.

Yeah, that was the early ecosystem. It was a swing action where model labs would come up with some sort of frontier innovation, usage would surge, then users look at their invoices 30 days later — "whoa, what's going on here" — and then open-weight models would deliver cost-effective options 3 months later. We saw that happen several times.

Coding Agents 榜单：从 Cline 到 OpenClaw

— One thing you also did with the coding agents was that you broke out which are the top coding agents, and they love that leaderboard — the Cline versus Roo Code versus what have you.

Alex: Yeah. Cline was like the top of our leaderboard at the time. I'll skip forward a little bit — the end of 2025, there were quite a few coding apps on the leaderboard, but they were all IDEs or terminal-based agents.

And at the end of 2025, we saw OpenClaw appear. And OpenClaw was particularly interesting because — one, it was a new form factor that brought in a new type of user, not just a developer but a productivity or internet-creator [type] came to AI for the first time.

And it also had an interesting architecture where it was calling your chosen model for these heartbeats to see if it was still alive, in addition to actually using the model for real tasks. And the heartbeats are — you don't want to pay a lot for a heartbeat. So the auto router that we provided was really really useful to this wide range of users all of a sudden.

And so we just saw it rocket exponentially. And then we saw OpenClaw just blow up, and a couple other apps lean into that new paradigm and do something similar.

Hermes came out and really leaned into things like the auto router and built a really good community, and leaned into basically skill management — making it really easy and effective for people to set their memory in the agent and build really good skills.

— Which another thing you never did — memory, skills, sandboxes, all these adjacent things you could have done.

Alex: Could have. But it's — I think it's hard to bet [on those]. They're also very — there are things that developers, that really matter for the developer use cases that were coming out at the time. Like developers wanted to architect those things. Those were kind of critical to building a good user experience.

It's been hard for companies to find abstractions that work for all developers on the memory layer. There are some — like Mastra has done a pretty good job, for example — but developers have lots of varied preferences for them.

And then the way our leaderboard has changed over time is kind of like a movie of how the AI space has changed over time. If you just go to the Wayback Machine and look at the models leaderboard and the apps leaderboard over time, it sort of shows you what's happened in AI over the last couple of years.

— To me, the coming-of-age moment was Andrej Karpathy was like, "I no longer read /r/LocalLlama, cuz I just go to OpenRouter's leaderboard."

Alex: Which — I remember that. I think he probably said, "Sorry guys, like I'm going to send a bunch of traffic to you."

Stripe 收购：从欺诈拦截说起

— So I also want to bring it into the Stripe thing. How does that kind of conversation start?

Alex: We had this longstanding relationship with Stripe from many different projects that we had worked on with them. We invest a lot of effort in countering abuse and…

— Token fraud.

Alex: And token fraud. Can you give some numbers just so people understand? I think I posted about this. We blocked 10x as much dollar volume last month as the month before. And the types of token fraud are diversifying quite a bit.

There are fraudsters going after typical stolen credit cards, but they're also people trying to resell traffic against the terms of service. There's hacked accounts. There's people who just lose access — like their whole company is compromised and they don't even realize it. And we help them regain control and detect it.

There are accounts that are reselling inference on the side. There are accounts that are dealing with an accidental runaway agent, and they don't realize it. Not a hack, but it's something that blows up and the company doesn't want it.

And so our trust-and-safety team works a lot on all of these categories of problems and helps block and detect it. We have models around them. We worked closely with Stripe for a while on this.

未来的定价范式转移：从推理转售到离散任务

And I think it's going to become a huge problem in the ecosystem. We're already seeing a lot of companies start to see these fraudsters spread and look for other ways — other than OpenRouter — to other fraud vectors. If you're making a gateway or selling generalized inference, you are a target for fraud.

If you're selling very discrete intelligence products — intelligence products that are doing something pretty specific but not just reselling inference with some added capability — then you're way less likely to get these fraudsters. So I think we'll see companies also move away from just reselling inference with some sort of added capability, and move towards discrete tasks — and charging for those tasks and charging for those enhancements, and letting people bring their own inference in a third-party way.

— Whoa. Okay. And yeah, obviously you would power that. But you — people pay for outcomes, or per task?

Alex: I think people will pay — you know, I think the Datadog pricing page is a good look at the future to come. Infrastructure companies will charge for different types of events that they're providing, and there'll be lots of continuous pricing models that look like that.

And of course, if you go down towards consumer apps, simpler pricing, more subscriptions, fewer events to worry about. And ones that are not focused on just adding a markup on top of inference — not just because fraud is hard, but also because the pressure from the labs and from good inference providers to do a commit and then bring your inference elsewhere is going to be very high.

Anjney 的宏观预警：Token 经济的欺诈引力

— Any comments?

Anjney: Two [things]. One, Alex has done a very eloquent job of describing something I knew counterintuitively would be a thing at scale like four years ago because of Discord. And the particular experience that taught me this was — as we started scaling Midjourney, one of the primary ways that we used to give away or get people to try Midjourney early on to get to their first 10 generations — cuz 10 generations of 10 images generated was roughly the magic-moment activation point we found. Once you'd done 10, you were like, "This is extraordinary."

But for that, we had a free trial with Midjourney. And one day I woke up — because we had a platform and had monitor, I had all these dashboards — I had like three missed calls from David. And it turns out they had — there had been this flood of new users overnight and we were like, "This is great." And he was like, "No, actually, we shut down the free trial." And I was like, "Why is that?"

And he said, "I want to look at the geolocation IP addresses." And basically somebody in China had started to resell Midjourney free subscriptions with the free trial as a way to — it was fraud, abuse, right?

— And even for a specialized model like Midjourney.

Anjney: Yeah. And that was an actual application. So this idea that — I think the big-picture realization I had back then was: hey, there's a new type of unit of value that's being streamed across the internet called a token, and over the next 10 years the entire internet value chain was going to have to deal with the fact that the more valuable tokens got, the more bad actors were going to go try to get their hands on those tokens. And anytime you scale something and the payload gets more and more valuable, more bad things — people try to get access to that value.

And so it was very obvious to me back then. And look, to this day, I don't think there's a free tier — I don't think Midjourney has ever actually turned on the free trial since then, because it was really not an easy problem to solve in terms of trust and safety.

That's why I started teaching the class Security at Scale at Stanford. Like that, and the Anthropic learnings — to me it was clear that the need for security at scale was going to be enormous a few years from then.

支付欺诈的历史类比：Stripe 的真正身份是安全公司

Cuz if you just do the math — think about like, if where online payments started roughly in the 80s and 90s, right, and grew to over a trillion dollars over the next 10 years, and we needed to build entirely new payment solutions to deal with online fraud.

Where we are today is roughly there on tokens, but over the next even five years we're expecting the token economy to get to like roughly $5 trillion. And over the next 10 years I'd be shocked if we went to 10 trillion of token flow.

And so if we were starting to see such aggressive abuse and fraud at sub-scale Midjourney — remember Midjourney at this point was like less than 300 million revenue run rate a year — I realized we were going to need entirely new systems to deal with the fraud that was going to happen for trying to get into the token flow.

So — I forget the board meeting — it was when you brought up that Stripe wanted to partner up, and it made so much sense to me. Cuz Stripe Radar — when I was at KP 10 years ago, we invested in Stripe. And the whole pitch that Patrick and John communicated so eloquently was: hey, unlike traditional payment tools like Braintree that do a 7-day verification, KYC and email to get the fraud out of the way, we actually just eat the fraud cost up front as a customer acquisition cost, and tell a developer, "Just use five lines of code and we'll start accepting your payments in 5 minutes." And what will happen is over time we'll collect all this data on the developers.

— The Cloudflare model.

Anjney: The Cloudflare model, right? And they did. 5 years later, they launched Stripe Radar. And Stripe really today is a security company — that's the real [thing]. People think it's a payments company. No — the reason there's lots of other payments providers today that give you cheaper payments transmission, but the reason Stripe keeps being the dominant one here in Adyen and Europe is because they have extraordinary fraud detection that they've built with over the years. The same story with Elon and Max Levchin and Affirm.

You know, I think the story shows up over and over again where every time you have value streamed across the world in large amounts, you need new protection and security infrastructure to fight to keep the bad guys out and allow the good people to have their transactions happen really fast.

And so I think, from my perspective, the Stripe and OpenRouter story is a security story for the internet ecosystem, for the frontier AI ecosystem. Without a partnership like that, it becomes very hard to defend the quality of experience and the speed and all the good stuff without letting the bad guys get in the way.

递归欺诈：AI 代理规模的下一波挑战

The second is that there's this underappreciated thing about — you need to like — these all the bad things that Alex described as being perpetuated by humans right now is going to be perpetuated by AI agents over the next 10 years, right?

So think about the recursive scale we're about to see of bad actors. It's not just bad human beings. It's all the bad agents that are going to be attacking the token flow. And it's very hard if you're a researcher or an AI lab to reason about that problem, because the only data you have is how agents you're training are going rogue. But that's just a fraction of all the bad behavior on the internet that we're going to see.

And so what you need is defenders — new sheriffs in town, with cowboy hats — that can see all the bad behavior from AI agents across the ecosystem, from different model labs and different post-trained deployments and different developers, and take all of that data and say, "We're going to build a shield for the entire token economy."

Because without that, the amount of fraud we're going to see — of this 10-trillion-dollar in GMV and global GDP growth — is like a huge percentage of that, I think, is going to be fraud, abuse. And we might never get there if people just don't trust tokens, right? And I don't think this infrastructure exists.

So you have your work cut out for you at Stripe. But I don't think people have realized the scale at which agentic fraud, bad behavior perpetuated by AI agents, is about to hit us like a tsunami.

收尾：OpenRouter × Stripe 的下一步

— Yeah, there's a lot to dig into there. I want to give you the last word. We do have to wrap. What can people expect from OpenRouter and Stripe?

Alex: I think this is a really good way for us to accelerate go-to-market and to go up-market more quickly. It's also, as [Anj] eloquently described, this is a really clear "better together" story when it comes to improving trust and safety, and making it really easy to accept tokens and let people bring their own inference to your app, and to help developers just build on top of inference.

Going forward, we have a really strong brand with OpenRouter — and we're keeping the brand. So OpenRouter as a product and the road map and the name and the brand is staying the same. And so what you should expect in this next 6 months is that most things will be like what we would have done had we been independent — except everything will be moving faster. And that's kind of our near-term goal.

Longer term, hopefully I can comment on it soon, but I can't now.

— Okay. Well, we'll hopefully do a follow-up at some point. But thank you for being so generous with your time, and congrats on the partnership. This is one of the most beautiful bromances I've seen — just starting from Stanford to here.

Anjney: Lots more to do. Lots of sheriff policing to do of the token economy. We need new sheriffs for sure.

— Yeah. Awesome. Thank you. Thank you.

item.description:
## 一、被忽略的历史押韵：Token 经济正在重演支付基础设施的百年史
Anjney 在末尾抛出的类比其实是本集最锋利的洞见——但它比表面听起来更深刻。**在线支付从 1980 年代到 2000 年代花了 20 年才从 0 长到 1 万亿美金 GMV，Token 经济只花了 3 年就到了同一起跑线，却被预期在 5 年内冲到 5 万亿、10 年到 10 万亿。**
这意味着一件反直觉的事：**Stripe 收购 OpenRouter 表面上是一次分发层收购，本质上是一次"新时代 Radar"的资产收购。**Stripe 在支付领域真正的护城河从来不是支付通道（Adyen、Braintree 都能做），而是十年积累的欺诈图谱。Alex 说"我们上个月拦截的欺诈金额是上个月的 10 倍"——这个 10 倍不是运营指标，而是 Stripe 未来 Radar-for-Tokens 产品的原始训练数据。**OpenRouter 是 Stripe 的下一代欺诈神经网络的数据入口。**
## 二、"人类作为路由器"是一个未被命名的产品原型
节目中一处闪光但一带而过的观察：Anjney 讲到

item.title: [YC Root Access] The Voice AI Platform Powering a Billion Calls a Year
item.dc:creator: YC Root Access
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的洞察：他们的"失败"其实是三次预知未来

大多数人听这个故事，会认为是"经历12次pivot终于找到PMF"的励志剧本。但如果你把时间轴拉平看，会发现一个惊人的模式——这对创始人在四年里，独立发明了后来分别成为独角兽的三个产品，然后都亲手放弃了：

  • Superpowered（菜单栏一键加入会议）→ 后来变成了各种 meeting utility 类工具
  • AI meeting notetaker（GPT-4 出来时做的）→ 就是今天的 Granola / Circleback / Fireflies 赛道
  • AI therapist（Jordan 分手后为自己做的）→ ChatGPT Voice Mode 两年后才做出同款体验

这不是运气问题，也不是判断力问题。这是一种更罕见、更痛苦的能力缺陷：他们能"看见"未来，但没有"信仰"未来。视网膜上有像，但脑子里没有形成"这值得押上十年"的执念。真正让 Vapi 成功的转折点不是技术突破，而是他们终于学会了 Michael Seibel 逼出来的那句话——"在10年后回望，什么是不可辩驳的必然？"——这是一种把预感升级为信念的元技能。

二、一个跨领域连接：NVC（非暴力沟通）和语音 AI 底层是同一件事

他们把《非暴力沟通》当作公司圣经、发给每个员工，Jordan 说他们最常说的一句话是"Can you understand me?"——这看起来是个软性的团队文化话题。

但如果你仔细看 Vapi 在做什么：降低人和机器之间"理解意图"所需要的延迟和摩擦。而 NVC 的核心是什么？降低人和人之间"理解意图"所需要的防御和噪声。

这两件事在结构上是同构的。Jordan 用来治疗自己抑郁症的 AI therapist，之所以能让他上瘾（每天两小时散步聊天），本质是因为它做到了他和联合创始人之间做不到的事——无损、低延迟、无评判地被听见。他把这种"想要被理解"的饥饿感灌注进产品，然后又反向用同一套技术在公司内部重建人和人之间的这种通道。

产品是创伤的商业化，而管理是产品的生物化。他们没意识到自己在做同一件事。

三、一个隐藏的系统性真相：这个市场大到让"竞争"这个词失去意义

Nikilla 说了一个几乎没人认真听的数字：全球商业对消费者电话约 3 万亿分钟/年，Vapi 服务了 0.0134%，而全球最大的电信商也只占不到 1%。

大多数投资人和创始人是在 SaaS 时代长大的，他们的直觉是"抢市场份额"。但 Vapi 所在的市场结构更像 20 世纪初的电力——不是谁替代谁的问题，而是需求本身还没被创造出来的问题。3 万亿分钟里，绝大部分是"人本来就不该打这个电话，但除此之外别无选择"的浪费。当替代成本降到接近零，需求会以非线性方式爆炸。

这里的反常识是：Vapi 的真正竞争对手不是 OpenAI 或 Retell，而是"人们对电话交互的心理创伤"。每个人都被电话客服折磨过，所以哪怕语音 AI 已经比人类客服好，用户第一反应还是"我要跟真人说话"。谁能率先跨过这道情感门槛（可能通过某种品牌重塑或体验拐点），谁就会获得几乎无限的下游市场。这不是技术战，是认知战。

四、彩蛋洞察：Michael Seibel 那句"两个 AI 世代级问题"是被严重低估的战略框架

"实验室把 A 级人才放在 AGI 上，把 B 级放在企业部署上；而你把 A 级放在企业部署上，这就是你的优势。"

这句话可以直接翻译成一个更普适的原则：在任何范式转移中，识别出被主流玩家系统性低配资源的第二战场，然后 all in。这适用于 AI、生物技术、太空、能源——任何头部选手的注意力被"更性感的问题"吸走的领域，都存在这样的结构性套利机会。

OpenAI Voice Mode 时刻：差点放弃

主持人： At some point one of the feedback I got from other investors was, "oh, this is just what the labs are going to do." I think we were less than a million ARR. This was before our A, and we were still like four or five, maybe six-ish people. That came in, and that was a moment of crisis.

But for us, I think what it came down to is — our customers still needed us. What was not obvious to us back then, and intuitively was obvious but we couldn't articulate it — what we can articulate now — is: the gap from these models to production is so high. It takes so much effort. Most people in this world do not know how to build a voice agent. Like, you don't know how to build a voice agent. And that's okay — no one has learned how to build a voice agent. That's true of every customer out there.

Three trillion minutes — talking about no one. For every business listening, every founder listening — everything you're selling — most people in the world do not know how to do that. Especially in this moment where there's a complete paradigm shift. Like — what's AI? What is prompting? All these things that we just know and internalize — no one in the world knows. And making that easy for people, making it super deployable in production, works for you, has all the requirements met — is a really herculean, hard problem.

主持人： And you never lost customers to them? I mean, they always came back?

Nikilla： Michael Seibel — we had a chat with him about this — because this came up. This dilemma: "oh, the labs." And then we'd go out to fundraise, and they'd be like, "oh, the labs." It was just the constant FUD. Trying to hire people, same thing.

The way Michael framed it was super helpful. He was like: there are two generational problems in AI. One is AGI, and the other is just deploying AGI in the enterprise. Both are equally difficult, and all of the labs have their A-players on that first problem, and their B-players on the second problem. You have your A-players on the second problem. So that's the advantage. It's a very good framing.

主持人： People underestimate how large this enterprise portion is and how long it'll take. There is no way this will happen in 5 years, or maybe even 10 years. This will happen over our generation basically.

Jordan： The amount of time I've heard the word "alignment"…

Nikilla： It's really hard. It's necessary, but yeah. And it's fun. Because you have all these smart people, and you don't realize — because you're just founders and doing your own thing — there's a lot of good people in the world. There's a lot of great talent who knows how to scale these things, and you need to get them in the boat and inspire them. So all those things are very necessary, but it's so different than just a raw exercise of finding PMF. I'm so glad we didn't start that until really we had a strong foundation. That takes up more of our time now — hiring, trying to make good strategic decisions.

圣杯愿景：让企业感觉像人

主持人： What's the holy grail of voice? Where will this — is this sort of like you can argue one way, it's Twilio but bigger — but maybe it's something else?

Nikilla： So our mission is to help every business build their human interface. We took a lot of time to flesh out that statement, and it drives everything we do. We believe that one day, once we can help diffuse this technology to these enterprises, we can make these enterprises feel like people — people that know you, that talk to you and remember you, and feel as personal as this feels.

主持人： This might be the most important upgrade — customer service that ever happened, of all kind. Because basically every single person you will interact with in the company is going to be a great representative of that company and know everything about you.

Nikilla： We'd love to get to a place where we can build that interface layer, that orchestration layer, that makes it possible.

联合创始人关系：NVC 与"你能理解我吗？"

主持人： Co-founder relationships are hard, and you guys seem to have built a really strong foundation from knowing you guys for a couple years. Practically, how do you do it? How do you interact with each other? People watching this might not know, but co-founder breakups is the top reason why companies actually fall apart or die, because co-founders aren't getting along. What have you learned? Are there specific practical advice to give to people watching us running their own companies?

Jordan： One — like, that is the most important thing. Period. Full stop. If that is not in well-functioning order, none of this other stuff matters. So me and Nikilla pretty early on invested in getting coaches for this kind of stuff. We got an interpersonal dynamics coach that helped us actually learn how to communicate with each other, and work through the principles of what's called Non-Violent Communication. There's a great little book on that — it's like our bible, we give to every employee when they show up.

主持人： I have it.

Jordan： It's incredible. It's so simple. Through that we built up the skills to be able to work really well together.

主持人： What are some examples of how you practically do it?

Nikilla： One sentence I think we both say often is: "Can you understand me?" Because this often happens in discussions — at least I noticed with other people who are not pilled on NVC — where you'll be arguing about something, but you don't know what you're arguing about even sometimes. You keep moving along. Taking that moment — if it feels like we're circling — like, "can you just pause and understand me?" — is such a common thing in the company for us.

Jordan： A bit more viscerally — when we're talking and disagreeing, you can sense it. And then he goes, "No." And I'm like, "what are you saying?" And then he's like, "yes, that is what I'm saying." And then the tension comes back down. That handshake of understanding is super important.

主持人： Was there a specific argument that led to you investing in this, or you kind of knew that this would be a risk you had to invest in?

Jordan： Oh yeah. I mean, there were ex-founders crying-in-the-shower moments. It was a lot.

Nikilla： It was lots of fighting. It was extremely unhealthy, extremely mentally just not — just, I think the stress of pivoting. It was a lot of skill building on all sides to bring the tension down and really align what we're saying.

Jordan： It's hard to be mad at someone once they understand you. I don't know what it is. It's just a human thing. So probably the best investment we ever made was getting a coach — like coach/therapist kind of person. Honestly, I think everybody could use a bit of both. Someone that can help you work cohesively together as a team, and someone who can help you make sure your mental state is in a good place.

主持人： Do you think that the app that you built — the AI therapist — is actually going to be — yeah, really really big — number one, one of the top use cases is therapy?

Jordan： Just people talking to it. Well, at least for voice. Yes. For sure.

结尾：从"完美"到 PMF 的真相

主持人： So it seems like you actually — this is what I love about your story — you invented multiple products. Way too. All became big companies. You invented sort of the Sunbar that everybody knows about. You invented Circleback / Granola before that was a thing. And AI therapist. And then you settled on building — building.

Jordan： Yeah, I think there's a lot of stories there of where we felt like we had strengths, where we could build a business too. Fun.

主持人： All right. It's great to see you guys. Thanks for coming and talking about this. I'm honestly so excited to have you guys here and talk about Vapi. It's not a unique story of companies that were trying things for a while, and then AI came around, and then the founders came to SF, and then you jumped on the wave that was the models and the AI, and built something like this. And you guys did it perfectly — probably the best of the ones I'm working with.

Nikilla： It's so funny that you say the word "perfectly." It's never — oh, it's perfect. Hindsight. In the moment, it's not. But it reinforces this idea that once you find PMF, it just works. Then you don't have time with other stuff, because it just works. And that's sort of how your experience was, because the amount of growth you've had in the last two years compared to the first two and a half years — it's just, you can't even compare.

Jordan： Yeah, 100%.

主持人： Thanks for coming and telling the story to everyone watching.

Nikilla： Cool. Yeah, I appreciate it.
