## 一、最反直觉的洞察：他们的"失败"其实是三次预知未来
大多数人听这个故事，会认为是"经历12次pivot终于找到PMF"的励志剧本。但如果你把时间轴拉平看，会发现一个惊人的模式——**这对创始人在四年里，独立发明了后来分别成为独角兽的三个产品，然后都亲手放弃了**：
- **Superpowered**（菜单栏一键加入会议）→ 后来变成了各种 meeting utility 类工具 - **AI meeting notetaker**（GPT-4 出来时做的）→ 就是今天的 Granola / Circleback / Fireflies 赛道 - **AI therapist**（Jordan 分手后为自己做的）→ ChatGPT Voice Mode 两年后才做出同款体验
这不是运气问题，也不是判断力问题。这是一种更罕见、更痛苦的能力缺陷：**他们能"看见"未来，但没有"信仰"未来**。视网膜上有像，但脑子里没有形成"这值得押上十年"的执念。真正让 Vapi 成功的转折点不是技术突破，而是他们终于学会了 Michael Seibel 逼出来的那句话——"在10年后回望，

item.title: [a16z] How to Spot Exceptional Talent Before Everyone Else
item.dc:creator: a16z
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、"只允许正面"不是让步，而是复刻了声誉的真实拓扑

产品明确说"这是一个只用来吹嘘的地方"——很多人会本能觉得这是内容审核上的懦弱。但仔细看，现实世界的声誉从来就是不对称流动的：赞誉走公开信道，批评走后台八卦。全球诽谤法几乎都把举证责任压在负面言论一侧，宗教里的封圣需要证人却没有"反封圣"程序，监狱里的名声更是完全靠"谁替你打包票"。cosign 不是在过滤声誉，而是在如实建模声誉本来的样子。真正被审查掉的不是负面信号，而是"人们说负面话时习惯用的隐蔽通道"——这个通道并没有被消灭，它只是没被这个产品搬到台面上而已。

二、这其实是一台皮格马利翁机器，不是发现机器

视频结尾提到 2009 年 Paul Graham 把 Sam Altman 列入"最好的五个创业者"。所有人都在把它当作"PG 眼光真准"的证据。但因果关系其实是反的：那次公开背书制造了 Sam 后来的机会集合，而不是发现了它。声誉不是对能力的测量，声誉是能力的因果输入——它决定哪些门为你开，从而决定你能做出什么。这一点跟诺贝尔奖引用模式惊人一致：早期引用最终获奖论文的作者会获得超额学术声誉，不是因为他们眼光独到，而是因为他们参与构筑了那份声誉。所以 cosign 的真实产品定位不是"人才发现引擎"，而是"机会分配引擎"——它决定的不是谁牛，而是谁被允许变得牛。这个区别很少有人愿意说破。

三、被埋在 David Prell 那句 quote 里的重磅指控

"我的 Twitter 账号比我的斯坦福学位更值钱。" 三位嘉宾轻描淡写地讨论了一下大学是"教育 + 网络 + 学分 + 社交"的捆绑包，就跳过了。但把它放在显微镜下看：Twitter 能替代的其实只有学分这一层——教育要师生反复辩证，社交要肉身在场，网络还得靠时间沉淀。所以 David 真正在说的是：大学最值钱的那部分，恰恰是学得最少的那部分。这是对高等教育系统一记轻声但致命的指控，也是 a16z 一边说"我们大爱高等教育"、一边刚刚开办自己学校的深层动机——他们看见了那个可以剥离出来单独定价的信号层，正准备把它变成产品。

四、跨界联想：这是硅谷偷偷回到了中世纪

正式合同体系无法胜任的场景，人类历史上一律退回到担保人网络——中世纪行会靠师傅担保学徒，修道院靠资深修士担保新人封圣，监狱靠老犯人替新犯人"背书"。共性是：当变化速度超过契约系统的处理带宽时，社会自动回落到熟人担保。硅谷不是发明了新东西，它只是快到没时间做完整尽职调查，被迫复用了一套非常古老的机制。cosign 在做的其实是给这套中世纪机制加上 API。这也解释了它的隐忧——凡是靠担保运作的系统，历史上都会滋生近亲圈层、恩庇政治、既得利益者卡位。行会有了徒工制却也有了行业壁垒，教会有了封圣也有了发放圣职的腐败。cosign 若成功，会不可避免地再演一次同样的剧本。

五、一个几乎没人指出的博弈论陷阱

嘉宾自豪地说"这就是抢先发现人才的赛跑"。但一旦声誉红利归属"第一个 cosign 的人"，博弈就会从"识别真正的强者"漂移到"识别别人将来会认为是强者的人"——这是凯恩斯选美博弈。时尚圈的 coolhunter、股市里的动量交易者、学术圈的早期引用者，全都掉进过这个陷阱：他们最终不再评估质量，而只评估他人的评估。cosign 的机制设计如果不引入担保责任的持久可见性（背书一个后来搞砸的人，你的名字要一直挂在那儿），就会不可避免地演化成一个镜厅式的二阶预测游戏。而讽刺的是，硅谷本身现在很多明星投资人的实际决策，已经在这么运作了——cosign 不是引入了这个问题，它只是让这个问题变得更清晰可测。也许这才是它最大的价值：它不是解决了声誉市场，它让声誉市场的失灵第一次可以被数据化审计。

📝 转录文本

Cold Open

"The most important skill in this industry or perhaps in the world is your ability to identify things before the market."

"There are so many people in the world who we want to meet who also want to meet us — and it's just an information problem."

"What's more impressive to you? Someone who went to Stanford, or someone who is followed by Patrick Collison, Elon Musk, Marc Andreessen?"

"A lot of people in Silicon Valley have a pretty high bar for who they're willing to publicly endorse."

"A lot of what we do — it's finding awesome people and connecting them to our companies, otherwise kind of getting them in the a16z network. And it allows us to really extend all that network and all that value and all that trust — and really that reputation that transfers and builds over time."

"There's this novel quote I love: 'Be so good that people do business through you.' In fact, if I co-sign two people, they might be able to meet and otherwise build something in a way that I enabled without even having to know about it."

"But it's always hard to match the needs and the skills at exactly the right time. What we've enabled is this…"

Announcing Cosign

We're super excited to announce cosign — a product that is around professional reputation for the startup community, and really just trying to be the most comprehensive directory of companies and people.

And I want to start with a story. My friend David Prell told me: he said, "My Twitter account is more valuable to me than my college education. Even though I paid, you know, a quarter million, whatever it is — my Twitter has given me more value to my career and also personally."

Now, we of course just launched our own school, so we are big fans of higher education. But I thought that story was profound because Twitter has been free for so long. And what he got behind it is of course: college is a bundle of education, network, and credential.

"And social life." Yes. [laughter] Of course.

Some of that is hard to recreate on Twitter, but yeah. The education — you learn from having conversations. The network — you meet people, you discover people. People are kind of proof of work: if they're interesting, if they're funny, if they build something cool, you can discover them.

Peer-to-Peer Credentialing

But the credential thing is really interesting, because here's a thought experiment. What's more impressive to you? Someone who went to Stanford, or someone who is followed by Patrick Collison, Elon Musk, Marc Andreessen?

People — I think most people — would say the latter, right?

And so this is kind of like peer-to-peer credential. Implicitly, although people also do this explicitly, it's a co-sign. It's an endorsement that this person is worth tracking. It's a public signal that this person is worth following.

We think there are lots of other ways to express that signal, and create this kind of reputational benefit that these people get — which is really an exhaust of "this person is not even trying to give them reputational benefit; they're just trying to read what they write, and the exhaust is this endorsement."

And this endorsement — if you're followed by these people — now your doors are open. People want to also read what you say. They want to work with you. They want to invest in you. They want to have you as part of their team.

There's benefit to the receiver, but there's also benefit to the giver too — because if you're the first person to discover someone, well, that's kind of how Silicon Valley operates. You're going to be able to hire them quicker, you'll be able to fund them quicker. And the cool thing about Silicon Valley is you don't know who the next big person is going to be. Sometimes they're 18, or they come from a no-brand school. So we're all in a little bit of a race to discover talent before anybody else.

Zack Frenkel has done an amazing job — so many people have done amazing jobs of building a reputation for discovering people. And the benefit talent gets is: they think, "Oh, I can get king-made by them." If Josh Elman or Olivia invests in my company, that's a signal to the market. Angel investing, or investing from a venture firm, is one way to express a co-sign or a signal — but a lot of people aren't founders, and a lot of people aren't investors. So we think there are lots of other ways to express this signal.

Three Kinds of Endorsements

Really curious as you've been building cosign — what are the kinds of endorsements you hope to get from the platform?

We want, on every profile, to have at least three:

1. Who shaped your career. Because we think this sort of mentor economy is what Silicon Valley runs on. If Josh Elman is my mentor, that means he put — which was true, actually [laughter] — you know, when I was a young person Josh spent a bunch of time with me. And that's a signal to other people that I'm worth other people spending time with too, because if you respect Josh, you respect me by association. And again the benefit to you: you get to be known for discovering talent early.

2. Who would you work with anywhere / who have you been in the trenches with. Because it's hard to tell from existing platforms — as you were saying the other night — who are you really in the trenches with, who have you really built bonds with, who would you go to war with, who would you work with no matter what you're doing. That's a much more granular signal than "do I follow them," which could mean any number of things.

3. Person to watch. Who do you think is going to really be emergent, ascend?

And we rank-order these too. The platform just started, so most of it's fair game, but if you build a great investor profile, it takes many years — and then you get credit for doing so. We think you can do that around people too. So you can say, "Hey, I think Olivia is going to be one of the greats. I'm going to put her on my person-to-watch list."

It's actually funny. I did this experiment seven years ago where I emailed a few hundred people — you were definitely one of them — and I asked them for their person to watch. I was just checking today. One of them was Russell Kaplan, who's now the president at Cognition. He was like a 22-year-old just engineer at Tesla. So there's actually signal in that too.

We're also excited for people to do it for companies too — like, what are the companies at seed that you think are going to be great? Because of course, if you're able to, you can express your conviction with your money — but not everyone's an investor. This is almost like fantasy investing, or social capital investing.

The Value of Conviction

I love this idea. I have long felt this — but as I've invested now for almost a decade, I believe it more and more every week, every day, every month: the most valuable data in all of Silicon Valley is who has conviction, and who can give you a real read on a person.

For so many decisions — who do you invest in, who do you hire, what company do you join — there's such information asymmetry right now. Our job investing every day: we are pinging people saying, "Hey, do you know anyone who worked with this person?" And we do it every day and we still have to work really hard to find that signal.

So — how can someone who is maybe evaluating between five startup job offers get that level of…? You just can't, especially if you're an entry-level engineer. And yet that could be the difference between joining a complete rocket ship and a company that isn't doing as well. The data has to be handled carefully around who says what about who, but I think there's a massive massive opportunity to add so much value to people's lives and careers.

The Sunday Startup Newsletter

Talk about the newsletter you did — because I think it's incredible stuff.

My twin sister Justine also works here at Andreessen on our infrastructure team. We have both been in venture for basically a decade now, and at our very first venture role we started a newsletter that we ran every Sunday for I think six and a half or seven years.

Subscriber. — Thank you so much.

It was basically just aggregating startup job postings. The thesis was: we both went to Stanford, we ran a startup incubator at Stanford, and even before we were working at a venture firm, we had no way to differentiate between all these startups and founders — who is legitimate, who's not, who's the most exciting. So we said: okay, we have some inside information now. Let's curate a list of the companies that we think are worth joining for young people.

And it really built up a real community, because people appreciated it — you can't get that information outside of Silicon Valley. We had a network of scouts on campuses that we recruited, and some of those people are now founders that a16z has invested in. They're all running fantastic companies in fantastic places.

That was the less-scalable version of this kind of network. And I'm excited for more people to have the ability to put their name behind ideas.

Signal in a Noisy Market

One thing I'd add: as it gets easier and easier to start companies, as it gets noisier and noisier out there, it's actually getting harder for people to do what you're describing. This kind of signal is more important than ever.

If you think about the average student graduating out of Stanford today, they're looking at the startup market and they have to rely on the signals that are given by firms who are investing — but even before that, given by people like you and hundreds of others we hope to empower here.

An example I love to point to on the site: Packy McCormick has always had a lot of very good signal around the deep tech and the vertical integrators in particular. Packy has 37 companies that he's chosen. He says, "These are the companies if you want to get into the space." In a way, he's co-signing some of his reputation against that company. He's saying: I trust this company. I'm putting my money where my mouth is. I'm writing about them. And I think that if you wanted to start your career off, these are the ones.

So it becomes a sort of living directory of companies and of people that are worth paying attention to — and free. Crunchbase, PitchBook cost money, etc. They're great products, they have to be businesses, but we have the luxury of being able to just offer this for the startup community.

A Positive-Only Product

We want it to be the most valuable place where people can see who invested in what, what is Olivia's set of deals, the most reliable company information — who are the co-founders, who are employees, what are the products they shipped.

One thing we've decided: no product can be all things to all people, and there are trade-offs. This is just going to be positive. This is going to be a place where people brag. It's going to be accurate — but…

How often do you go to someone's LinkedIn and text someone: "Hey, you're connected to someone on LinkedIn, can you tell me about it?" And they're like, "Ah, I don't really know them." We're going to have much more granular information to make sure there's real signal there. That is one product decision we've made.

Investing Your Own Social Capital

David — this is something we experimented with seven years ago and decided not to pursue because we got busy with other stuff. What has always struck you about this idea — the need for it, what we're really trying to do here?

One thing I've always believed: the most important skill in this town, or in this industry, or perhaps in the world, is your ability to identify things before the market. And those things — if you're an investor, it's companies. If you're a hiring manager, if you're a founder, it's people. Sometimes it's products. If you're in charge of procurement for a growing company, maybe you need to identify which product is better for the market. But there's no way of recording that. There's no hipster leaderboard that says "this person found this coffee shop."

For angel investors, of course, they want to be non-consensus and right, and they're rewarded for doing so — I can invest in your pre-seed round; if I'm right, then it's lucrative for me.

One of the things that's always drawn me back was the idea that I can't invest my personal social capital in you. I am very willing to make an introduction for you. If I really really believe in someone and no one else has heard of them, I can make an introduction to, say, Josh Elman, and he will hopefully take that introduction because he sees me putting my reputation against it. He has no idea who this person is, but he knows that David thinks highly enough of them to take a chance.

The thing that stood out the first time around, and that we're really trying to lean on coming back: when I co-sign something, I take it seriously. I want that person to be able to take the co-sign I've given them — and they might be able to go straight to Josh, they say "Hey, David co-signed me," and Josh might reply to that cold DM. That sort of lubricates the wheels of social capital, and could empower a lot more people to achieve a lot more.

There's this novel quote I love from a long time ago: "Be so good that people would do business through you." In fact, if I co-sign two people, they might be able to meet and build something, or otherwise hire each other or invest in each other, in a way that I enabled without even having to know about it. Which is very exciting.

The SV Angel Conference Story

Related to that — I want to talk about more features of the product. Sort of the more granular ways of expressing reputation.

One of the best events I ever went to was this SV Angel conference in like 2018. Before I went to the event, they had this list of 150 people that they sent out. Everybody was a baller, and they said: swipe who you want to meet, who you want an intro to. I swiped on almost everybody — I was up and coming, eager to meet great people. And basically if they swiped right on me, then we would get an automatic intro: "You guys have full context, you should chat."

I ended up meeting with most of those people, and they became really great friends and collaborators. Of course I couldn't have met 40 people at an event and had deep conversations, but that event provided the context for us to become friends and collaborators.

I say that to say: there are so many people in the world who we want to meet, who also want to meet us — and it's just an information problem.

If you can reduce the friction to make that introduction — because right now it's "I have to DM them, but I have to think about something to say, are they interested, I don't know" — but this is just sort of passive: "here are people I would meet."

What we've enabled is a bit more granular. It's not just "I want to meet them" (though there is that) — it's also "I would fund them if they start a company" or "I would hire them if they consider leaving." There's a lot of people I would hire, but I can't reach out to all of them; it might be inappropriate, I'm too busy, and I'd only want to talk to them if they want to join me. Having more granularity around professional intent, passively, with no risk — because there's some cost in sending a DM: rejection, time — if they also express interest, then it's an introduction with high intent that can unlock a lot of good stuff.

Everyone Becomes a People-Matcher

That conference example is so interesting because I feel like the other takeaway is: we can all be people-matchers now with a product like cosign.

In all of our jobs, we meet so many people every day. I often meet someone and I'm like, "They are awesome. They have this really specific skill set." Then I meet someone else three months later who's looking for that skill set, and I have to figure out — remember this person, check if they still want the intro, make the intro. That store of information, somewhere more persistent, that can work across time, is really really interesting.

I agree completely. So much of what we like to do — both as investors and around Silicon Valley — is make these connections, but it's always hard to match the needs and the skills at exactly the right time. Being able to codify this: "Here are the people I think are truly great designers." "Here are the people I think are truly great PR people who can help you through a crisis." "Here are the mentors I go to when I face a career decision."

Being able to actually endorse that now, and have it available so that when you're looking for that, you don't just have to go: "Josh — who can help me think through this decision?" — and I have to see who I've recently talked to. I can go back and say, "Hey Josh, I'm looking through those co-signs and you said that this person really helped you in this one situation — do you think they'd be open to helping me?"

It allows us to really extend all that network, all that value, all that trust. And yet still, you're trusting me to try to make that introduction. It's not that any of us want to say, "Hey, everything's open to everybody." It's really still part of the trusted community and the reputation that transfers and builds over time.

Private Signals × Public Signals

Building on something Eric said — the private signal is one core piece. What you're talking about here is, in a way, the public signal. We've built both.

The product is so fun — you can go rabbit-holing around. It's a bit like Wikipedia, clicking from link to link to person to profile to company to investor and back again. As you go, you're collecting — maybe it's Pinterest that I'm going to put this person on my personal, private list of people I want to work with in the future. And I'm going to put this person on my public list of designers that I rate.

Every time a founder comes to me and says, "David, I need a new designer, I need a growth guy, I need an engineer," I can say — well, do I consult my private signals, or do I send them my public list? Hopefully everyone has this habit: if I really believe in someone, I'm putting them on my private list. It's utility both ways. It tells them that I believe in them, it tells their network I believe in them, and it's also something I can use — I can turn around and give it to a founder or someone I respect. I can shortcut the work every time someone asks a question.

Two-Sided Matching Across Time

What's so interesting to me: there's this timing discrepancy that happens in networks. I'm like, "Oh my gosh, I know this person has been trying to get their startup off the ground; this other startup would love to merge with them or welcome them to the team." But if I go to that founder and say, "Hey, are you thinking about exiting your company?" — that's a big risk. It could be offensive or insulting; maybe the company is working and they want to keep going.

So the idea of a two-sided network where there's information on both sides, and they can match when the time is right when both indicate — really really great on hires, acquisitions, job changes, tons of things.

The company-to-company one — I didn't even think about, like, I would buy stuff. [laughter] We'll get to product features tomorrow. — We just extended the roadmap.

Feed = Questions + Announcements

We thought a lot about: should there be a feed? What is on the feed? Is it free-form? Josh helped us really nail down the focus of the feed to be around questions and announcements.

Announcements is so interesting because we think a way to differentiate there is to make reputation durable. A lot of reputation is built on social media, but it's ephemeral. When Josh joined the firm — he wanted me to focus on other people, but you're such a good example — a lot of people came out of the woodwork who've been working with him for a long time, but who maybe hadn't publicly said anything recently because they didn't need to. They said, "Wow, I really endorse Josh. You should work with Josh. Josh helped me in my career." I said that, Nikita said that, a bunch of other people said that. Some people saw it, some people didn't. But that type of stuff is so valuable, and should exist on someone's profile the first time you look them up.

So for us, any announcement is going to be tied to their durable reputation. When companies fundraise, when people switch jobs — these are opportunities for co-signs, for endorsements.

On the question side, it's this thing we were talking about earlier: "Who's the best comms person for this?" "Who's the best angel investor in fintech?" "Who are people I should work with for this?" Very specific questions of some person or company or product you're looking to either surface to you or learn more about. And in that way it will also build durable reputation, because you get added to a list through that.

Celebrating the Invisible Work

I see a lot of great comments for you, for Olivia, for David — but they just get lost. This idea of tracking those co-signs and making it feel like this fundamental network of Silicon Valley, of the tech industry, is really powerful.

Do you know the meme where the guy's walking into a party as a stick figure and he's like, "They don't even know that I got a baller co-sign"? Like — Marc Andreessen wrote a blog post about me joining the firm. That's pretty dope. [laughter] I want that on my profile. I want the first thing when you think about me to be "Marc endorsed her professionally."

Honestly, it wasn't until we actually hooked up the internet fire-hose to this product that I realized how many of those moments there are. Every day: fundraising announcements, talent transitions. Thanks to our good friends at X, we're plugged into a lot of those. Whenever somebody quote-tweets an announcement or replies with a genuinely thoughtful, positive comment — we're filtering them — those are pulled through, from a person, on the profile of the person the comment came from, and it goes to the person it's about.

The reason it's all positive is because products have to win on some dimension, and this product is going to win on people using it to show off — in a good way. Like, this represents the full manifestation of what I'm capable of, on a personal level and on a company level.

It's about celebration. So much of what we do — there's so much hard work that goes into making every single product. It's a toil of somebody's love, their idea, the coding they wrote or maybe worked on with their agent now. But putting that out in the world is a very vulnerable moment. "Do you like what I've tried to make?" We need to celebrate that effort. There's plenty of places for critique — we see all that too — but that doesn't need to be recorded for posterity in the same way.

One thing that's interesting: a lot of awards and a lot of shine go on founders — justifiably so. But a lot of other people build the companies too, and are critical to those companies, and they're unknown or not celebrated to the same degree. This is an opportunity to do that as well.

Positive signal is going to be incredibly informative, because a lot of people in Silicon Valley have a pretty high bar for who they're willing to publicly endorse. If you endorse someone who's not great, that reflects poorly on you — natural reputation-cyn mechanism. There's a whole thing about "do you share something you haven't even played with?" — "have you even read the article before you retweet it?" The key: you'll get to know pretty quickly who's just spouting things versus "I've actually played with this, I've spent time with it, I've heard the backstory."

Flashback: The Rise Awards

I want to tell a story — or nudge Eric to tell it. One of the first times I heard of Eric, and then went on to meet Eric, was the Rise Awards — 2015, 2016, thereabouts. Over a decade ago now. Around this thesis that founders get a lot of publicity, a lot of credit, but it's actually the people who are the operators behind the scenes.

The Rise Awards were a series of awards meant to be for everybody else — for the engineers, the designers, the product managers. Josh was a judge, along with many others. We had thousands of submissions, and discovered and selected some great people because of it. We're going to bring that back in some capacity.

There's this phrase — "fear not the guy who has a thousand moves, but the guy who does one move a thousand times." [laughter] The samurai — the kick a thousand times. So — Rise Awards, cosign — a lot of these ideas have been in the ether for us for a while.

The thing that stands out: a lot of the Rise Award recipients got to know each other and built lifelong relationships through the retreats they attended, the groups they were added to. There's something around the connection too.

We often meet people who are spitting out of great companies to start their own — and often if you get really deep, if you call everyone they've ever worked with, it's like: "Wow, this person who was engineer number four was actually a huge determinant in this company being successful." But to your point about legibility, that's not something they can publicize. They're not going to be the face of every article about the company. And yet — I'd love to see them, when they leave that company to start a new one or go to another, carry that accomplishment with them. They can't really do that right now.

We're making the reputation market more efficient and more liquid. Efficient: there are people with amazing reputations, but not a lot of people know about it. Liquid: if it were known, a lot of people would want to hire or fund them. Fix that information asymmetry.

Long Talk on LinkedIn

Let's talk about existing platforms for a second. X — such a great platform, and the exhaust is so valuable. But there are times where I'm like, "Man, I wish I could just download my followers." Where a few thousand people liked this thing about joining my company — I wish I could see this. Why is it so difficult? It's not built for this use case of discovering people to work for. "Okay, you follow me — do you want to work for me? Do you want to invest in me?"

And then LinkedIn — it's such a valuable utility, we're on it all the time, and yet everyone hates it. We love LinkedIn. We love LinkedIn. Josh used to work there. LinkedIn is one of the most iconic products of all time. Marc famously defended it — I remember when they got acquired, only $26 billion, but a great outcome and iconic product. And yet people have frustrations. Even before the feed — some say the feed is cringe — people were like, "I wish there was just more we could do here."

I worked at LinkedIn back in 2004 and 2005 when we were just starting to form the network. Reid Hoffman, the founder, used to talk about it very much as three stages of the company: growth, usage, revenue. First, growth: figure out how to have the largest professional network, give everybody value even if they have nothing to do — for a lot of users, sign up, make your profile, don't do anything else for a while until something comes to you was a perfectly good usage. Then usage: build products on top of the network. The network is just the substrate — we need to go build a real job service. I helped launch the first LinkedIn Jobs. Then revenue.

The challenge: as we built the network, it was very single-signal — are we connected? At the early days, the beauty was: we really know each other. I'll vouch for Olivia — if David is asking me for an intro to Olivia, and Olivia says David's really good, will you take this intro? Great. Even better if you imagine this whole table — David asks Olivia, "Hey, can you introduce me to Eric?" Olivia says, "Josh, David's my really good friend. It looks like you know Eric — would you be willing to pass him on?" This idea of a trusted graph — I'm so happy to connect with you, and I'll pass you on to somebody else.

But over time it faded from that strength of connection to "yeah, we met once at a party, we high-fived, we had a good email exchange." Everybody got into collecting, and the challenge with collecting is it makes it much harder to figure out where the real signal is.

On the other side, it still is the iconic representation of who each of us is professionally.

One thing I remember when we were first building LinkedIn Jobs: the goal was to take a current job service where someone just applies and gets a resume, and go, "How do we use the power of your professional network to make it better?" Reid would push us: what is a social resume? When a job application comes in, it wasn't just here's who this person is — it was here's who this person is, and here's who else in your company might also know them, here's who worked at similar companies, here's who knows people who also worked at those companies. You wouldn't just get a flat resume — you'd get one annotated by who else can help you reach that person.

Then when you're looking at jobs, instead of a faceless job you're throwing your resume over the wall to — we put the hiring manager on. Their profile is on the job. You're going to get hired by this person, and here are the ways you might have connections to that person or to others who work at that company.

What has been missing though is the set of things that happens ephemerally through X — the set of things we all have but don't figure out how to strengthen and put into LinkedIn anymore. The true connection. The reason we were in the trenches together. You bailed me out of a crisis. When we can have that information in the network, all these use cases happen so much better.

The Granularity Problem

There's kind of a hierarchy of connections, and LinkedIn — for good reason — treats almost every kind of connection the same. Especially as products like endorsements on LinkedIn haven't really taken off.

For example: 90% of the time when I say to someone, "Hey, I saw you're connected to this person on LinkedIn, can you intro me?" I will get, "Hmm, I don't think I know them. Maybe I met them at a party. I'm not sure." So — did you actually know the person? Did you work at the same company? At the same time? On the same team or adjacent teams? Did you manage them? All of those are treated as one "connection or not connection." I love the idea for cosign of being able to break that into the granularity it deserves — cuz it's so much more useful.

AI, Endorsement Scarcity, and Broadcasting

Seems like the greatest time in history to be building products generally that can accumulate context that was otherwise unavailable. The social CV. Agents are an interesting way to accumulate a lot of context around a person.

A lot of what we do — both our investing teams and operating teams — is just finding awesome people, investing in them, connecting them to our companies. Right now a lot of it is scraping existing profiles and networks and doing manual work: who actually is the best strength of connection? That kind of manual work — that's truly external-signal-based, and it's binary versus really granular — is only going to get harder.

Recently I posted on LinkedIn: "Hey, I'd love to help my portfolio companies hire. If you want to work at a startup, fill out this Google Form." When it works it's almost harder — I get 2,000 results. That's going to happen to every person who posts a job or any opportunity. It's going to be 2,000 now, 10,000 a month from now as browser usage gets better, 100,000 as more people use browsers. So — how do you even, using Astra at maximum strength, sift and sort?

In an age of endless outreach and interest with AI, the scarce thing is the human endorsement, the human conviction, the human knowledge.

We've sort of gotten to a place where there's only broadcasting networks to the whole world, or group chats with 50 people. There's not really a much more vetted 10,000-person community. That's where we are to start — growing slowly, so that when you put out a post you'll be more confident in the signal that comes in.

What LinkedIn Still Misses

Some things I wish LinkedIn had: - A MySpace Top 8 for business — who do you have trenches with, who do you talk to regularly, who are mutuals, how do you know them, how'd you meet, what do they think about you. - More context on the relationship, more context on people's reputation.

LinkedIn is about personal identity. We hope cosign is about professional reputation. LinkedIn says it's people you know. Twitter is people interested in knowing you. We hope cosign delivers both, in a more granular way.

At the same time — to give props to LinkedIn — it started 20+ years ago, and no one has even come close to competing with it in any capacity. Charles Hudson, great investor, wrote a blog post 12 years ago: "Where are the LinkedIn competitors? It's time to disrupt." We've seen tons — we backed some at the firm individually — people tried crypto, all sorts of different incentives to break LinkedIn, and it's just fascinating. I was joking when I said everyone hates it. People use it obsessively, yet they have low NPS on it, and they know a better version can exist — and yet it's been impossible to disrupt.

But I think the real thing with LinkedIn is that NPS is actually really high for the people who aren't actively in the flow. LinkedIn's always served two audiences: people who want to find people, and people who want to maybe be found at some point. All of us would love to be found for the right opportunity. Not a lot of us might be actively unhappy — we used to talk about the mildly happily employed. They like what they're doing, they're not in urgent need to do something else. But if the right thing popped, they might consider it.

For those mildly happily employed people, they aren't constantly checking LinkedIn. But if you're in sales, BD, venture, an investor — you're using it all the time. That was special. And moving hundreds of millions of happily employed people who are maybe open to the right opportunity — that's the kind of network effect that really sticks. As you're building, think about a 20-year network effect.

We've looked at and invested in some attempted LinkedIn killers. What LinkedIn does remarkably: switching costs are very high, both because they're famously good at bot detection [laughter] — so you can't scrape it in real time, and whole businesses are built off scraping LinkedIn and selling that data — and because it's such a tight and dense network that ultimately, if it's something as important as your career, you're going to want to be on the platform where everyone else is.

That said, there's a massive opportunity when there is new information or new value to be gleaned — high-quality endorsements and high-conviction people. Generational shifts. And niche — the hyper-niche that needs its own LinkedIn. For example, GitHub is arguably a better LinkedIn for engineers than LinkedIn itself. Is there an emergent niche here? The individual trying to build their reputation as a talent scout? A founder who wants to break through?

What gets me excited about cosign isn't that it has to be a better LinkedIn — it's that it pulls together all this information that's already latently happening in our industry. Silicon Valley is so special for this pay-it-forward, this belief in somebody — the stuff we talked about at the beginning. Someone who may not have had a previously strong reputation, but has an insight, an idea — that alone can gather momentum and change the world. If cosign works great and it only serves the tech community, that's a huge win. If other communities and industries figure out they should take part in this too and bring some Silicon Valley energy to more places, even better.

Wikipedia, AngelList & the Cold Start

Eric from Benchmark had this comment on the Patrick O'Shaughnessy podcast where Patrick was asking him about every category, and he's like, "It's all going to work — everything is going to be huge. Not every company, but as an index, every category." We've come to a similar conclusion. When people say, "Does the world need another podcast? There are too many podcasts" — and yet another great podcast comes in and it doesn't kill the others. It just all works. Everything that's great works.

Similarly — we just launched a school. Stanford's going to be fine. Our thing's going to be great. LinkedIn's going to be great — it's going to keep doing its thing. We're inspired by them.

We're also inspired by AngelList — 10 years ago when they owned the investor graph, really really focused on the startup community — companies, investors, and talent. They made a series of other bets that made them focus on other parts, or deprecate the free public social network that used to exist. We think it's an opportunity to bring that back.

We're also inspired by Wikipedia — in terms of how we're going to do this. One: people want Wikipedia profiles, they're aspirational. Two: we're creating profiles for people. That's where we're starting, and we think people will be excited because we're bragging for them on their behalf in an exclusive way. If they don't want it, we'll take it off — but you're going to see your profile fleshed out with people giving you compliments, and people expressing their interest in funding you or working with you, even before you go to the profile.

Only because of AI can we generate all of this information on people and recreate a professional graph. If we didn't go that third-party route, we'd have the cold-start problem: it's the place people go to update their profiles — often people say "what's the daily behavior?" Well, we're brute-forcing it by covering every transition. We'll also have reliable profiles with more reputation benefits.

The best — for consumer products — the easiest way to acquire users is to tell them that someone else is saying something about them on the product [laughter], especially the Nikita Bier "your friends just answered this question about you" strategy, which worked so well three times. It wasn't possible before AI for a network as big as Silicon Valley. Now it is, which is awesome.

Someone was calling me today the Nikita Bier of founder communities. [laughter] That's a real compliment.

Everything being pulled in is coming from public sources — what people have posted, funding announcements. Really high-quality information spread across the publicly available internet, uniquely aggregated and structured in one place.

AngelList — very early in my career — was probably the first wedge I took into Silicon Valley. The ability to see which companies, which geographies, which people at those companies. For a long time it felt like it could be the LinkedIn for this little niche of people ambitious in technology. Then it moved away from that for a number of reasons, and that's been missing — a place you can go as a founder saying, "Which angel investors do I want to get to know over the next 6 months before my round?" A public utility.

An Invitation to Build Together

We're putting this out into the world. It's a thing we'd like to build with people — not something being presented as a fully finished perfect product. It's an invitation. To everybody who wants to come in and edit, submit an update to their own or someone else's profile. A real ask: let's build this thing together for everyone. Submit things to profiles, co-sign the things you endorse on people. And even if somebody has feedback — co-sign that feedback so it gets back to David and the team to keep improving things.

The Long-Term Positive-Sum Case

To end on a higher-level note — a lot of the industry, but also other industries, run on co-signs.

Paul Graham co-signed Sam Altman famously — I feel like 2009 or something. He said the five best entrepreneurs: Steve Jobs, three other people, and Sam Altman. At the time, Sam Altman hadn't had a huge exit yet, but that really gave him such a reputational boost. Him running YC, etc., was critical to him going on to build one of the most important companies of all time. Ben Horowitz cosigned Ali from Databricks. So many examples of people who got their co-sign from someone older and more senior and were able to rise up because of it.

Ryan Hoover, founder of Product Hunt, co-signed Eric and brought Eric on to become one of the leaders of building the community there. It was such a great endorsement of you early in your career.

I'm grateful for him. It's fascinating because one of the things that makes Silicon Valley so special is how much of a meritocracy it is — you don't have to pay your dues for 20 years before you're taken seriously. One of the most important intellectuals right now is Dwarkesh — he's 25 years old, has never had a job as far as I'm aware, just came to San Francisco, started podcasting, and someone — I don't know if it's Patrick Collison or Marc — a number of people going on his podcast early co-signed him. Then Zuck and others could go on. One of the most important founders is Michael Truell — a young guy in his mid-to-late 20s. One of the most important labelers is Alex Brenner — I think 24, 25. If you're talented, if you're smart in this industry, someone will discover you, co-sign you, and make your career. We hope that happens in ours.

The Critique — And Why the Long Game Wins

Talking about social capital and positive-sum mindsets, I think it's really important — there's a critique I wanted to talk about. Someone might rightfully say, "Why would I share this co-sign? This is my alpha. This is my private knowledge. Why would I tell you that person's good?"

If you take a very long-term view: sure, if that person is raising a pre-seed round right now and you want to do it — don't co-sign them right now. But the person you want to co-sign is the one raising a pre-seed round two years from now, five years from now. And when they do, they remember you. They say, "Yeah — the reason I'm able to raise this pre-seed is Olivia co-signed me two years ago. She helped me meet my co-founder, my five early believers. That's why I'm here today. And of course I'm going to call her first on my pre-seed round." If you turn it around that way and take a very long-term mindset — it's such a long-term game.

100%. The benefits accrue to you, in the sense that people always remember, by orders of magnitude more, the people who believed in them first. When Brian Chesky went public with Airbnb, who does he write about in the blog post? YC — Paul, his first investor. He's had so much investment throughout the book, so much more money, so much more time into the company. But you remember the first person.

If you are the first person — especially publicly, because that's where the value is — they will remember you, and more people will come to you.

Wrap

So let's wrap on that. Thank you so much. — Thank you. — Thank you.

## 一、"只允许正面"不是让步，而是复刻了声誉的真实拓扑
产品明确说"这是一个只用来吹嘘的地方"——很多人会本能觉得这是内容审核上的懦弱。但仔细看，现实世界的声誉从来就是**不对称流动的**：赞誉走公开信道，批评走后台八卦。全球诽谤法几乎都把举证责任压在负面言论一侧，宗教里的封圣需要证人却没有"反封圣"程序，监狱里的名声更是完全靠"谁替你打包票"。cosign 不是在**过滤**声誉，而是在**如实建模**声誉本来的样子。真正被审查掉的不是负面信号，而是"人们说负面话时习惯用的隐蔽通道"——这个通道并没有被消灭，它只是没被这个产品搬到台面上而已。
## 二、这其实是一台皮格马利翁机器，不是发现机器
视频结尾提到 2009 年 Paul Graham 把 Sam Altman 列入"最好的五个创业者"。所有人都在把它当作"PG 眼光真准"的证据。但因果关系其实是反的：那次公开背书**制造**了 Sam 后来的机会集合，而不是**发现**了它。声誉不是对能力的测量，声誉是能力的**因果输入**——它决定哪些门为你开，从而决定你能做出什么。这一点跟诺贝尔奖引用模式惊人一致：**早期引

item.title: [Business of Sport] Why are Spurs Still Bad, Man Utd’s Accounts Released, Hearn’s Rugby Takeover, & WTA in Big Trouble
item.dc:creator: Business of Sport
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、隐藏的镜像：热刺、曼联、切尔西、女子网球、英式橄榄球——都在犯"同一种错"

表面看这期节目是五个孤立的话题拼盘，但如果把它们叠在一张X光片上，你会看到同一副骨架：跳过"机器搭建"，直接往里灌汽油。

  • 热刺：以为问题是"没花够钱"，于是花 3 亿+ 请来 De Zerbi，赋予他 1980 年代式的"魔术师全权"。
  • 曼联：Ratcliffe 以为可以像收购化工厂一样重构一家足球俱乐部——低估了"文化—技术—青训"这台机器修复的时间常数。
  • 切尔西 Clearlake：把本该投向球场基建（一个能提升"发动机排量"的东西）的 20 亿英镑，烧进了球员市场，现在只能通过溢价 20% 的关联交易，来"保住估值面子"。
  • WTA：把 CVC 给的 1.5 亿美元一次性抵押未来的钱——本应用于国际化、品牌、产品开发——几乎全部倒进了奖金池。
  • Eddie Hearn 想干的橄榄球：主张"去掉薪水帽，让球员多赚钱"，而现实是 Prem 十支球队里六支资产负债表已经技术性破产。

出人意料的观察：这五个案例中，决策者都是极度理性、极度自信的商业老手——Levy、Ratcliffe、Boehly、CVC、Hearn 都不是傻瓜。但他们全都做了同一件反常识的事：把"支付端"（工资/奖金/转会费）当成了"驱动端"（收入/结构/文化）的替代品。这是一种系统性的认知偏差，我称之为 "支付幻觉"（Payout Illusion）——当一个系统的引擎升级太慢、太痛、太不性感时，人们会本能地转去调节"输出量表"，因为那能带来即时的、可炫耀的进度感。热刺球迷欢呼签约、WTA 高管在会议上收获掌声、Pollock 拿到 40 万英镑合同上头条——这些都是"糖果"，而不是"食材"。

二、跨领域连接：Brighton 的哲学 = 丰田生产系统 + 婴儿依恋理论

Fabian Hürzeler 那句 "We don't replace players, we find new solutions" 听起来像足球圈的鸡汤，但它其实是跨了三个学科的原理合流：

  1. 丰田精益制造：Brighton 提前 2 年就把"下一代 Van Hecke"外租到德甲/英冠去磨合，这就是Just-In-Time 的球员版本——库存在别人的仓库里成熟，需要时刚好交付到产线。
  2. 儿童发展心理学的依恋理论（Bowlby / Ainsworth）：Charlie 讲到"球员与理疗师、后勤、食堂阿姨的关系每周稳定持续，才能长出 mentality"——这是安全依恋（secure attachment）在企业组织里的直接映射。热刺的"旋转门"让每个新球员都处在回避型依恋的应激状态："我下一个会不会被赶走？"
  3. 组织行为学的隐性知识（Polanyi）：Vušković 案例里，Charlie 无意中触及了一件事——一个 18 岁被引入、22 岁被卖掉的中卫，带走的不只是他的身价，还带走了俱乐部四年间在他身上编码的隐性知识。Spurs 是在做知识资产的资本减记而不自知。

惊人的连接：Brighton 之所以能用一半的钱击败热刺，不是因为他们有更好的数据科学家（其实差距没那么大），而是因为他们把足球俱乐部当成了一个"人际生态系统"来运营，而热刺还在把它当成"一支球队" 来运营。这是一次元层级的认知差。

三、最让我意外的一个观察：Clearlake 已经"举白旗"了，只是没人听见

节目里两个人差点漏掉了这一段的重量级信号——Clearlake 已经把自己对切尔西股权的估值内部下调到 1x（也就是"投多少收回多少，不赚钱"），而且是在牛市里。

这在私募股权语言里几乎是一种公开的哀鸣。因为：

  • LP（有限合伙人）恨死的不是亏损，而是"锁死的死钱（dead money）"。
  • 一旦一个资产被内部标记为 1x，基金经理的唯一理性动作就是加速退出，而不是继续做多。
  • Boehly + Walter 的"体面退场"其实是 Clearlake 亲手买回的——Clearlake 是在为自己未来的退场路径打样。它需要一个"股权换手参考价"来向 LP 证明"资产还在流动、还有价值"。

跨领域连接：这个动作和 中央银行"锚定预期" 的操作是同构的。当央行不能真的把利率降下去、汇率稳住时，它会做声明式操作（jawboning）——通过一次干预性交易，让市场相信"价格是这个"。Clearlake 那笔 20% 溢价的股权回购，不是投资行为，是金融锚定行为。它保护的不是切尔西的价值，是Clearlake 自己在下一次募资时的叙事权。

这意味着：切尔西大概率会在 2028-2029 年之间被再次出售，比市场预期的 2031 早得多。而且卖方的谈判筹码正在每周被英超赛场上的比分持续稀释——这是一次典型的"时钟站在买家一边"的估值博弈。

一个贯穿性的元洞见：这五个案例其实共同指向一个更深的系统性真相——现代职业体育的"资本化"，正在遭遇它自己制造的悖论：钱越多，越难分配；分配越急，机器越坏；机器越坏，就越依赖钱来掩盖。这是一场缓慢展开的、正在被时代记录的"体育金融业的能力危机"。而 Brighton、Brentford 这些"小而美"俱乐部之所以逆袭，本质上不是他们更聪明，而是他们穷到没资格犯这种错。贫困，有时候是治疗傲慢的疫苗。

"The last point I want to make here, perhaps I don't understand vast amounts about rugby but I probably understand more than Eddie Hearn, is that who gets paid the big bucks in American football?" "The quarterbacks." "The quarterbacks. What's the nearest equivalent in rugby to a quarterback?" "The fly-half." "And who's the best fly-half in the world?" "Finn Russell." "Right. So you're talking about—give or take, there are two or three of them—but you're talking about one of the three most valuable players in the world in Finn Russell, who's playing in the key position that impacts, influences every single game. Totally different from someone who plays at flanker."

该由 Eddie Hearn 干什么？——"要认清自己车道"

"So Charlie, it's exactly to the point of really know your lane, right? For now. And this—what do I want from Eddie Hearn in this situation? Why were we excited potentially? Because as we said, and as he's—Rugby's biggest problem over the years has been its inability to make stars out of its biggest talents and those talents transcend boundaries. How many Jonah Lomus have we had? And even at that level, you still would say there was a huge amount left on the table for an athlete of his quality. Even your Johnny Wilkinsons and your Dan Carters—those players, they did a little bit. Johnny Wilkinson's probably thing was Hackett or, you know, was—" "Gillette, maybe." "Bryan Habana with Gillette, you know, but—" "One—and he hated when he came on the show. He said, 'Look, you've been one of the very, very few. I could count them on one hand. Athletes to break out of that.' He just couldn't admit it. He couldn't accept it. And that's part of the rugby player's mentality: it's team ethos. Individuals sticking their head above the parapet, being more than the sum of the team. It's a massive challenge."

"So what do I want from Eddie Hearn going into this? I want him to do what he's best at. I want him to try and build as much hype around some of these individuals as possible. I want him to get brand dollars in. But wanting to show people that rugby stars can be valuable, that money should be put into the broader sport of rugby, because if you can really capture what makes this sport good—i.e. the top professionals throwing themselves for 80 minutes a match into each other, there is something extraordinary still about what that product actually is. If you can show that, then you're going to give the sport, the Prem, Saints, whatever, a chance to improve on their revenues."

"You're trying to build a business case, right, before you come to the point of 'we have to pay everyone more.' And Charlie, why we laughed at this really from the start—and we're going to talk about it in a sec—is because there's just this assumption that you walk in, you say 'the players are great and there's all this attention, we must pay them more' is going to mean that the business of that sport improves. No. Let's be very, very honest here with this whole thing that Eddie has to understand coming into this: six out of 10 clubs are balance-sheet insolvent in the Prem. What that means is that their liabilities exceed their assets."

"And what happens when that happens, as we know in English football, it means that the owners have to put in a significant amount of cash to try and offset that. Now, rugby doesn't have the billionaire owners on the whole in this country, doesn't the Pro 14 in France, but that creates different problems for them. So if you don't have that, eventually you're going to be in a position where the owner cannot keep putting money in. And hey, guess what happens? A quarter of your division goes out of business in just a few years."

"So if you want to just give them free rein, if you want to leave it to the whims of ownerships who want to chase titles and try and do everything that they shouldn't do for good business on the pitch, then yeah, remove a salary cap and let them do that. But it's not actually going to help the sport and it's not going to help Pollock in the long run, because they're going to be sitting in an environment which ultimately is screwed."

"全球明星"的门槛：不是市场营销问题，是能力问题

"But you know, Charlie, I mean, stick to basics here. I totally agree with everything you've just said, by the way. That's absolutely correct. Like, if you are in a non-massive sport—and I'm sorry, rugby isn't. Football is. American football is because of the country it takes place in. Golf is. Rugby is not. Rugby's the next tier down from there. Cricket. Sorry—cricket is a proper global sport with massive audience. Rugby's the next tier down from there."

"If you're going to be one of the stars that breaks out, one of the prerequisites is you have to be one of the very best in the world. You've got to be able to actually walk the walk rather than just talk the talk. Henry Pollock is not even a guaranteed player for England, let alone in a world 15. He's definitely not a guaranteed player in the British Lions."

"The thing that makes me slightly queasy about this whole thing is that effectively you've got a situation where we're being told that a player who is not the very best at what he does should be being paid a vast amount because he wears a headband and because he dances around and this type of stuff. That is not how—I don't want to say, like, I love boxing and I love snooker and I love darts, but they are all slightly in the circus bit of sport." "Yes. And they are show—the show—" "They're a show, and they have always been done by promoters, which the Hearns are. They are promoters." "They're also individual—" "And they're individual sports as well. But again, you need to be the best. Luke Littler doesn't make money by being the 10th best player in the world. He makes money by being the best darts player in the world."

"In a team sport, which is not at the very very top, if you are going to get breakout stars, they are going to need to be players who are conspicuously stars. Jonah Lomu burst on the scene and he was the player. He wasn't the 10th best player, he was the best, and therefore everyone wanted to watch him because he was going to go and score three or four tries and run all over people. Now Henry Pollock is a very good rugby player, but he's got some way to go before he's in the Dan Carter, Johnny Wilkinson, Jonah Lomu type stratosphere."

"So I don't even think, taking on its merits as a sports marketing person myself, if I was advising rugby right now, I would not be saying go and stake all your bets on a player like Henry Pollock. Whatever he brings he brings, and that's great, fantastic. We've got to focus on the players who are the genuine global stars. We've got to focus on the ones who can actually inspire people by being something out of the ordinary on the pitch, by doing things that take people's breath away. And sad to say that is somewhat unlikely to happen with a flanker."

"It's probably the least glamorous position on the entire pitch pretty much, right? Doing the dirty work, doing the hard yards, doing the turnovers, making the tackles, all this type of stuff. It's going to be a fly-half. It's going to be a wing or a fullback or whatever it might be. If it is going to be a forward, it's probably going to be someone like Eben Etzebeth, who's absolutely massive—and Martin Johnson, who just carries that vast presence with them and wins line-outs and all this type of stuff. I think it's going to be super, super difficult to make a global star out of Henry Pollock no matter how charismatic he might be."

空杯之谈？

"So it just seems to me like a sort of storm in a teacup that's been blown up for no obvious reason. And it doesn't seem to have any underpinning. Like, if he does go in to see Prem Rugby and if he does go in to see the RFU and says, 'I should be running rugby. I could do it, like I run snooker, like my dad runs snooker and darts'—if I was at the RFU, I'd be saying, 'Right, can you actually explain what that looks like in terms of how that actually translates through into dollars for the sport?' I can see how you could make some more endorsements for your player, and by the way, knock yourself out. We've got no problem with that whatsoever. If you manage to get Henry Pollock a bunch of endorsements, great, fantastic. But if what you're saying is that we should build a marketing strategy around a player who might not even be selected—not sure about that."

"But you know, when he's talking about this, I think in this statement, he's talking bigger than Pollock. And that's the bit that just—again, as I said, I'm a big fan, big Matchroom fan, big fan of everything, but it doesn't mean you can walk anywhere and be a success in it. There has to be a respect. Now, do I think that the structures in rugby are correct and are well positioned and optimized? Absolutely not. But for you to be able to affect the change, you have to appreciate what the landscape actually is on the day you walk in. And I have met a lot of people who are either running rugby or have invested in rugby, and the thing that comes up every single time is: 'I didn't realize how hard it would be for me to do my job.'"

六、WTA：一场"用未来抵押现在"的破产危机

"Okay. Well, look, we'll watch with interest. We need to catch up about the Women's Tennis Association, right? The WTA. And it's actually along slightly similar lines. So just to go back on what's happened in the last few weeks: during the run-up to the US Open, which was two weeks ago, so the week or two before that—over the last month—there have been meetings between the Women's Tennis Association and representatives of the players and various others, which has been made pretty clear that the Women's Tennis Association is potentially on the edge of bankruptcy."

"And the reason it's potentially on the edge of bankruptcy is because they have done exactly what Eddie Hearn is advocating that rugby should do, which is that they've started paying their players far more than the revenues that they have would support. And they've effectively mortgaged their future to do so because ultimately if you're not getting the money to increase the pay through revenues, where do you get it from? Has to come from somewhere else and that doesn't come for free."

数字：明年 8–9 月现金见底

"So what actually happened in women's tennis—just to be clear on that, because this is not inflammatory. They've basically at the current financial rates they will run out of money by about August to September next year." "This time next year." "This time next year. Right. Yeah. That's what the figures show. 11 million in cash at the end—pounds, 11 million pounds in cash at the end of this year." "They got 11 million in cash at the end of this year and their current run rate is around about a 20 million pound loss a year. So in other words, they are projecting that next year they are basically going to be short of money."

一场"因追求平等而生的融资"

"What's led up to this is that I think it was about four years ago, 3 to four years ago, the WTA decided that they wanted to pay the players more. Right? It's not immediately clear to me why, because there wasn't an alternative tour. There wasn't a LIV equivalent that Aryna Sabalenka, Iga Świątek, and Elena Rybakina were about to go off onto. It more was to do with this vexed topic of equality of pay. 'We want the female tennis players to be paid the same as the male tennis players. Why? Because that's equality.'"

"Anyhow, in the absence of the revenues that would support equality of pay, what they did is they went to CVC—ironically the entity that also pumped a lot of money into rugby, English club rugby that is—and said, 'Can you make an upfront payment of $150 million, which is $30 million a year over five years, and in return for that, we will give you 20% of the proceeds from our commercial rights in a separate vehicle called—' in a separate vehicle called Ventures. So effectively they were doing what we call in football 'factoring.' They were saying, right, we will give a chunk of our future revenues away to you in return for you giving us money up front."

比 factoring 还糟：永续 20%

"But it's worse than factoring." "Oh, way worse than—" "It's way worse than factoring because in factoring, once you've paid back the original amount that was fronted up to you plus the interest—" "It's done. Yeah." "Goodbye. You're done. In this thing, it's 20% in perpetuity. So CVC get 20% of the proceeds of the WTA commercial side in perpetuity in return for 150 million bucks."

"Now, that's something that you might do if you're trying to build a new stadium, if you're trying to construct some other major piece of infrastructure, add value, or potentially if you're about to go on a massive new marketing push that's going to open you up into new markets, which is then going to drive bigger commercial revenues, which is then going to exceed the 20% that you're losing in future. Whatever it might be."

"Instead of which, they took CVC's money and they pumped it into prize money. The WTA borrowed effectively their future, mortgaged their future in return for short-term injections of cash into prize money. And that money has almost all now gone. The commercial revenues have not risen." "Of course not. Why would they? Why would they? You haven't done anything different other than say, 'Cool, there's a few events here where they value the joint events on the ATP tour.' ATP tour which generates nearly $300 million a year, and the WTA which stood 142, I think, last year. Hey, they value the women's game at 40% of the men's game, which is not fair."

三种赛事结构解释

"So I just wanted to just—you skated over that, because it's core to the buckets of events. You have the Grand Slams, which do have equality of pay. The Grand Slams are independently owned, massively profitable, make a huge amount of revenue, and slightly grudgingly, they've said, 'Okay, we'll give the women the same amount of money as the men.' You've then got a pot of tournaments which are much smaller tournaments that the WTA runs, which are standalone women's tennis tournaments over here, which have much lower prize money."

"There's then a bucket in between, which are the events outside of the Grand Slams where there is a men's event and a women's event. And this includes most of the biggest tournaments outside the Grand Slams—whether it be the Madrid Masters or the Miami Masters or Indian Wells and all these sorts of things. And it's at these events that what Charlie said has historically been the case, which is that broadly speaking, the women's prize money is about half that of the men's prize money."

"The reason being that those events have to make their own finances work. They can only pay what they make. They can't do more than that. And because most of their ticketing and most of their commercial revenue is linked to the men's side of that particular event, they have to be careful to pay enough of the prize money to the men."

"So the WTA have stepped in and used their pot of money that they've raised from CVC to bump up the prize money in those events, which effectively—think of it this way—under the previous dispensation, the likes of Sabalenka and Rybakina who win these events at the end of the year, their annual prize money level might have been 14 or 15 million. As a result of this 30 million a year that's been pumped in, those players have been earning 5 or 6 million a year extra each during that period. And that's where the money's gone."

结论：把明日的钱塞进今日最有钱球员的口袋

"So effectively the players of tomorrow are going to have 20% less commercial revenues in the tour that they're playing in, to pump up the prize money packets of athletes who are already the highest earning female athletes in the world now. It is bonkers."

"Charles, it's really—do you know, rarely do you actually get annoyed?" "You look sad." "I'm sad." "Well, do you know why I'm sad? Because women's tennis is great as well. It is the most successful—as a product, women's sport. I said to you when watching the Sabalenka–Raducanu match for the US Open final, I enjoyed more than I enjoyed the Shelton–Alcaraz match. You have seven of the top 10 most marketable, highest earning athletes—" "Female athletes." "Female athletes in the world in tennis. The only three that are in that top 10 that aren't are Eileen Gu, Nelly Korda, and Caitlin Clark."

"Yeah. The WTA have chosen to put money into the growth of those pay packets rather than the growth of the sport as a whole, to capitalize on all of this opportunity that comes from having athletes. We've just spoken about rugby's need to have talent that can really bring the value of the collective together. Tennis has that. Does. The WTA has six commercial partners. The ATP has 18. The WTA does not have a single female-only brand behind it to capitalize on it."

"Meanwhile, Aryna Sabalenka is walking around the US Open with about $1.5 million worth of jewelry on her, proving the value that she has, the power that she has to brands. Why is that exclusive to individuals when the WTA could bring some of this value into the broader collective game now?"

CVC 的失职：没有条款保护

"To do this, as you said, to take that investment would make sense if the ambition and structure and strategy was really clear on how we are going to develop this so that CVC—that money is not only going to help us be a better business but it's also going to increase the future value of your investment. So, I'm really also pissed off from the CVC side because how were there not stipulations that prevented this from happening? How did CVC not put something in place which said, 'you cannot put all of this money we are giving you into prize money'? Because what we need to see on this investment is an increase in what we are putting in."

"Well, there's a number of reasons. Firstly, was it 150 million in funds that are 16 and 22 billion size, recently? Is that a big enough investment that they really give a—really? Who knows? And within these plays when you're making them, right, they've also put 2 billion into La Liga." "Much more." "Much more. On a similar kind of basis—" "On a similar kind of basis, with many more strings attached." "Exactly."

对照 La Liga：条款怎么设计才合理

"So I just want to read that out. The injection—and this is on the La Liga site as well—when the deal was announced with La Liga: 'This injection of nearly €2 billion euros commits the clubs to allocating up to 70% of the funds to investments linked to infrastructure, international development, brand and product development, communication strategy, innovation and technology, and content development plan for digital platforms and social media. Up to 15% can be used to sign players with the remaining 15% used to reduce debt.'"

"Now, the WTA doesn't own stadia. So, front-up we can say it would be very hard for you to put that money towards an infrastructure play like we've said in football. But the rest of it—international development, brand and product development, comms strategy, innovation in tech—they could have had a strategy around all of that to improve the product 'women's tennis' owned by the WTA. They didn't."

"CVC made this mistake when they went into Prem Rugby and they bought 27.5% of Prem Rugby in 2018 or 2019—2018 I think—for 200 million, and they didn't put the protections in place to stop that money being spent in ways that do not grow the overall value of the sport. And unfortunately—and it was unfortunate when COVID hit—a huge amount of that money went to the OpEx and attempted survival of these clubs rather than the traditional growth capital that it was designed for. But there was nothing that CVC could do about it because there was nothing in the contracts that prevented that money being spent in those ways."

"给孩子十块钱"——一个让人心痛的比喻

"So from an investor's perspective, it drives me mad because, Charlie, it's a bit like a child. You give a child a tenner and tell them to go into a shop, they're walking out with a bag of sweets. They're just walking out with £10 worth of sweets. You know that. They're not going to go in and buy ingredients, are they? They're not going to go and buy what you need for dinner. No, because ingredients mean time. They take skill and knowledge to put together. Much better for you in the long run, but it doesn't give you that immediate hit and that feeling that makes you go, 'yeah, do you know what, I really enjoyed that.'"

"This is how I kind of look at that. You—the sports organizations—and it's not letting them off the hook, but you know, are they genuinely proving capable of managing this amount of money responsibly? I don't think so in a lot of cases. I really don't think so. If you're putting that money in, you have a responsibility. And as I said, you could look at this and go, do they really care? You know, it's one of those—they had big fund, they had a big exit from Formula 1 and there was a few of these investments that they've made off the back of it. Okay, let's just give it a crack."

"There's also the flip side, which is everyone hates the old models of private equity and they think they're asset strippers and they think they're bad money. Well, this type of behavior doesn't help the argument that institutional cash coming into sport is a good thing, because there is a responsibility when you do invest in these types of organizations."

"I think naive, maybe. Yes, but there is a responsibility that you have to the sports that you invest in, the fans that follow it, to actually try and do best by that organization, by that sport. And if it does—I mean, I don't know, short of them selling more equity and trying to find more value in this Ventures, which obviously is just going to reduce the value that they can extract from this—I don't know where the solution could lie. It's a sad state." "It is a sad state of affairs."

结论：奖金必然大幅缩减，可能引来"挑战者赛事"

"Sorry, a bit of a rant." "Yeah, it's actually 9 months in, that's the first time I've heard my ginger friend really go off on one. Normally he belies the reputation of red-headed people for hot temper. He's normally a very calm person, but he absolutely went off on one there. By the way, I totally agree with the gist of what he was saying."

"Whatever happens, there's going to need to be a significant reduction in prize money outside of the Grand Slams. That's absolutely clear. But I'm worried that even with that, with them having sold 20% of their future revenues, that the reduction in prize money is going to be very, very extreme and may even be getting to the stage where you do start to look at potentially a challenger of some kind coming up and saying, 'well, actually we don't need to carry that baggage of the past.'"

为什么这个故事没上主流媒体？

"Charlie, I don't know about you, I'm quite surprised that this hasn't got more attention. And maybe it hasn't got more attention in the main—and when I say attention, I mean the mainstream media attention. Maybe because it's just—it does sit in that uncomfortable area of you have to really reflect on the things that we've been pushing for, when people have been pushing for for so long, pushing against—" "And we've been pushing against purely for the reason that to be able to do this, as this shows, you have to have the business behind you to support those kind of changes. This is a total non-sequitur, say in professional sport."

"So just to make clear what happens in professional sport: people like me, who are operators, sit in the middle, and people who pay to watch either live in a stadium or on TV through their subscription—pays, they pass money to me and I then pass money to the performers. That's what it is. That's professional sport. And the more money that we get from ticketing and from TV rights revenue, the more money we can pass to the performers. And generally speaking, the operator who sits in the middle doesn't make very much if anything, and sometimes even loses money. Okay? That's just the reality of sports business."

核心谴责

"What you cannot do is start chucking money to the performers, which isn't justified by the ticketing and the TV rights. It's not just bad business in terms of putting your organization in a very precarious state. It's bad business because it means you're not confronting the fact that you're not making enough revenue. So you're not actually doing the hard yards of thinking, how are we going to drive more revenue because ultimately we would like to pay the performers more."

"Instead of which you're reaching for, as you put it, the sweet shop. You're saying, what's the short hit? And the short hit here is that various executives want to go to various conferences around the world and say 'equality of pay' and everyone claps and goes, 'Yeah, yeah, great, fantastic, equality of pay.' It's just meaningless. It's absolutely irresponsible."

"Well, it's meaningless if it means the end of the product itself." "Yes. Which realistically, if we're being—" "Well—" "As direct as possible—" "What they've done here is they've taken pay which should have been paid to players in 5 years time and forwarded it to players who are playing now. In what way is that responsible or ethical? It's not. It's absolutely terrible. Anyhow, there we are. Let's see what happens. I think for all of us who like women's tennis and watch women's tennis, we hope that they do sort it out. It just at the moment is looking pretty precarious."

收尾

"Thanks guys. Thanks as always for tuning in and we will see you next week. Thank you."

item.description:
## 一、隐藏的镜像：热刺、曼联、切尔西、女子网球、英式橄榄球——都在犯"同一种错"
表面看这期节目是五个孤立的话题拼盘，但如果把它们叠在一张X光片上，你会看到**同一副骨架**：**跳过"机器搭建"，直接往里灌汽油**。
- **热刺**：以为问题是"没花够钱"，于是花 3 亿+ 请来 De Zerbi，赋予他 1980 年代式的"魔术师全权"。 - **曼联**：Ratcliffe 以为可以像收购化工厂一样重构一家足球俱乐部——低估了"文化—技术—青训"这台机器修复的时间常数。 - **切尔西 Clearlake**：把本该投向球场基建（一个能提升"发动机排量"的东西）的 20 亿英镑，烧进了球员市场，现在只能通过溢价 20% 的关联交易，来"保住估值面子"。 - **WTA**：把 CVC 给的 1.5 亿美元一次性抵押未来的钱——本应用于国际化、品牌、产品开发——**几乎全部倒进了奖金池**。 - **Eddie Hearn 想干的橄榄球**：主张"去掉薪水帽，让球员多赚钱"，而现实是 Prem 十支球队里六支资产负债表已经技术性破产。
**出人意料的观察**：这五个案例

item.dc:creator: 投资TALK君
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、瓶颈迁移史：AI 最终被 19 世纪基建卡住了

过去三年 AI 的瓶颈迁移路径本身就是一个反讽的隐喻——H100（芯片）→ NVLink（互联）→ HBM（内存）→ 现在停在了新墨西哥州的一份天然气管道审批上。整个视频最容易被忽略但最惊人的一个事实是：人类最尖端的技术堆栈，最终被一份州级空气质量许可证和几段管道钢管卡住了。

跨领域连接：这几乎完美复刻了 2010 年代德国的太阳能革命——最终不是电池技术限制了转型，而是输电线路审批限制了扩容。每一次能量密度革命，最后败给的都是地方规划委员会。AI 表面上是硅+算法的战争，本质上正在变成能源+规划许可的战争。这也解释了为什么 GEV、Caterpillar、Bloom 这些"老经济"公司突然被拉进了 AI 定价链条——它们是新瓶颈的守门人。

二、"泡沫延缓论"——最反常识的市场自愈机制

本次分析最反直觉的洞见值得单独拎出来放大：Oracle 的执行失败，反而在系统层面降低了 AI 泡沫风险。

  • 直觉链：项目延期 → 营收往后推 → 坏消息 → 拉低估值
  • 但真实链条：需求端持续增长 + 供给端因物理/审批瓶颈跟不上 = 供需缺口继续存在 = "供给过剩"的泡沫论证据被削弱

这构成一个奇特的悖论：Oracle 越"不行"，行业整体越"健康"。市场在周四已经用 CoreWeave 和 Nebius 的上涨定价了这个逻辑——单个玩家的执行失败，反而是行业稀缺性的价格确认。这几乎是"负面消息=正面信号"的教科书案例，能看懂这一层的人才真正理解 AI 周期还没到顶。

三、Oracle 正在扮演"AI 基建的准主权信用"

更深一层、几乎没人明确指出来的观察：Oracle 在这套 SPV 结构里扮演的角色，与 19 世纪美国州政府为跨州铁路建设提供收益担保是同构的。

SPV 借了 180 亿美金，抵押品不是数据中心的物理资产，而是 Oracle 未来的现金流承诺。这本质上是把 Oracle 的公司信用证券化并注入基建融资链条——就像州政府用未来税收担保铁路债券一样。

由此推出一个尚未被主流讨论的问题：当 AI 基建融资规模持续膨胀到 Oracle 市值的相当比例时，Oracle 的信用曲线就变成了整个 AI 基建圈的"影子国债曲线"。这也是为什么那笔 180 亿贷款跌到 89 美分并不是简单的流动性折价——市场正在重新为"Oracle 作为 AI 基建准主权担保人"的信用打价。加息只能解释 2–3%，其余 8–9% 的折价是这个身份的估值重估。

四、被忽略的结构性真相：Oracle 的"影子资产负债表"

一个几乎所有报道都漏掉的会计洞察：Oracle 在整个木星计划里几乎没有直接资本风险——它不是 SPV 股东、不是贷款方、不是开发商。它只是用"未来营收承诺"换取当下的算力优先权。

这在会计报表上是天才设计（不并表、不负债），但在系统层面创造了一个"影子资产负债表"：Oracle 真实的敞口远超财报数字，因为它的品牌、信用、股价都被绑定在一个它并不直接控制的物理施工时间表上。

跨领域连接：这与航空业过去 30 年用飞机租赁 SPV 持有飞机的结构完全同构——表面轻资产，实际重敞口。当年美联航、达美的租赁 SPV 结构在 2001 年、2020 年两次危机中都反噬了母公司。今天 Oracle 走的是同一条路：一旦木星计划从"延期"滑向"永久搁置"，那 180 亿贷款的债权人一定会通过合同追索链把风险反向压回 Oracle——force majeure 警告本身就是 Oracle 提前在打这个防御桩。

五、一个属于 2026 年的时间悖论

最后一个让人后背发凉的观察：审批周期正在变得比技术周期更长。

天然气管道审批推到 2027 年 2 月——这意味着从"决定建"到"能通电"的时间，已经超过了从"H100 发布"到"B200 出货"的整个 GPU 换代周期。监管时钟正在变得比摩尔时钟慢。这在人类工业史上是极其罕见的错配——通常是技术慢，规则跟得上。而现在，最快的技术被最慢的官僚流程套住了。

这才是 AI 时代真正的深层瓶颈：不是算力，不是数据，不是能源，是"批准速度"。
