item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、无法解释的价格，本身就是信号

小涛开场那句"我不知道为什么"，其实是这一整期视频里最有价值的一句话——比后面所有的分析都更值钱。

大多数分析师面对14~15个基点的收益率跳涨，会本能地把 PMI 超预期 + 拍卖不及格拼成一个"合理故事"。但当解释和幅度不匹配时，强行拟合叙事等于制造虚假信号。这里有个反直觉的观察：市场最凶险的时刻，往往不是"看不懂"，而是"看得太懂"——所有人都拿着同一套故事下同样的注，多头集体缺席，空头目标高度一致。这时候流动性的塌方，才是那多出来的10个基点的真正来源。

跨领域连接：这和情报分析里的"信号噪音比"是同一个问题。CIA 的分析师训练里有一条铁律——当证据无法解释事件量级时，不要去补齐叙事，而应该假设存在一个"你尚未看到的变量"。小涛在这一点上做的比99%的宏观博主都要诚实。

二、黄金-真实收益率的"脱钩"，可能是货币史级别的裂缝

视频里一笔带过的一张图，其实是全场最重要的图：真实收益率破新高，但黄金没破新低。

传统教科书告诉你，黄金和真实收益率是-0.8的负相关关系——因为持有黄金的机会成本就是真实利率。但这个关系已经被打破一个多月了。40个基点的实际利率上行，正常情况下应该让黄金跌8-12%，但现实只跌了3-4%。

这里有个让人不寒而栗的解读：当"避险资产"和"债券"分道扬镳，市场正在悄悄给美元本身定价违约风险——不是形式违约，而是货币购买力的隐性违约。真实利率上升本应吸引资本回到美债，但资本在同时买黄金，这是"我承认收益率高，但我不再相信这个尺子"。

跨领域连接：这和新兴市场货币危机爆发前6-12个月的"影子信号"极其相似——1997年泰铢崩盘前，泰国国债收益率上升但泰铢仍在贬值，本地精英在同时买入黄金和美元资产。当利率工具无法把货币"锚"回来，就是主权信用重定价的开端。贝森特"会不会干预"其实已经晚了——真正的干预窗口，在市场停止相信"利率信号"的那一刻就关闭了。

三、高盛的"消费者惯性篮子"：一个金融版的反射性陷阱

彭博披露高盛推出这个篮子，然后 Expedia、Airbnb、Allstate、Intuit 集体大跌——小涛看到的是"作妖"，但底层机制更精妙。

高盛不需要预测未来。它只需要创造一个 Schelling Point（谢林焦点）——让所有对冲基金看到同一张名单，然后大家心照不宣地一起做空。篮子发布本身就是自我实现的预言：股价下跌 → 分析师补上叙事 → 更多资金抛售 → 逻辑被"验证"。

小涛的反驳很有力——AI Agent 改变的是"入口"不是"蛋糕"，Airbnb 的房源、Expedia 的库存、Intuit 的报税知识库并没有蒸发。但市场在杀跌时不看基本面，看的是共识坐标。

跨领域连接（这一段最值得展开）：这个模式在AI叙事里已经出现过两次了——年初 Anthropic 每发一个模型，SaaS 就被杀一遍；六个月后回头看，SaaS 营收增速几乎无一放缓。市场反复犯同一个错误：把"渠道颠覆"当作"价值毁灭"。这是一种典型的范畴谬误（category error）——就像把"报纸从纸质变成 App"误读为"新闻业消亡"，或者把"支付宝取代现金"误读为"消费需求下降"。真正会被 AI Agent 消灭的，不是有真实履约能力的平台，而是那些本质是"信息中介 + 广告变现"的公司。旅行社（做履约）活得下去，比价工具（做信息套利）活不下去——但市场把它们一起卖了。

四、麦当劳的隐藏杠杆：不是利率，是油价

小涛提到一个被严重低估的细节——加息对麦当劳客户"几乎没影响"，因为他们的痛点是油价，不是利率。

这背后是K型货币政策传导：美联储加息，其实是通过几乎完全不同的渠道分别打击高收入和低收入群体。高收入被资产价格和抵押贷款利率打击，低收入被通胀和油价打击——而这两个渠道的相关性可以是负的。这就是为什么"美联储调控总需求"这个说法本身是个抽象泡沫——美国不存在一个"总需求"，只存在两个各自独立震荡的经济体。

麦当劳三季度美国负增长的指引，其实是低收入端消费的先行指标，比任何政府数据都提前3-6个月。当汉堡都卖不动了，Dollar Tree、Family Dollar 的财报可能就在路上。这是一个跨消费板块的连锁警报，值得比麦当劳本身更认真地看待。

📝 转录文本

开场：为什么我无法解释周三的美债走势

今天在社交媒体上有人问我，能不能聊一下周三的美债市场。那我回答他是：如果我告诉你，我并不知道为什么周三美债市场的收益率出现了那么大幅的一个上涨，能不能接受？

那其实我想表达的是——我们不一定一定要强行去解释每一天市场的一个走势背后的一个理由到底是什么。我觉得没有必要完全去理解，相反，很多时候其实没有办法给出这个理由。

我要给的话，我当然可以给。我说：周三市场 PMI 数据超出市场预期、大幅超出市场预期，所以美债收益率出现上涨，所以美元指数出现上涨。但有什么意义？我说实话有什么意义？因为我个人认为，这组数据没有办法去解释上涨的这个幅度——你可以解释上涨，但是没有办法解释上涨的幅度。

那么，所以在这种情况下，包括周三市场的美债拍卖也不是那么的好，但是这两件事情加在一起，能不能解释那么大的一个幅度呢？我个人认为是解释不了的。所以在这种情况下，我就没有办法给出这个理由。但不妨碍我们去理解一下当下市场的这个定价是如何、包括当下市场的一个参与度是如何。

本期三大看点

所以我个人认为，过去这段时间价值股的这个下跌是和利率相关的，但是彭博在周二的那一篇文章里边解释了，似乎高盛也是背后的这个推手。所以这是第二部分。

然后最后，和一只价值股是相关的——麦当劳。麦当劳在周三出现了比较大幅度的下跌，我们去看一下背后到底发生了什么。周三的一个市场还是有很多的点值得我们去展开的。

好吗？欢迎大家来到一个不只聊新闻的专业美股频道，我是市场分析师小涛。

在开始之前，大家记得留言、点赞、加转发。昨天我上传了最新的一期会员视频，在那些会员视频里面有详细地去聊了一下我现在自己的一个仓位，包括接下去的一些调整。

今天的仓位调整

那今天其实我做了一些调整，主要是卖出了非常小一部分的亚马逊，然后加上自己手里的一个现金，在周三的时候加仓了谷歌。好吗？这是我周三唯一的一个仓位调整。

一、美债市场：无法解释的收益率飙升

然后我们回到资产价格这边的一个走势。就像我前面说的，两年期美债收益率和十年期分别上涨了14个基点和15个基点，10年期上涨这个幅度高于两年期，就整条利率曲线出现了往上的这个平移。TLT 出现了1.6%的这个下跌。

那么大幅度的一个涨幅，我个人是没有办法做这个解释的。有两组数据确实是我们可以参考的：

第一组是在周三早上发布的 PMI 数据大幅高出市场预期。你可以理解为是经济增速高于市场预期，那么所以美债收益率逐渐上涨是合理的。

第二部分，美债的拍卖的结果也非常的差，那拍卖的结果差，利率也会出现上涨。

但是能不能够解释那么大幅度的一个上涨？我个人认为是没有办法解释的。那这背后可能债券市场这一块的空头现在的目标比较的一致，或者市场里面其实缺少了一些多头。

关于贝森特干预、黄金与美债的选择

讲到这边，可能有人会问：我是不是还期待贝森特会去干预美债市场？我个人认为是会的。

然后另外一点我觉得比较重要的是，因为我现在也并没有去做多美债，那么我现在是有一部分的一些非常小部分的一些黄金上的一个交易仓位，是做多黄金的。

另外一部分我觉得比较重要的是，你看今天虽然美债收益率出现了非常大幅度一个上涨，那其实黄金下跌的幅度还好，下跌了1.7%。那稍后有一张图和大家分享，其实黄金并没有去破过去几天的一个新低，但是美债收益率却不断在破新高。

所以从这段时间的一个走势，其实是可以和七月份的走势有点类似的——就是真实收益率不断地破新高，但是黄金的一个价格却没有破新低。那这也解释了过去这段时间有人问我了：你既然认为贝森特会干预美债市场，为什么不去做多美债，而去做多黄金？那这段时间的走势，我认为也解释了一部分——明显黄金是更加的强势，相对于美债来说，明显黄金更加的强势。

二、周三的下跌：价值股是重灾区

那周三的市场，随着美债收益率大幅度的一个上涨，标普三大指数都出现了下跌，而这个下跌其实主要是集中在价值股板块：

  • 银行板块下跌 1.2%
  • 公共事业下跌 1.9%
  • REITs 下跌 1.5%

那一些派股息比较多的一些价值股公司或者价值股板块，出现下跌的幅度可能就会大一些。为什么？因为美债利率这个上升，对于这些派股息的公司来说就是一个利空。

前七大科技股周三下跌了 0.8%，等权指数下跌了 0.7%。整个周三的一个市场，其实下跌的一个范围和参与度是比较的大。

前面我聊到了这两个板块：一个是银行板块 KBWB，看一下银行板块现在 RSI 日 K 线的这个走势也进入了超卖的这个区间，其实上一次进入超卖的区间是在今年的 3 月份。然后另外一个价值股板块的 ETF——XLU 基建板块，那基建板块现在也是进入了一个超买的区间（注：此处原话如此），而且超买的这个幅度也是比较的大，在过去一年，我们是没有看到过基建板块进入超买的区间。

黄金 vs 真实收益率：一次值得警惕的背离

然后我们来看一下黄金。图里两条线：白色这条线是 10 年期美债的一个真实收益率，蓝色这条线是黄金的一个价格走势。

你可以看到白色这条线现在再次去破了一个新高，但是黄金的这个价格其实并没有破新低。那这段时间的一个走势，其实黄金这段时间真的是强势的——因为美债收益率从 8 月底的一个低点，相对的一个低点，到现在整整上升了 40 个基点，一个多月的时间，差不多正好一个月的时间上升 40 个基点，这是非常大幅度的一个上涨。

而黄金的这个价格，我认为总体来说相对是比较强劲的。我这边画了另外一个时间点，就是整个 7 月份，当时你可以看到白色这条线真实收益率也是在一个上升的一个空间里边，但是蓝色这条线黄金的这个价格基本上是保持在 4000 点左右。

三、市场对加息周期的定价：极度鹰派

讲到债券市场，讲到真实收益率，我们来看一下现在市场对于这一次加息周期的这个定价。我认为，现在市场已经超出了我理解范围以外的这个鹰派。

上一次点阵图里边，美联储成员就已经说过了，他们认为在今年会加息两次，然后明年是不会加息的。但是现在市场定价是什么？是现在市场定价整个加息周期在 9 月份已经加息了一次的情况下，还会再加息将近 4 次，也就是总共会加息 5 次——美联储的 SEP 里面预测总共会加息两次，也就是比美联储的 SEP 整整赢了三次加息。

并且随着这段时间两年期美债收益率的一个上涨： - 10 月份加息这个概率来到了 71% - 今年加息的这个次数来到了 1.5 次 - 整个加息周期接下去来到了 3.76 次，就将近于 3.8 次

市场现在的一个定价，期货上这块的一个定价，隔夜利率或者美联储的这个联邦利率将会停在 4.8%。

MOVE 指数：债券市场的"恐慌指数"也在爬升

另外，随着最近这段时间债券市场的这个波动，我们来看一下 MOVE Index。MOVE Index 类似于股票市场里边的一个 VIX，MOVE Index 衡量的是债券市场这块的一个波动率。波动率在最近这段时间也出现了上涨，来到了 95.45。

那上一次波动率去到一个高点是在 110 以上，是 3 月份，当时市场的一个下跌。所以我们从这张图明显可以看到，债券市场的这个恐慌指数也开始慢慢上升。

传统"利率涨—股票跌"的逻辑，其实已经破产

但是在这种情况下，如果我就告诉大家说：哎，如果美债收益率的上升——就这个逻辑本身是没有意义的。什么逻辑？就是美债收益率上升，美股就一定要下跌。

我其实上次和大家看过，从 7 月份以来整个市场的一个走势，我说是不可思议的。美债收益率在大幅上升的情况下，你看一下大科技是出现上升的，软件板块是出现上升，比特币是出现上升，黄金是出现上升——你是没有办法去理解这种宏观的一个逻辑，完全打破了以前这种逻辑。

但是你会发现，从周三的走势你就可以看到：利率的确在上升，包括过去一个多月的走势，利率不断在上升，但是反而是这些价值股板块受到影响。

其实我在 22 年的这一波加息周期里边，我就不是非常认同市场的这个看法。市场当时的一个解释——我当时在留言区里边还和很多观众有过一定的一个交流——市场的一个解释是："哦，因为这些科技公司，他们的盈利比较偏向于比如说在 5 年、甚至在 10 年之后，那么所以他们受到利率的这个影响会比较的大。"

但是我们如果从 DCF 现金流模型这个角度去出发的话，任何一家公司，只要你是有现金流的，你都会受到利率这个影响。只要利率上升，你的折现的一个价格、你的 Present Value 就是会降低。

然后我们回过头去看整个 22 年结束之后的这个走势，其实有一些价值股板块反而是上涨了，即使在一个那么强的一个加息周期里边。科技股是下跌，但是当时因为科技股下跌，所以市场说因为加息影响到这些科技股的一个现金流，所以科技股下跌。但是这一轮你看到这个加息周期也好，或者利率这个上涨也好，上涨的幅度很大，四五十个基点这种上涨幅度，那为什么大科技的价格反而出现上涨？

所以这个逻辑，或者我们如果死套这个逻辑的话，也是没办法去解释的。

真正的核心变量：EPS 增速 vs 宏观逆风

那我个人的一个理解就是，最终你会发现影响到股价、或者影响到 PE 的这个走势是什么？是公司的一个 EPS 增速或者 EPS 的体量。

所以我认为这一轮的加息周期也好、或者这段时间利率的一个上涨也好，为什么没有影响到科技公司？这背后的一个核心逻辑（包括接下去我认为的一个核心逻辑）就是——这些科技公司、这些 AI 公司，他们盈利的增速和整个市场宏观这一块的一些逆风会成为一个抵消。就你看宏观的逆风比较的厉害，还是说盈利的增速比较的厉害，到底哪个是占主导？

如果盈利增速占主导的话，股价仍然可以出现上涨；而如果宏观逆风占主导的话，那价格就会出现下跌。

那反过来看这些传统的价值股公司，因为他们并没有接受到 AI 的这波红利，那所以他们受到了利率上涨这个影响。

所以我认为接下去也会是这样的一个逻辑：AI 的一个基本面 VS 宏观这一块的一些逆风（包括这些模型公司上市对于市场的一个抽血等等）。

市场参与度：指数新高，广度却在悲观区间

那我们回到周三市场的一个参与度。实际上我前面说周三市场的参与度其实比较低的： - 纳指只有 20% 的公司出现了上涨 - 罗素 2000 只有 15% 的公司出现了上涨 - 标普 500 只有 30% 的公司出现了上涨

那我们对参与度做一个更新。三大指数 20 均线和 50 均线的参与度： - 纳指分别在 30% 和 32%，正好卡在一个悲观的位置 - 罗素两千 25% 和 27%，已经在一个悲观的位置，或者仍然停留在一个悲观的位置 - 标普 26% 和 29%，也是停在一个悲观的位置

这和我们当下整个指数的一个感觉是不一样的。因为指数是新高，纳指刚刚破了一个新高，然后市场的参与度在一个低位。

那在这种情况下，我们更加应该相信什么？我觉得这种情况下是最好持股的一个时候。为什么？明明自己的账户也是在昨天破了一个新高——因为昨天英特尔涨了，周二的时候英特尔涨得比较好——就明明自己账户刚刚破新高，但整个市场的参与度却是在一个比较悲观的位置，那在这种情况下，我并不觉得有很多东西是我们值得去担心的。

但是与此同时，因为市场本身非常的撕裂。即使大科技走得好，Mag 7 走得好，但 Mag 7 里边也有一些分歧，并不是所有的 Mag 7 都走得好——这段时间唯一走得比较好的可能是 Meta 走得比较好一些。

所以在这样的一个市场下，在板块非常撕裂情况下、即使在一个板块里边也非常撕裂这种情况下，我个人认为如果从投资个股这个角度去看的话，确实会比较的难。其实今年到现在为止，我认为都是一个高难度的一个挑战。

但在这种时候，如果对于很多标的本身没有那么信心的话，我个人建议还是持有 ETF 或者持有指数的这个占比稍微大一些，这样的话会大大减轻选股的这个风险。而且现在板块与板块之间的这个轮动非常的快。

四、高盛的"消费者惯性篮子"：又开始作妖

那我前面聊到，我说我个人认为这段时间价值股的一个下跌是因为利率的这个上涨。彭博在周二写了一篇文章，他说高盛他们又开始作妖了——高盛现在又建了一个一篮子股票，这个篮子股票叫做消费者惯性篮子。

他们认为因为人工智能代理的一个广泛使用，而这些股票、或者这一篮子股票将会受到损失。所以他们的一个解释，你可以看到他说 Meta 他们上线 MUSE AI Agent 的时候，就是这个股票开始下跌的时候。

那这篇文章是写在周二。他说到主要银行、保险公司和在线旅行社的股价下跌，因为投资者担心像 Meta 这一类的个人智能体代理的工具，可能会颠覆那些受益于所谓消费者惯性的一些股票。

我为什么认为这个逻辑不成立

我觉得这是不 make sense 的。比如说他下面举了很多的例子——像 Allstate 也好、像 Intuit、像 Expedia 也好——它这边的一个下跌幅度是周二下跌幅度，周三这些股票、这些标的，有些标的下跌的幅度更大：比如说 Expedia 周三下跌了 5% 吧，然后 Airbnb 下跌了 7%。

我认为这是不 make sense 的。为什么？什么意思？Meta 的这个 MUSE、Meta 的个人智能体，它绝对不会是第一个，也不会是最后一个。那接下去，我相信 Siri 的这个推出，包括谷歌也会推出自己非常强劲的这个个人智能体，一定会推出的。

但是，如果我们今天拿 Expedia 来举这个例子，Expedia 或者 Airbnb 或者 Booking.com 都是一样——人们在旅游这一块的需求不会因为有了 AI Agent 之后增加或者降低，不会的。只是我们去选择订购这一次旅游的一个渠道有可能会出现了这个改变。

那么原本我可能是直接去 Airbnb 上进行订阅，现在的话我可能通过 MUSE，然后 MUSE 通过 Airbnb 去进行这个订阅。所以对于像 Expedia、Airbnb 这类的公司，他们的业务本身，只要你的业务本身没有依赖于一些广告费等等，它其实核心的业务本身是不会受到任何影响的。因为今天 Meta 是不可能去破坏这类的公司的。

这一幕似曾相识：半年前的 Anthropic vs 软件公司

但是市场背后交易这个逻辑线有点类似于什么？有点类似于可能在半年前，起码今年年初的时候——还记不记得今年年初的时候，当时 Anthropic 只要发布一个模型，这些软件公司就下跌，只要他们发一个模型，软件公司就下跌？

但是我们回到现在，6 个月之后，我们会发现 Anthropic 到底有没有破坏这些软件公司？我们有没有看到这些软件公司他们的营收增速放缓？几乎大多数的软件公司营收增速都没有放缓。那么与此同时，Anthropic 他们所推出的这些模型本身有没有一些非常好的一些 adoption？其实并没有看到。

那我能够理解彭博这篇文章背后的一个逻辑，对吧？因为入口不一样了——原本你是直接去 Expedia，Expedia 就是一个入口，Airbnb 就是一个入口，现在你的入口变成了一个 AI Agent、变成了智能体。那你的入口改变之后，对于这些公司，你说他们的核心的一个营收是不是受到影响？我觉得（市场是）和软件公司都同样的一个逻辑去杀跌这些公司，但是和软件公司背后的一个逻辑其实不一样的——就是换句话说，Anthropic 还有一定的可能性去破坏一些软件公司，但是 Meta 是绝对不可能去破坏这一类的平台公司。

什么时候平台公司才会真的被颠覆？

直到什么时候？直到未来有一天……我们拿 Airbnb 举例子会比较的好。Airbnb 它背后的客户是谁？它背后的客户是个体，同时它的一个客户是谁？是房东。

如果未来有一天，每一个房东都有自己的这个 Agent，那 Airbnb 还负责什么？还负责打扫啊、然后服务啊、包括监管，那么每一个地区都需要有牌照的。那如果未来有另外一家 AI Native 的公司能够把这些东西全部搞定，然后所有的房东又有自己的这个 Agent，那我们可能会有另外的这个平台去替代 Airbnb 这类的平台。

但是我认为我们距离那样的一个时间点还有比较长的一段距离。所以直到每一个人都有自己的这个 Agent、都有自己这个 Agent 的一个标签，直到每一家企业都有自己这个 Agent 之前，我并不认为这一类的公司会受到像 Meta 这一类个人智能体的破坏。

那恰恰相反，因为整个蛋糕是不变的嘛——蛋糕并不会缩小、然后也不会扩大。如果说像 Airbnb 这类的公司，他们如果可以把 AI 和自己的产品有一个非常好的这个结合，甚至于他们有一些自己的一些智能体，自己的智能体可以和个人的 AI 智能进行交流的话，反而可以在整个蛋糕、整个市场里边抢占更多的一些市场份额。

那么但是没办法，市场下跌，高盛他建了一个一篮子的股票，一篮子的股票出来之后就给市场去做空的。那如果市场因为 MUSE 这个上线去杀跌这些消费者惯性股，我认为市场是真的太会做现金外兑了。

五、麦当劳：不是估值问题，是基本面预警

最后我们聊一家公司——麦当劳。那麦当劳正好也是最近这段时间下跌，所以最近这段时间你会发现整个板块其实走的都不好，那不在板块里面那些标题走的其实也不好。

我看了一下，因为麦当劳在周三的一个市场走势：首先第一点它是放量的，第二点它下跌的幅度比较大，将近最多是 5% 左右。

我去看了一下新闻，首先它未来要加大这个投资，但是加大投资可能并不是主要下跌的一个原因。主要下跌的原因我去看了一下，是管理层给了三季度它美国这边的一个增速，他说有可能是一个负增长——而现在市场的预期是增速。我这边圈出来是 0.11%，也就市场原本的预期是正好是没有任何的增速，就接近于 0%，但是管理层给了一个指引是负增长。

也就说明什么问题？说明美国这边原本在策略上的这个错误——就是在 promotion 这一块策略上的一个错误——并没有因为他们纠正，在短期之内营收就出现一个反转。甚至我们都可以这么去理解：因为第三季度马上就要结束了，在这个节骨点管理层说美国这边的一个营收非常有可能会低于这个预期，就是财报——你可以把它理解为是财报提前公布了——美国这一块的营收低于市场的预期。

估值回到接近 2020 年 3 月的水平

然后我们来看一下估值。这张是 Forward PE，截止到周三的收盘，是 17.4 倍。麦当劳的股价在今年为止下跌的幅度比较的大，主要是从今年的一二月份开始下跌的，从最高点的估值 25 倍以上下降到现在 17.4 倍，估值本身下降了 31.6%。

那这一波下跌主要就是定价他们在美国这边 promotion 上的一个策略上的一个错误。现在的一个估值离 2020 年的 3 月份 16 倍左右吧还是有一段距离，但是已经非常的接近，而这一波的下跌已经非常的大。

今天我再看到麦当劳下跌，我看了一下成交量又是放量了，其实我是想开仓的。但是我看了一下我没有开仓的原因，是因为我现在没有仓位了，我也没有现金仓位了——因为我现金仓位今天加了谷歌嘛，所以我现在没有仓位。我要思考的是我要换哪些标的出来，然后去购买麦当劳。那这个问题我还没有思考清楚，我思考清楚之后我再去考虑要不要去建仓麦当劳。

那但是我个人认为在这个位置去压麦当劳未来有可能会出现基本面上的一个反转的话，我认为这个 risk 对我来说已经是非常性感的了。只是我还没有找到有可以替代的一个标的。如果我找到这个标的的话，那我就去做替换。如果我没有找到这个标的的话，那我就不会去做一个替换，我就不会去开仓麦当劳。

关于加息对麦当劳的影响：真正的痛点是油价

最后关于麦当劳我想聊的是，因为有一部分的观众担心现在进入一个加息周期，加息对于麦当劳可能会存在一定的一个利空。但其实加息对于麦当劳的客户来说几乎是不受影响的——因为麦当劳的客户相对都是低收入人群的，对于这些低收入人群来说，股市也好、或者楼市也好，对于他们不是最大的一个负担，对于他们最大的一个负担其实反而是油价。

所以加息本身对于麦当劳的基本面 EPS 来说，其实影响是不大的。

从另外一个角度，你说加息本身对于麦当劳的 PE 有没有可能会有一些影响？这是有可能的。就像我前面聊到，因为最近这段时间利率的这个上涨，导致很多派股息的这些公司，它的价格逐渐下跌。因为市场原本是把这些公司认为——你我买 5 年、买 10 年，你每一年的股息 4%、5%，我拿着非常的开心。但是现在如果我去买美国国债，每年就有 4%~5% 的话，那这一类的标的相对来说就没有买国债有吸引力了，对吧？

所以这些标的它的一个估值下降，那当它的一个估值下降、当它的一个价格下降之后，它的一个已有的股息率反而出现上升了。那直到这个股息率再次变得有吸引力之后，它的股价从 PE 这个角度去看，就能够找到一个低点。

结束语与推广

好吧，那今天最后的一个活动来自于 Seeking Alpha：

首先是 Seeking Alpha 他们这个量化选股策略现在有立即的一个免费试用，首年有 50 美金的一个优惠。

另外是 Seeking Alpha 在过去这两个月最新推出的量化选股策略，这个量化选股策略它叫做 Quant Growth and Income。它主要集中的这些标的就是我前面聊到的那些派股息的一些标的，所以这些标的本身相对防守属性是比较强的。那大家对于这一个量化选股策略感兴趣的话，现在也有第一年 50 美金的这个优惠。

所以两个订阅的链接我会放在置顶的留言里边，大家感兴趣的话可以去进行订阅。那今天这期呢就到这边，下期见。

item.description:
## 一、无法解释的价格，本身就是信号
小涛开场那句"我不知道为什么"，其实是这一整期视频里最有价值的一句话——比后面所有的分析都更值钱。
大多数分析师面对14~15个基点的收益率跳涨，会本能地把 PMI 超预期 + 拍卖不及格拼成一个"合理故事"。但当解释和幅度不匹配时，**强行拟合叙事等于制造虚假信号**。这里有个反直觉的观察：市场最凶险的时刻，往往不是"看不懂"，而是"看得太懂"——所有人都拿着同一套故事下同样的注，多头集体缺席，空头目标高度一致。这时候流动性的塌方，才是那多出来的10个基点的真正来源。
**跨领域连接**：这和情报分析里的"信号噪音比"是同一个问题。CIA 的分析师训练里有一条铁律——当证据无法解释事件量级时，不要去补齐叙事，而应该假设存在一个"你尚未看到的变量"。小涛在这一点上做的比99%的宏观博主都要诚实。
## 二、黄金-真实收益率的"脱钩"，可能是货币史级别的裂缝
视频里一笔带过的一张图，其实是全场最重要的图：**真实收益率破新高，但黄金没破新低**。
传统教科书告诉你，黄金和真实收益率是-0.8的负相关关系——因为持有黄金的机会成本就是真实

item.title: [硅谷101播客] E252｜硅谷睡眠外挂：富人的玩具，还是预防医疗的入口？｜对话Eight Sleep创始人
item.dc:creator: 硅谷101播客
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

反常识观察：他们卖的不是"追踪"，而是"无为"

大多数健康科技公司都在往你身上"加"东西——手表、指环、贴片、CGM。Eight Sleep 反其道而行之，把技术藏到你身下。这是一个被低估的战略洞察：当整个行业都在争夺你的手腕和手指时，最大的未被开发的界面是"无意识的六到九小时"。 Matteo 说得很直白："data is not the endpoint for us but is just a mean to an end"——数据不是终点，响应才是。这一句话其实把他们和 Oura、Whoop、Apple Watch 划清了界限：穿戴设备卖的是"知情"，Eight Sleep 卖的是"代劳"。这背后是一个更大的哲学转向——从"量化自我"到"外包自我"。健康科技的下一波，不是让你更了解自己，而是让你不用了解自己。

跨领域连接：床，正在变成一台隐形的 MRI

访谈里最容易被忽略但爆炸性最强的一段是 Matteo 提到的斯坦福论文——一夜睡眠数据可以检测 130 种疾病，准确率接近 90%。把这句话和他"first principle"式的追问放在一起看："一个人在一个大表面上静止六小时，上下都有空间、有 Wi-Fi、有电——你能对它做什么？"这不是床的思路，这是扫描仪的思路。类比一下：MRI 之所以昂贵，是因为医院时间稀缺；而床垫则是世界上唯一每天让每个人主动躺进去六小时的医疗器械界面。他们真正在做的事，其实和 Google 早年做搜索一样——用一个免费/便宜的日常行为，采集出全世界最贵的训练数据。搜索采集意图，床垫采集生理。当他们说"下一步 8 Medical"时，你要意识到：这可能是消费硬件史上最长的特洛伊木马——用助眠的名义，建造一台家用癌症早筛机。

出人意料的数据点：伴侣在床上时，女性的 HRV 更好

Alexandra 顺嘴讲的这个发现，值得单独写一篇论文。女性只是因为伴侣在同一张床上，恢复指标（HRV）就系统性地更好。 这不是浪漫叙事，这是可量化的共调节（co-regulation）。它把一个心理学/依恋理论概念，第一次通过消费级传感器变成了统计事实。跨领域看，这和最近关于"孤独是一种炎症状态"的研究、以及母婴间心率同步的研究，属于同一条隐藏的科学暗线——神经系统并不止步于皮肤。这也解释了一个反直觉的商业现象：为什么 Eight Sleep 的"救婚姻"叙事其实卖得比"睡得更好"更有力——它悄悄触及的是"人是社会动物"这件事的生理证据。

深层模式：意大利卓越 × 美国规模 = 苹果

Matteo 讲定价时透露了一个真正精妙的心智模型："意大利品牌追求品质、小规模、高毛利；美国品牌追求规模但容易牺牲品质；乔布斯是极少数把两者调和的人。"这个二元框架比它听起来更深——它其实是手艺文明 vs 工业文明的当代和解方案。有意思的是，Eight Sleep 从技术上（液冷循环 = 超跑发动机技术下沉到卧室）到商业上（不卷价格卷"outcome"）都在复刻这条路径。这也是为什么中国市场对他们反而是加分项：中国消费者刚好完成了从"性价比"到"要最好的"的心智跃迁——他们此刻的消费心态，比十年前的美国消费者更接近"米兰高定"，而不是"沃尔玛"。

隐藏的反差：癌症患者是他们最意外的用户群

访谈里最人性的一句话是 Matteo 承认——化疗患者是他们没预料到的一个大客户群，因为化疗破坏体温调节，导致夜间盗汗。把这个和孕期潮热、更年期潮热放在一起，你会发现一个尴尬的医学盲区：人类温度调节系统在生命中最脆弱的三个阶段（怀孕、化疗、更年期）都会失灵，而主流医学几乎没有非药物解决方案。 这三种人群共享同一个生理问题，却分散在三个完全不同的科室里，从来没有被"温度调节缺陷"这个统一视角看待过。Eight Sleep 无意间做了一件很有意思的事：它用一个消费产品，把三种从未被并列的医学困境统一到了同一个 SKU 下面。 这是消费产品反向定义医学分类的罕见案例。

E252｜硅谷睡眠外挂：富人的玩具，还是预防医疗的入口？

对话 Eight Sleep 创始人 Matteo & Alexandra

开场：欢迎来到 Valley 101

主持人：Alex, welcome to Valley 101.

嘉宾：Yeah, thank you for having us.

主持人：I am really excited for this. Great to meet the people behind a product that I sleep on every night. I was really excited when I unboxed the product. A lot of my friends have been telling me about it. I feel like you guys have really made the brand known not only in the tech circle but also just in general. But for the viewers who are not really familiar with Eight Sleep, tell me a little bit more about what you guys are building here.

Eight Sleep 是什么？

Matteo：Yeah, we invented a technology that improves your sleep. Everything starts with a mattress cover that you can install on top of your mattress, but then we added other technology that will help you mitigate snoring and also help you fall asleep. But in general, we have this vision about really enhancing sleep performance. What if you could sleep only six hours and get more rest than when you were sleeping eight hours? And in the meanwhile, we also want to track everything about your health so you can live a healthier and longer life.

主持人：So I guess the core technology here is temperature control. You mentioned that it was cooler. Tell me a little bit more about how that idea came about for you guys — when I guess when you guys started building that. That was like when you guys were 20, 24, 25.

核心技术：温度控制 + 打鼾缓解 + 助眠

Matteo：We started working on this in 2014 the first time and we had this vision about the ability to track everything about your health and respond. The big difference between what we do and wearables is that the data is not the endpoint for us but is just a means to an end. The end is the ability to respond. Temperature is one of the ways we respond and is one of the most effective.

So each side of the cover — each side of the bed — can have a different temperature and that temperature will dynamically adjust based on your biometrics, sleep stages, preferences and whatever you did during the day, so sort of activities. So temperature is the first big one, and through temperature we can give you up to 30% better sleep.

Then there are other technologies. There is one for snoring mitigation. This is a base that goes underneath your bed and if you're snoring, we are going to raise your head and that should mitigate your snoring. And then we also have a speaker in the base and we are able to play certain sounds at certain moments of the night to help you fall asleep.

Alexandra：And all of it is really personalization. So as you saw, it's all these different factors about your environment. But when we started working on what is now Eight Sleep, it was because of this clear vacuum in the market where, like Matteo said, wearables may give you data. There are pharma companies that create drugs to help you fall asleep and help you stay asleep. But the reality is that no one was using technology to solve this problem of humans struggling to sleep well. And modern ways in which we live are getting a bit in the way of our ability to sleep really well every single night. So we wanted to solve that. And we realized that we have to personalize the night for every human in order to do that, and that's what we do.

睡眠文化的转变：从"熬夜可耻"到"睡眠即身份"

主持人：I wanted to talk a little bit more about just sleep in general. I feel like we're kind of in like a sleep maxing world. Everyone suddenly started to care about sleep a lot more. Was that the case when you guys started the company?

Matteo：No. No. No one was talking about sleep back in 2014. And I mean the world was so different in terms of health and wellness. The trends have really accelerated I think over the last six years. But no one would talk about it in public as well — like it wasn't something you discussed with your friends, or it was sort of very private. There were no technologies that were really tracking sleep. Wearables were starting to do it. There were a few companies — Apple was not even in the wearable space at the time. So, it was a very different world. And as you're saying, now, everyone cares about their sleep and people are talking about sleep maxing. People are talking about recovery as a key component of performance and health. So, the world has really changed.

主持人：I feel like previously there was this grind culture. Everyone is proud of not sleeping, you know, waking up at 4:00 a.m. and all that. And that has really changed. What have you noticed over the years of building this product in terms of the cultural reception of this?

Alexandra：Yeah. Well, I think a lot changed since 2020. Social media has given us the ability to discuss in depth so many topics about health that maybe previously were not. The explosion of formats like podcasts and YouTube vlogs — you just have so many great individuals who are sharing some of the science behind why you should be sleeping and why it matters for your longevity. We have people who are friends of the brand like Brian Johnson who are out there experimenting with all these things around how can you live longer. That has fueled the conversation for the average consumer where they are seeing that media and then they're also thinking, well, what does that mean for me? Obviously technology companies like Eight but many others that are providing that data every day has sort of opened the eyes to people of, wow, actually I do feel better when I sleep more. So it's been a combination of factors, but it has changed significantly I think post-2020 to where we were before in the first years of the company.

Matteo：I would almost simplify saying — look, 10, 20 years ago, sleeping 8 or 9 hours was seen as weak, as like you're wasting your time. You're not probably driven enough. Well, instead now, is literally perceived like going to the gym. Okay, you're a healthy person and then probably during the day you will be also a top performer because you will be sharp. And so this shift is because of the reasons Alexandra just described. And it's pretty incredible — and true, which is the most important thing — is literally what science proves.

Biohacking 与 Wellness 的融合

主持人：How does it fit into the biohacking culture? I was in SF a lot. I went to a lot of the peptide parties where people inject stuff into their bodies also to like optimize sleep. Have you seen examples of people kind of biohacking their own sleep?

Alexandra：I think we're a bit past that, which is interesting. I do think that biohacking as a movement was very strong in that 2020 to 2022 and then it really just blended with general wellness. And what we're seeing now around the world when we travel to all these countries where we sell Eight Sleep is that everyone's talking about wellness in the sense of they want to live healthier, longer. So the sense of longevity. And so I think that sleep has become more quote-unquote mainstream compared to say peptides that are sort of more right now on the edges — they're being adopted by people who are in the early adopter circles. Definitely in Silicon Valley you see a lot of that because people tend to have appetite to take risk and experiment and they're doing all sorts of things.

睡眠指标：数据 vs. 结果

主持人：You mentioned wearables. I feel like right now we use so many technologies to track how we sleep. I have a Garmin on my wrist right now and I feel like we have so many metrics — like REM, deep sleep, HRV, all of those words. What do you think are the most important things when it comes to sleep metrics, or holistically, are metrics important?

Matteo：Well, a couple of things. The first one is people obviously like metrics but at the end of the day what they pay us for is to do the job for them. That is what we do through this form of responses — temperature and elevation. At the end of the day, another metaphor I like to use is: we built a sleep butler for you that will do continuous adjustment while you are unconscious to deliver better sleep. So this is an AI that is behind the scene. It looks at the data for you and in real time adjusts temperature, elevation, noise, and in the future other factors.

So number one thing is you shouldn't even look at the metrics. We just need to make sure that when you wake up you feel great. Then if you want to look at the metrics — because we all want, I'm a metric geek — I think the key thing is to simplify things and highlight when there are what we call internally "anomalies." So at the end of the day what you want to know is: is everything on track? Yes. And then most of the people are fine.

Then if something is changing in your body and our AI or our intelligence is able to detect that you have a certain likelihood to be sick within two, three days — that is what we should surface. And then there are people like me and maybe you and we really want to go deep into the data, and there is when you should have a dashboard with HR, HRV, deep sleep or REM and so on.

主持人：How does it predict when you were sick?

Matteo：We have models that look at a bunch of different biometrics. Usually the most relevant are HR and HRV. And so you start seeing a trend where your heart rate at rest starts going up usually three, four, five days before you get fever, and your HRV starts going down. And so those are what we call anomalies, and that is how we are training our models to be able to detect some of the shifts in your biology.

为什么选择"床垫罩"这个形态？

主持人：I wanted to talk a little bit more about why you guys chose mattress cover. I know that you guys pivoted a little bit — cover, then mattress and back to cover — and there are so many variables. Why did you guys choose mattress cover in particular?

Alexandra：Well first, we wanted it to be seamless. So for us when we think of sleep, we didn't want to have to ask you to do something else, right? Even wearing something while you're sleeping, or having to remember to charge your Garmin or your wearable every x days and remember to do that, or activating it or anything like that — like was out of the question. We don't believe that that's the right way to go, especially when it comes to sleep. When you feel tired, you should just be able to go to bed. And like Matteo said, this sort of sleep butler takes care of you. So embedding something on the surface that you're sleeping on felt the most natural design option. And so that's why the mattress cover — that's the form factor we've had since our very first product, before the pod. And we've sort of gone back and forth in whether we sell it integrated to a mattress or not. But in the end, consumers wanted the flexibility to put it on top of any bed they already had at home. So it turned out to be the right bet.

专利技术：液冷 + 40+ 项专利

主持人：I would love to talk a little bit about the technology that allows us to do that. And what are your proprietary technologies that kind of optimize this temperature control and help us feel comfortable?

Matteo：We have filed many, many patents. I think we have over probably 40 patents in that range. We really reinvented the technology from the ground up. We came up with this technology that is liquid-based. The science behind what we do and the fact that temperature will improve your sleep is something that has been proven for probably 50 years by now. So we didn't invent that. That was already proven. What we did is we were the first company that was able to create a consumer device at scale that could deliver this value to the average user.

And another thing we noticed was the need for couples. What we see is 80 to 90% of the couples they have different temperature preferences and different needs. And that is where we immediately found the product market fit. So people like to joke saying that we saved their marriage because they were fighting with their partner about different temperature needs — I want it colder, I want it warmer, and so on. And so we built this technology that has a device that sits next to your bed and there is where the whole intelligence lives, and then there is this cover where liquid cooling is circulating. So think of having the most sophisticated liquid cooling technology ever built, but instead being maybe for your top car or supercar, is just for your bed and for your sleep.

主持人：Yeah, I was actually quite surprised how easy it was to assemble. Like I kind of just poured water in and it worked. Was that a conscious decision between liquid cooling and other methods?

Alexandra：Yeah, I mean ultimately because water is the best material to actually absorb the body heat. Our bodies are quite hot. They're dissipating heat throughout the night — you're in bed for 6 to 9 hours every night — and so the water can absorb that and remove it from the surface of the bed. So it's much more successful at achieving and maintaining cooler temperatures than air would be, for instance. So that's why liquid was important to achieve our goal. But then, like Matteo said, it's really sophisticated because we had to also make it comfortable. When you're speaking about being on the surface of the bed you need to make it comfortable. You need to make it reliable. We wanted it to like disappear so that it wouldn't bother you — go in bed and it just feels like your regular mattress that you had bought previously, but now you have these added benefits.

伴侣与睡眠：一个被低估的生理学发现

主持人：Going back to that couple point, I thought that was really interesting as you said people have different temperature preferences. Is there any scientific evidence proven that how sleeping with a partner kind of affects your sleep, like your partner's sleeping habits would change your sleep quality?

Alexandra：Yeah, I think we have data. Yes. Yeah, there's definitely a very close connection. One because of habits. So couples who are going or not to bed like are keeping the same bedtimes or wake up times — they will influence their sleep significantly. But even while you're in bed, one thing that we have seen in our data is that women are actually heavily influenced by having their partner in bed and their HRV — so their recovery — tends to be much better when they have their partner in bed than when they don't. And so you start seeing all these sort of physiological effects of having your partner with you that are very interesting.

And so you would hear anecdotally women would say like, "Oh, it's much easier for me to fall asleep with our partners with me, or like I sleep better." But then we actually see in the data that it's true. The challenge is that when you're sleeping with someone, again, their bedtime routine, their wake up can bother you, their temperature preference can bother you. And those are some of the things that we're solving here by giving each partner the ability to define their own side of the bed, their microclimate, their own conditions, their own silent alarms so that they interrupt each other's sleep as little as possible.

女性健康：孕期与产后模式

主持人：To build on that, I wanted to talk a little bit about women's health as well because you guys launched the pregnancy mode. Tell me a little bit about how you guys discovered that use case and how sleep quality differs in those periods of their life.

Alexandra：Yeah. Well, I think everything that we're doing in women's health is really fascinating because there's a lot of conversation about how little women are really studied in anything related to our health and wellness. It's sort of harder to run clinical studies for women because of the variations that we have in our hormonal cycles. And we said, well, that doesn't make sense to us. Like, let's just figure out — given that we have this incredible scale of being in consumers' homes, let's figure out a way to recruit women who want to participate in studies with us. They're already part of our user base so that we can learn how women sleep. Let's actually start contributing back to science and sharing some of this data.

So women anecdotally would say that as they go through pregnancy, they start feeling warmer. They start feeling sometimes even sort of hot flashes or night sweats that they wouldn't have before pregnancy. And then as they go into postpartum, they have those effects again, which almost feels like a little bit of a perimenopause moment because their hormones are starting to go back down to where they were pre-preg. And we saw that in the data. It was very clear.

So as the pregnancy advances and every week of pregnancy, you do have different needs in terms of what environment temperature is going to keep you comfortable at sleep. So we said, well, why don't we build that? Let's actually use AI to create this algorithm that's just going to run automatically. If you tell our product what week of pregnancy you're in, what is your due date, it will just manage the temperature of your bed for you automatically. You don't have to do anything.

And beyond that, we have the value that we have the data. So we can also tell you here's how your heart rate is looking compared to pre-preg benchmarks. Here's what your HRV looks like, your breathing rate — all of those biomarkers change as a pregnancy advances. And we can benchmark you. We can tell you for the week of pregnancy you're in whether those metrics are looking quote-unquote normal, which also gives women some peace of mind, which is so important in that phase of life.

主持人：When you train the algorithm, what is the training data? Do you think we have enough data from pregnancy and women in general to train this algorithm to make sure it's accurate?

Alexandra：We do because the thing that we have is obviously all the people that sleep on the pod, we recruit from our user base. So we have women opt in. That's what's amazing. So we don't need to go and get that data from any external source, which obviously, as you said, sometimes there's not enough or there's not enough of the same quality of data for us. We have this incredible product in people's homes and our user base is excited because we're going to build something that's going to actually benefit them because they end up using it.

主持人：What kind of feedback have you been hearing?

Alexandra：So those two cohorts, it's incredible but they're some of their like highest engaged cohorts. They just love the features. We're building something that no other technology company has done for them because it's beyond tracking. So, it's not just the data, but we're actually solving a problem for them through this response. And so, that's just amazing for them. It's like someone's finally building what I needed and that is giving me a pregnancy that means I can sleep better, a postpartum where I can recover better. And when you think about it, in those moments in your life, sleep is so fundamental to your well-being. It really is critical. It's probably the most critical thing that you have to do.

十年迭代：数据护城河的规模

主持人：So, I guess it has been over 10 years. Looking back, are there versions of product that failed and what did you learn from that experience?

Matteo：Well, it's not that there was a version that failed. I think over the years, we always kept improving what we had, both because technology became better in general through AI and sensors. Every iteration — now, for example, with the pod, we are on Pod 6 — each iteration of this device is better than the previous one.

主持人：When it comes to the algorithm, how large is the data set behind the algorithm? What specifically is hard to replicate about that data?

Matteo：Well, it's billions of hours of health data and so we collect multiple terabytes of health data per day, and the only way you can do that is to be at scale. So even if you were starting a company today with a large amount of cash in the bank, it's literally something you cannot buy. Even because in our case we don't have off-the-shelf sensors — the sensors have been developed in-house by us. And so to train your algos on this specific type of sensors, there is only one company in the world that can do it, which is us.

8 Medical：从睡眠数据到疾病预测

主持人：I do also want to talk a little bit about the endgame here. In a podcast I think two years ago you mentioned that you wanted to solve cancer with this technology. Tell me more about that connection. How do we get from tracking sleep data to solving one of the hardest diseases?

Matteo：So first of all, recently — like probably six months ago — there was a paper published by some scientists at Stanford, and what they proved is that with the data of one night of sleep they can detect 130 diseases. And we started seeing that in our back end, meaning we started seeing correlation between sleep and diabetes and hypertension and other diseases, and we started seeing an accuracy that based on an early test is close to 90% accuracy. This is something that is happening just because of AI. It's fairly incredible how AI is triaging different amounts of data and finding correlations that maybe us as humans we wouldn't have found.

Then specifically for cancer, we have a vision for full body scanning. We believe that while you're asleep we could scan your body and detect certain types of health conditions, including certain types of cancer.

Alexandra：Yeah, it's really cool. At the end of the day, if you think you're standing still in the same position for six hours and you are on a surface, lying down on a surface that is really big, we have space underneath your body and potentially above your body. Then you start thinking first principle in terms of technology: okay, what can you do to a body that is standing still when you have all this space, Wi-Fi connection and electricity?

FDA 审批与睡眠呼吸暂停

主持人：To follow up on that, you are also pursuing FDA clearance for this product as part of preventive care and you guys published an independent study. Tell me just more about that process and why did you decide to pursue this role?

Matteo：We are moving towards what we know internally we call "8 Medical." And so, how can we pursue our medical mission? How can we help millions of people to really extend their life or at least maybe even save their life? One of the first steps will be through sleep apnea. Step one of a journey that hopefully will last many decades. We have a technology that is able to detect if you have sleep apnea while you're asleep, sleeping on the current technology — so it's a software update. And then we also developed a technology that mitigates sleep apnea, and we're pursuing FDA approval for both of them.

意外的用户群：化疗患者与早期心脏病发现

主持人：Have there been any examples of anyone benefiting from seeing signs of diseases early from using your product, even in your own experience? Because I assume you guys are the first users of the mattress cover. What has kind of surprised you while you were using this product?

Matteo：Well, the most unexpected case is for people going through cancer. We didn't expect that, but we discovered that when they're going through chemo, they have hot flashes and the body also becomes less accurate in temperature management. And so we started seeing a lot of people with cancer buying the product. We didn't expect that. We didn't know anything about that, and now we fully understand the why. And our goal is to start helping people with those conditions as well.

Alexandra：And there have been cases too of people who have written to us where they say, "I've been sleeping on the pod for a while." And so they have their data, right? So it sort of builds this repository of what's happening while you're sleeping to your body, and they were not feeling great. They checked their metrics on the Eight app and they saw that it had been a few days where something was off. I think in this case specifically it was their heart rate at rest, and they decided to go to the hospital. In the case of this one person I remember, he said that he ended up needing heart surgery. And so I think that's an example of what data is doing and sort of empowering us where it might not be something that you're interested in checking every day, but the fact that you can passively track your biometrics — it becomes such an important signal when something does feel off, or when we can flag a certain trend like Matteo was saying earlier, and then people can go and do something about it.

消费硬件创业：YC、中国工厂与"naïve 的红利"

主持人：I wanted to move on to you guys building this company. Being a consumer hardware company, I think we can all admit it's pretty tough. When you guys were in YC back in 2015, I assume there weren't that many hardware companies in your batch. What are the biggest challenges of building a hardware company, a consumer hardware company in particular?

Matteo：Well, the first part is to really understand the manufacturing, how long it takes. Then you need to understand the unit economics. It's not something you can adjust quickly. So being able to nail what is your BOM cost or the cost of production of manufacturing of the device and what the margins will be, and then you need to have enough cash or capital to handle returns, replacement, the whole supply chain, the net terms or non-net terms you get from suppliers in the early days.

I think we were lucky to be naïve because it's one of the things that if you know before you start, maybe you don't even start. In our case, we were so naïve, then we had to figure it out as the problems were coming in and we did it. So now 10 years later, the company last year was profitable — strong unit economics, we sell in 35 countries, strong growth.

主持人：You mentioned that you flew to China to tour the factory?

Matteo：Yeah, I moved to China for multiple months because at the time we had prototypes that were working, but I don't think we were fully aware of the delta between having a working prototype and something that can be fully shipped and manufactured. And so we had to learn that, and I moved there. We selected the manufacturers. We also hired our first employees in China, which are still with us — they're actually the longest-tenured employees in the whole company outside the founders. Jack and Tony. And yeah, those people that I found back then, they're still leading our group in China.

主持人：What have you learned about manufacturing from that trip in China?

Matteo：Well, the first one and the biggest is really this delta between a working prototype and a final product. And the main reason is that there are certain steps that you cannot skip. It's called EVT1, EVT2, and DVT, MP, and so on. But more than anything, these steps are really key for the quality and reliability of the device. So you literally cannot skip them. At the beginning, founders, entrepreneurs — they always try to find shortcuts and they think they can cut certain steps, but obviously manufacturing is something that now has been tested for hundreds of years from very smart people, and some of these things can literally not be cut.

进入中国市场：最快增长的地区

主持人：I wanted to talk a little bit about the Chinese market, which is one of the main reasons we are having this conversation here. So you guys started selling in China since April. How has that been?

Alexandra：It's been great. It's been our fastest growing market. I think the reception has been incredible. We were really excited to get into China because in one way or another, China has always been a part of our journey as a business. Like Matteo said, he moved there for many months at the beginning, and the reception has been great — just far beyond what we expected. I think a lot of excitement that the pod was finally available.

主持人：What did you do like in preparation for this launch? Did you go to China and talk to the market there?

Alexandra：Yes, definitely. I mean, we've been going to China now for years, so I think we were familiar enough to know sort of how different it is, right? That's the first thing that I think any brand coming from outside China realizes and why I think most brands are scared to enter — because it's really different than marketing to the rest of the world. But for us, it was an exciting challenge. And what we did first was build a team. So we built a marketing team that would know the market, that would be in China, that could actually take the leadership and guide us through what it would mean to build the awareness of the brand and also all the different advertising channels and how they performed. So that was our strategy: hire the best people possible to make it happen.

主持人：Was there a reason why you guys decided to do this now in this market?

Alexandra：I think it just felt like the right time. I think the brand's reaching a certain point of maturity. We're in over 35 countries and so when we think what is the next big market to tackle, China's always at the top of the list, right? Like it's a huge market. It's a market that's very exciting. There's a lot of innovation. I think the Chinese consumer right now is definitely into everything related to their health and their well-being as well. So, we didn't want to be left behind. We are taking the leadership around the world on everything related to sleep and so we want to be also the leaders in China.

主持人：I would love to hear a little bit about what about the market surprised you. Growing up in China, I always thought it was a very competitive consumer product market. When you were doing market research, what about the market surprised you, even pleasantly surprised?

Alexandra：Yeah, I think it's a pleasant surprise, but it definitely was a surprise to see how demanding the Chinese consumer is. Because as you're saying, it's a market where you find so many products, right? And there's this availability of almost anything that you would want, because it's a country that is manufacturing so much of what we use around the world. But it's really positive to see that the consumer still demands high quality and they want high quality products, right? They're not just compromising. They want the best. They want the best service — and that's something we have to build for. The fact that the way you interact with a brand, you expect a very six-second response on WeChat, and people just need to be available 24/7 is something that in other markets people don't expect. And so it's something of a learning curve, but it's been great because we've also been able to bring those learnings to the service that we provide outside of China because we think that should be the gold standard.

主持人：What cities in China are you in now, or is it mostly online?

Alexandra：Yeah, it's all online right now. And we have a pop-up store in Shenzhen and now we're looking at other locations as well so we can bring the product to life in person and people can try it and buy in person too.

跨文化偏好：中国用户其实更喜欢"暖一点"

主持人：Going back to the Chinese market, and really the global market — because sleep is something where individual physique matters a lot and varies a lot. I, for example, am a pretty hot sleeper. I cannot stand any coldness. But a lot of people in western countries may have a different preference. How do you guys account for those preferences across cultures and regions and countries?

Alexandra：Yeah, it's something that we saw actually when we were doing the pre-market entry in China, that we did have to adjust our understanding of preferences for humans in terms of what they want to feel like when they get in bed. Because actually the Chinese user does prefer the bed to be slightly warmer than what we see in the rest of the world. And so the beauty of it is that the way we account for it is we just see the data and you see the usage. So it's very easy — when you're onboarding to the product you give the product your preferences because it starts from there. Like, who are you? Male, female, age, etc. But then also what do you prefer? So then the AI is just adjusting automatically to that, and then we can start seeing patterns as the user base grows in a certain market — distinct patterns from what we have seen in the rest of the world.

主持人：And as you get more data, does the algorithm keep improving?

Alexandra：Yes.

定价哲学：意大利卓越 × 美国规模 = Apple 模式

主持人：I do want to talk a little bit about the pricing strategy. The price point. So you guys sell in the US right now for around $3,000 for a mattress cover. That is quite expensive for a mattress cover. And China is a market where really all the consumer hardware companies compete on prices. Even with AI models they compete on prices. How do you guys account for that difference? How do you guys think about the pricing strategy?

Matteo：Well, the way we think is just to use some references, right? Think of Apple or think of Tesla. Obviously, right now we are at the Model S if we were Tesla. So, you should imagine the Model Y, X and 3 to come. The idea is to democratize sleep for 8 billion people. And so over time we will do it. The point is when you develop a technology that is so sophisticated, usually at the beginning it is slightly more expensive, but then over time you find ways to optimize through better engineering and that is how you make it affordable.

Then the brand — and our brand is aspirational — and that is where you can make reference to an Apple. So we are not the type of device that wants to be sold at the cheapest price. That is not our position. We just want to build the greatest product, and even if that requires a slightly higher price, that's what we want. That's not our focus, but at the same time we want to make it more, I would say, democratic for 8 billion people.

Alexandra：Yeah. I think ultimately we don't think of competing in price but we compete on outcome. So if we are the product that is going to help you sleep better, we are confident people will buy our product.

主持人：You mentioned in a previous interview that you really look up to the luxury brands from your home country in LA, where when they raise prices they actually receive more demand. Is that kind of the model that you guys are going after as well?

Matteo：I don't think it's luxury — meaning we don't want to be positioned as a luxury brand. Then one of the things I learned from great Italian brands is this obsession for quality and also obsession for building a company that is sustainable, with margins that can take you IPO and make sure that we are going to be around for the next 30 years. But the position is not specifically luxury. It's more what Alexandra said: it's all around delivering the greatest product for sleep enhancement.

Because usually in Italy is all about excellence, quality, slightly higher prices but smaller scale, and that is how they generate enough bottom line to have a great company. Well, instead in the US is all about scale. But then sometimes there is the risk of compromising quality. And so I think there are very few companies like Apple — with Steve Jobs — that was able to almost find the balance between the US way and the American way, where they created a product that is still incredible, is technologically advanced but is still premium and something that people desire, and they don't want to compromise on product just to compress margins. And so that is where Apple sits and that is exactly what I love.

名人与运动员用户：F1、NBA、环法冠军

主持人：You guys have a lot of celebrity users as well. This has kind of become like a status symbol. What are the pain points when it comes to sleeping for those high-performance individuals — the athletes, executives?

Alexandra：Well, I think it's the same as a regular person, right? Like what's fascinating is to see that after all these years working in the sleep space, we see that humans, we sort of all share the same sleeping problems. But obviously, the one caveat would be like professional athletes and athletes that travel often. So we have a lot of F1 drivers who use the product, and a lot of them travel with it across all the races. They're traveling across multiple time zones. They have what, like 20-something races in a season? So it's like very grueling, and so for them recovery is important mostly because they're just traveling so much and they're sleeping away from their bed. So they want to have the same conditions wherever they go around the world. Or we have NBA athletes — in the United States, they're traveling all around the US, but they may have a match on Tuesday and then they have another one on Thursday, late at night. And so those are very particular cases. But we're all sharing the same physiology, which is temperature is still such an important factor in our ability to fall asleep and stay asleep.

Matteo：Another great story is Pogačar, the guy who has won multiple Tour de France. This is the second year in a row where he installs our product in each hotel of each stage of the Tour de France — which is what, probably 20 to 30 hotels every single night — because he can't sleep without our product to recover and deliver the performance he needs to win the Tour de France.

睡眠优化建议：优先级、一致性、光与温度

主持人：For someone who travels a lot, what would you say they should do to optimize their sleep?

Alexandra：Well, I think the first is making enough time for sleep. Wherever you're in the world, just making sure that you're prioritizing that in your day schedule. The second is consistency. I mean, we travel often as well, and I think when it comes down to beating jet lag is trying to stay consistent with your bedtime and wake up time regardless of where you are in the world. And the cues around temperature and light are really the two most important signals for your brain of when you should be sleeping and when you should be awake. So, use those cues to your advantage. So exposure to light and then also the temperature — so dropping that core body temperature in the evening so you can fall asleep, and then raising it in the morning. That's what's going to help you adjust as you go through the different parts of the world.

主持人：So for you guys, after over 10 years, do you feel like you have figured sleep out?

Matteo：Definitely.

Alexandra：Yeah, we do pretty well. We just came back from the West Coast the other day, slept 9 hours and 12 minutes, and that is how I started my Monday.

主持人：Wow. What do you do during the day to keep your sleep consistent?

Alexandra：I think it's just prioritizing it, right? It's basically saying at a certain point of the day, no matter how busy you are, you have to just go to bed. You need to put away your phone, your computer, and go to bed. And as long as you do that and you do it at a consistent time, it becomes a routine for your body. So your body knows that by 10:00 p.m. you're tired, you're going to go to sleep. And then also I rarely use an alarm. My body just wakes up naturally, because we are quite consistent with our schedule.

主持人：How long do you guys sleep every night?

Alexandra：Eight to nine hours.

主持人：Oh, wow. Every night.

Matteo：Yes. Less than eight for us is very difficult — is a disaster.

主持人：Wow, that's fascinating. So you really know your body well.

不规律作息的人如何优化睡眠？

主持人：I actually want to build on that and talk more about the culture, because we talked in the very beginning about how the culture surrounding sleep has changed, starting from Silicon Valley and now around the world. Keeping a consistent sleep routine, it's somewhat of a luxury. For a lot of people who have to work maybe night hours or not consistent hours every day, it is kind of hard to keep that. What does sleep optimization look like for people who may not have the luxury of keeping a consistent schedule?

Alexandra：We get that a lot because we definitely have some members who are even people who work at hospitals or doctors and they have changing shifts. And so what we know is that as much as possible just still prioritizing sleep in your day makes a big difference. So even if the schedule is changing continuously, if you just make enough time for sleep, that will help you. Because the biggest challenge people have who have night shifts or who have changing schedules is that they end up not making enough time for sleep. They try to live the life of a person who has a regular schedule but they actually don't have one. So that would be our first recommendation.

The other one we do see with our product specifically that because of the influence that temperature can have in helping them fall asleep faster and get deeper sleep, that it gives them a boost. So those hours that they are sleeping — even if they may be a little off to their regular circadian rhythm because maybe they were sleeping in the middle of the day — the influence of that temperature coming from the pod can help them achieve higher quality sleep even if it's in the middle of the day.

未来愿景：更多产品、更多国家、IPO

主持人：So my last question is: what is the vision now that you guys are in 35-plus countries around the globe, and over 10 years of making this product — what are you planning to do in the future?

Matteo：More products, more countries, more channels, and at a certain point probably an IPO.

主持人：Yeah, totally. And I guess more people to realize the importance of sleep.

Alexandra：Yes.

主持人：Great. Awesome. Thank you guys so much for joining me.

Alexandra：Yeah, this has been great. Thank you.
