item.description:
## 反常识观察：他们卖的不是"追踪"，而是"无为"
大多数健康科技公司都在往你身上"加"东西——手表、指环、贴片、CGM。Eight Sleep 反其道而行之，把技术**藏到你身下**。这是一个被低估的战略洞察：**当整个行业都在争夺你的手腕和手指时，最大的未被开发的界面是"无意识的六到九小时"。** Matteo 说得很直白："data is not the endpoint for us but is just a mean to an end"——数据不是终点，响应才是。这一句话其实把他们和 Oura、Whoop、Apple Watch 划清了界限：**穿戴设备卖的是"知情"，Eight Sleep 卖的是"代劳"**。这背后是一个更大的哲学转向——从"量化自我"到"外包自我"。健康科技的下一波，不是让你更了解自己，而是让你不用了解自己。
## 跨领域连接：床，正在变成一台隐形的 MRI
访谈里最容易被忽略但爆炸性最强的一段是 Matteo 提到的斯坦福论文——**一夜睡眠数据可以检测 130 种疾病，准确率接近 90%**。把这句话和他"first principle"

item.title: [All-In Podcast] Luca Ferrari, Bending Spoons CEO: The $40K Start, Buying Product-Market Fit & Beating Private Equity
item.dc:creator: All-In Podcast
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的观察：Bending Spoons 不是"科技公司"，而是"科技界的银行"

大多数人把 Bending Spoons 归类为"连续收购者"或"科技版伯克希尔"，但真正的隐喻其实是银行——他们的核心业务不是造产品，而是把"僵尸资产"的现金流重新定价。

传统 PE 做的是财务套利：低价买、砍成本、高价卖。Bending Spoons 做的是技术套利：他们建了一套 50+ 的专有"操作系统"，把这套 OS "刷"进任何被收购的公司里，就像银行用同一套核心账务系统处理不同储户的钱。这套 OS 才是真正的产品，被收购的品牌只是"应用层"。

这解释了一个非常有趣的悖论：Luca 直言几乎不做"客户侧协同"（AOL 卖 Vimeo 广告之类），但疯狂追求"后台协同"。因为前者是营销幻觉，后者才是复利机器。这与传统 conglomerate 的思路完全相反——GE、Berkshire 都强调品牌间的看得见的协同，Bending Spoons 恰恰放弃了这一层，反而胜出。

二、跨领域连接：他们复制的其实是"米其林三星厨房"的模式，不是"投资组合"的模式

我给你一个可能让你意外的类比。听 Luca 描述"800 人的核心团队在不同产品间流动、同一套工具、同一套文化"时，我立刻想到的不是 Danaher 或 Roper，而是Alain Ducasse 或 Joël Robuchon 的餐饮帝国。

Ducasse 拥有全球 30 多家餐厅，但他不是"投资人"——他是把一套烹饪方法论、一套供应链、一套培训体系复制进每一家餐厅。厨师团队在餐厅间轮换，形成"厨师界的通才培养场"。这正是 Luca 说的"一个员工可以花一年重建 AOL 的邮件基础设施，然后七个月重构 Vimeo 的订阅系统"。

这个隐藏的联系揭示了一个更深的真相：Bending Spoons 真正的护城河不是资本、不是技术、也不是并购能力，而是"跨场景通才工程师"这一稀缺人力资产的培养机制。硅谷训练的是"深度专家"（在一个产品上做十年），Bending Spoons 训练的是"高频重装工程师"。这类人才在市场上几乎不存在——因为你必须自己造。这也是为什么 Luca 说"用 5 年可以复制，2 个月不行"。

三、被忽略的宏观信号：为什么 Milan 而不是硅谷是这套模式的必然发源地

这里有一个反常识但极其重要的观察：Bending Spoons 只可能在米兰诞生，不可能在硅谷诞生。

硅谷的整个人才市场结构是"零和抢人"——每个工程师都在追逐下一个独角兽的股票期权，跳槽周期 18-24 个月，任何"运营型公司"根本留不住顶尖工程师。而在米兰，Luca 面对的是80 万份申请对 300 个岗位（0.04% 录取率，比哈佛还低）。因为在欧洲，顶尖工程师没有 100 个平行的 AI 独角兽可以跳，Bending Spoons 成了唯一的"知识密集型雇主"，形成了硅谷永远无法复制的人才引力井。

这与 Chamath 提到的 Charles Koch（Wichita, Kansas）的洞察形成了完美的镜像：顶级复利机器往往诞生在"人才市场供给过剩、需求单一"的地缘经济洼地里。这不是"意外"，而是一个可预测的结构性规律：在人才市场竞争最激烈的地方，反而不可能建立需要"长期人才复用"的组织；在人才被"低估"的地方，才有可能建立起沃伦·巴菲特式的"人才复利"。

一个大胆预测：下一批 Bending Spoons 式的公司，最可能出现在里斯本、华沙、布宜诺斯艾利斯、班加罗尔的二线城市、成都——不会出现在旧金山、纽约、伦敦、新加坡。硅谷的胜利机制本身，注定了它无法孵化这种物种。

📝 转录文本

Luca Ferrari, Bending Spoons CEO: The $40K Start, Buying Product-Market Fit & Beating Private Equity

频道：All-In Podcast
链接：https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6t5yF8ansoQ

开场介绍

You are the reason that NASDAQ exists. [music]

They went from zero to $1 billion in revenue in just 10 years. Bending Spoons CEO Luca Ferrari. We have never lost a bid before. Well, AOL has a new parent [music] again. Milan based tech company Bending Spoons announced it will buy ticketing platform Eventbrite. Bending Spoons is stirring up the market. [music] They go from fixing one zombie app to reviving 20 of them. Half a billion people use our products. We're trying to build a generational company.

Please welcome Luca Ferrari. [music]

寒暄与开场

Hey, here he is. Nice to see you.

You got fans.

All right, Luca, you have uh a great company.

Don't make fun of Luca Ferrari.

I'm not. I'm just —

This is a great Italian entrepreneur, so shut the up.

Absolutely. Absolutely.

I asked somebody yelling like it's Super Mario Brothers in the audience.

We could have another presidential moment here at the All-In podcast. So, if she picks up, if she calls you, then just run the phone over. [laughter]

Got my phone here.

Okay. Just in case.

Yeah, it's ready.

起点：$40,000 与第一次失败

Um, I mean, there's a lot of us that have actually been tracking you for a while. I originally heard about you because you were in Milano, where, you know, my wife's family is from. And you had this incredibly progressive, methodical approach to growth. You did this fantastic podcast with Patrick O'Shaughnessy, which was great. I encourage all of you to listen to it. And you explained the arc of Bending Spoons. I'd love for you to explain to folks the first few years and just all the misery and failure — the nadir of the company — and then the beginning of the ascent.

Yeah. So most of the — I mean the pain — there's been plenty of pain throughout, as for most entrepreneurs I think. But the biggest failures were in the previous startup. So with my co-founders, we launched an AI company in 2010, very early, too early clearly. Crashed and burned three years later.

We're left with about $40,000 in capital we raised from the VC. And, you know, clearly there wasn't a lot to salvage other than our relationship being stronger, and that money that the VC pretty much gifted to us as they didn't want to go through the liquidation process too much in legal fees and too many headaches. They had seen us work pretty hard, and so they told us, "You guys keep it. We'll sell our shares to you for $1, like nominal value, and you go and get a nice vacation. We're clearly a little bit sick in the head." And so we took the money and enthusiastically turned it into seed financing for Bending Spoons.

And we came up with —

You started with $40,000.

40,000 exactly in 2013.

核心战略："购买产品市场契合度"

And we had this strategy which has remained pretty much the same. Obviously, you get smarter, you refine it in time. The idea was: we are not very good at finding product-market fit, or maybe luck plays a big role. Probably both things are true. But we have become pretty good at engineering, design, monetization, marketing in just three years of hard work. And so we should be able to be among the best in the world at that, and we should be able to buy product-market fit from people. They get a good price, we got a good asset we can make more valuable, and then we deploy more capital into making our platform...

The first acquisition — and how much did you pay and how did you get the deal done?

So the first acquisition was — we paid $10,000 give or take — and it was a mobile app for iPhone specifically that you used to personalize your keyboard. Very simple. One kind of developer sold it to us. Obviously very amateurish operation, not that difficult at the time to make it better and more successful.

What were you buying? Were you buying one times revenue, were you buying the revenue, were you buying the app?

That one specifically I think had negligible revenue. It wasn't even really monetized.

Okay.

Which of course is never the case for scaled businesses,

but it had users.

It had users. So what we bought at the time was an app with a bunch of users and good positioning on the app stores. So it would get an influx of new users. And that's remained broadly speaking similar over time — we keep looking for great brands, user and customer bases where we can improve everything ideally and make those assets even more valuable over time. We just do it at a much bigger scale these days, but the underlying concepts have not changed.

技术架构：50+ 专有技术的"操作系统"

Did you rebuild that app? Did you take over the code base and redo it? Just help us understand technically what's going on in the organization — from that business through to some of the bigger ones today. Is it a code business? Are you doing engineering, product, design, marketing, all of the above?

Yeah, most of what we do is engineering and product. We have a core team at this point about 800 people, and I would say probably three quarters of them are either engineers or AI researchers or product designers, product managers. Most of what we do is actually improving technologies and products.

And of course that app, we wrote it completely. But it's very early days. Today we're much more sophisticated. What we do is we bring in — call it an operating system — of 50 plus proprietary technologies. We built an engine to run technology businesses very effectively and efficiently. Really our core product — we swap out the technological foundation of the businesses we buy with that one so we can run it much better. And also the people we transition across our various businesses always play by the same rules; they're more efficient because they find the same tools.

These tools cut across what — HR, finance, tech ops, devops?

Pretty much everything. Orchestration of AI models — check. Recruiting tools — check. Ing platforms — check.

And then do you bring all of the technology spend up to the top co so that you're doing one deal with AWS, one — all the licensing becomes scaled across one entity?

Yeah, that's a lever for value creation. I'd say that's a relatively small one. It probably adds one, two percentage points in EBITDA margins. The more important aspects are being able to drive revenue increases through better product, tech and monetization, sometimes marketing, cost reduction through leaner teams — so more talent-dense teams. But yes, vendor optimization is helpful too.

精简团队的方法论

You were doing the Elon X playbook before he did it. There's some stories that were written about how you right-sized Vimeo's workforce, you right-sized Brightcove...

He called me before doing the X — no, I'm joking.

Oh, he did? Oh — [laughter]

But explain — how do I cut all the people?

No, no, [laughter] he didn't do that. I don't know Elon.

How did you figure out that you could cut 80% of a team and it still works? How do you figure that out? Is that accidental where you're just pushing to a threshold?

I think it's something we learned partially because early days when we were acquiring smaller businesses, typically these people would sell us the asset — say the product — but not the team, because for them it was very small teams. They wanted to move on to whatever other project they had. And so we didn't really know any better. We were establishing teams internally to carry on the work, and the number of FTEs was much smaller than —

the original footprint.

Well, also that. But then when we ended up buying businesses with established teams, we had perhaps naively built teams to run comparable businesses that were much smaller, and so we couldn't explain why you necessarily needed more people.

Partly, yes, through experimentation, we have found call it the sweet spot. Obviously it's never perfect. But overall, the key thing for us is: we want our businesses to be run at a 10 out of 10 level. And we find that generally you're more likely to get that level of performance if you have very very small teams, super high bar for talent, and sense of ownership.

资本结构：从现金流到杠杆

You have a $40-odd billion dollar market cap-ish right now, I think plus or minus.

I don't know actually. I haven't checked the ticker since we —

I think it's roughly in that zone. Which is incredible from starting with the $10,000 acquisition. When did you transition from scaling on cash flow to then using debt and using more sophisticated financial engineering so you can go after these bigger fish?

So historically, we started using debt in 2017 I believe — either 2017 or 2018 — very basic bank loans, TLAs, and then as we — free cash flow, the reinvestment of free cash flow, had always been a thing for us. We have redeployed pretty much 100% of our free cash flow toward acquisitions since the beginning. From 2017, as we got more credible, a little bit wiser and more sophisticated, we went for TLBs, and maybe in the future there'll be bond issuances and other more complex instruments.

We haven't used a whole lot of equity. Actually when we IPO'd, we had only quote-unquote "only" raised about half a billion dollars in primary equity and we were at roughly $20 billion in valuation. And even that half a billion, we had raised pretty much all of it in the previous six months or so. So almost all of our track record we've achieved through reinvestment of free cash flows. But going forward, I think particularly as a public company, using equity tactically here and there could be a good idea.

利率风险与竞争加剧

So with that equity — you're taking loans, I guess, five, six points over Libor — so 10%, 12% loans — and then you buy a business like Airtable, but that means you have to pay $100 million in debt payments per year. If interest rates go up, and there's a 90-some-odd chance they're going to start going up, what does that do with the business? Has to throttle a little bit?

And then my second question: people have been pretty enamored by the progress you're making, and I think you're now facing some Bending Spoons competitors. Maybe you could talk — are you seeing more people show up at these auctions, and it's not just you and two other players?

Yeah. So that is an accelerant to our growth. We would still grow pretty fast if we only used free cash flows, but definitely being able to use debt is a good thing — prudent levels of debt.

I would say I'll give you two parts. First, the risk with the existing indebtedness. All of our debt currently — the average cost, the blended cost — is about 9% give or take, and it's fully hedged. So increases in interest rates would not impact our cost of debt. It matures in 2031. So we are in a position to pay it back completely before maturity. We're currently at two-and-a-half times leverage approximately.

Now if interest rates were to go up substantially, then new debt would be more expensive. I think that would be under most scenarios a net positive for us for a couple of reasons. Our returns unlevered historically have been pretty high — consistently above 25% unlevered. So whether we pay 9% or 12%, of course I'd rather pay 9, but it doesn't break the model. And the second aspect is: typically when interest rates go up, the value of assets goes down. And so as a serial acquirer, I think we're more likely to benefit more from the lower valuations than the higher debt.

Now that depends — I'm generalizing and simplifying a bit — but overall we feel we are fairly well protected and robust when it comes to indebtedness.

We have — all of the processes we have participated in have had other buyers, or almost all of them. I'm sure competition will intensify — or I'm sure it may intensify, who knows. It could also get weaker, seeing private equities' woes historically down. Softer actually — raise less capital to do the same. And so on balance, we might be better off.

It's also I think important to note that it's really painful and time-consuming to replicate what we've built, because a lot of it is based on those technologies which you can't build overnight. You don't even know what to build really if you haven't gone through many years of painful experimentation, mistakes, try and repeat. A lot of the value we create is thanks to those 800-odd people we have painstakingly selected over time — the culture of high performance and a scientific approach to business we have developed. Those things are — there's no shortcut. I still remember hiring the first one person, and then two people, and then four people. You could probably do it in 5 years rather than 13, but not in two months. So I think we'll face competition, but I'm pretty optimistic.

创始人角色的哲学

Follow up if I may. In our industry — the venture capital industry — and even going into public markets, we covet the founder. And if a company loses its founder and the founder authority they have, like Elon to say "hey, we're not going to make the Model X, we're not going to make the Model S, we're going to convert those to Optimus" — those kind of bold bets only made by founders.

You have a slightly different philosophy here. You don't want founders inside the company. You're not looking for that founder authority in each of these brands, based on what I've heard you say. So what is the expectation for your brands? Do you want to create cutting-edge version twos of Eventbrites and Vimeos, or do you just want them to grow at a predictable rate and throw off that cash flow? Talk about the founder role.

Yeah. So I think if you can have a founder with that level of passion and that mentality, it's nine times out of 10 will be a major net positive. Generally, when we end up acquiring companies, these are businesses that have been around for 10, 20 years, even more than 20 years in some cases. And for the founders, if they're still on board — sometimes they aren't on board — for them it's really a moment of "okay, this is a chapter I'm closing, I want to move on."

So the real question there for us: we win if that business does better with us than it would have under previous ownership. Obviously if we could have exceptional founders stay on board and pour their hearts into it, it would be even better. But we can still do well by being a better home for that business than that business staying with the same ownership group and maybe losing the founder anyway. So it's not that we don't want founders, but once companies are sold, the people are generally looking to move on.

M&A 筛选流程

Can you bring us into the M&A deal? Walk us through your screening process. What are we looking for? Are we looking for synergy and integration with the assets that we've bought before? Are we looking purely at cash flow? How do we stack-rank these things? Just walk us through the deal desk.

Yeah. So there's qualitative criteria we use to slim down the long list of businesses that would be interesting targets.

One is scale. That process of integration and profound transformation takes a lot of operational effort. So we can't do a million of these. And by the way, the amount of time and effort it takes to transform a business — we have found it doesn't really scale linearly with revenue. So we're much better off acquiring relatively few sizable companies than a million small ones. So we look for scale.

We look for predictability in earnings — it's a big topic in and of itself, but we like businesses where we are pretty confident we can project at least the next five or six years directionally.

And then we look for businesses where we can create a lot of value. It could be technology, org, product, monetization, marketing — ideally most of these.

协同效应与有机增长的抉择

Does value include the integration with these other assets that you have, or value just means economic value, operation?

Well —

Let me just ask a detailed point of that. Like if you own AOL, you could put ads for Vimeo or Eventbrite or Miro on AOL. If you own Vimeo, you could probably have a sales team that's selling ads on AOL that you can use. How much synergistic effect is there? And if there is synergistic effect, and you've got all this capacity to do design, build, product management, agentic orchestration, testing, AB testing — why not also build organically at the same time and leverage the network effects of the existing businesses?

So historically, we have created almost no value from — let's say — customer-facing synergies. What you described. Plenty of behind-the-scenes synergies. Like I said, it's all built on the same technological foundations, and then there's this large core team of people we move around fluidly.

Going forward — and by the way, the reason why we haven't unlocked a lot of value through customer-facing synergies being that the portfolio wasn't necessarily large enough for good overlaps to materialize — but as it grows more and more, for example now Airtable and Miro are both quite appealing to a lot of enterprises. I think what you are describing could become an additional value creation dimension.

You haven't tried, or you've tried and it hasn't worked?

No, we've tried and it's worked but marginally. So maybe it's helped 3%. But the bulk of it has been bringing 10-out-of-10 excellence in operations, product, monetization, technology on an individual business basis.

And then why not build organically products?

Yeah. So first of all, you can't do everything. I mean Elon can, I — my colleagues and I, we don't think we can. Maybe we should be more ambitious with ourselves, but —

You got a lot on your plate.

There's so many different kinds of products already.

We launch a lot of new things on top of existing brands, but it's not like completely radical innovation. We don't do a lot of that. We try to stay focused on one thing to try to be the very best in the world at it. Also at the scale we are at at this point, we're on a proforma with Miro close to a run rate of $4 billion in revenue. It's difficult — if you look at the percentage of new startups or products being launched that would move the needle, it's very very small. So we would have to deploy a lot of our resources and very unlikely to work.

人才与文化

Sorry, let me — can you just talk about the thing you and I talked about, this point on the talent exodus that happens in Silicon Valley companies when they start to stall out — and that the talent maybe that's working on the business isn't the quality of the talent that you've built in your core platform. How much of that is assessed in that M&A process that Chamath was mentioning?

Well, it's difficult to assess from the outside in, but you can form first-principles opinions. Businesses that are more in a saturation phase, they tend not to be as appealing to some of the most entrepreneurial engineers or designers. And so you can assume that the level of talent will be maybe good, but perhaps not what Anthropic would have. I'm not saying anything shocking here.

They have a very unique kind of talent, but we'll talk about that another time.

Yeah. Okay. We have a big advantage in attracting talent because if you work at Bending Spoons, it may be one of the very few places in the world where we can spend say one year rebuilding the email infrastructure for AOL, and then seven months helping rethink subscriptions on Vimeo, and then build a platform technology to manage payments — all with the same employer, mostly the same colleagues, same culture.

You get broad technical scope.

Exactly. So career opportunities, just staying motivated because it's fun and new. Very high talent density begets high talent density. So there is an element of virtuous cycle. So we have been able to attract a ton of people. Last year, 800,000 applications, we hired fewer than 300 people.

Are they all in Milan? Where are they?

No, no, we are fully — very international as a company. Milan for historical reasons remains like the biggest pool of talent, but London for example is coming up faster. Madrid. We'll be hiring plenty of people in the States, I think starting next year.

欧洲 vs. 硅谷

Brings up an interesting question. Europe as a tech center isn't exactly something that venture capitalists — even late-stage investors — are pursuing. They kind of look at the market there as maybe slower and maybe just not as good of an opportunity, is I think their decision. Rather be in Silicon Valley or American companies, or perhaps Asia. So what's it like being the most aggressive, successful company then in Europe? Or one of them?

I think you're right. No, I think it is the —

I mean Spotify obviously is much better, but Klarna — you're in the top 10 probably. Clearly in the top 10.

What's the talent pool like there? How is it different? Specifically Italy. I noticed when Chamath goes to Italy, maybe there's a little bit less working going on.

An extra button. He goes from three unbuttons to four.

Yeah. The buttons go down and the number of hours in front of a laptop.

Italy changes Chamath. We see it.

How do you keep these Italians working? What's the secret? No, but tell us about the talent pool in running a company in Europe.

So I think Europe has a lot of problems. But I think there's pretty good talent. Half a billion people live in let's say the main part of Europe. So a lot of people have pretty good education. It's not Stanford, but it's solid. And a lot of these people have a chip on their shoulder to prove "we're not necessarily less smart or capable." So you do find a lot of good people.

I do think — the fact that Italians don't work hard is mostly a false stereotype. Yes. I mean my wife, she doesn't work with me, she works in another company. She works a lot of long hours. At our company, we work pretty hard. We generally find that when we acquire companies and we work with existing teams, more often than not, the team we bring in works substantially harder. So — I don't know — we just try to hire people who are intrinsically motivated, very ambitious, hungry, entrepreneurial, and then give them a good reason to do their best work.

为什么不搬到硅谷或纽约

Because they see that they can have — Have you thought of having the headquarters anywhere other than Milan and that it might be an accelerant for the business? New York City where the banking capital is, Silicon Valley the tech capital — have you thought about moving the headquarters?

Why? Luca is totally right. You get like these people — the problem with people in the — like you go to these typical places, typical schools, they think they're geniuses. And it's like, when you actually just look — even just look at AI — who are the major contributors? These are not like — they're not from MIT, Stanford per se. You know, they, uh, they were at CMU. It could well — it could be an advantage.

No, that's sort of what I'm getting at — a huge advantage. When I interviewed Charles Koch, you and I talked about this. What I found so fascinating is he built that business, probably the most extraordinary wholly-owned business on Earth, from nothing effectively in Wichita, Kansas. And I say it's like the Wichita mindset, because he basically kind of ignored everything that was conventional, and he was able to do things his own way.

I don't know anyone that thinks and does things the way you do them, that are based in Silicon Valley. And that might be the reason — because you're in Milan and you're not indoctrinated into cultural thinking.

在科技领域首次成功的"复利收购者"模式

I mean, look, I'll just say — what I find so incredibly interesting about your company and what you're building is: in all of our generations, we've seen these incredible examples of companies that have run your playbook, but in traditional industries. Amphenol, Roper, Danaher, Berkshire. And we've never seen a successful implementation of it in tech. I think you're the best-scaled example.

I mean, Expedia tried. Barry tried. I think it was a little complicated. So it's really exciting to see that this thing can work, because the structural issue was always: how do you underwrite these cash flows? And I think you're proving that they're underwritable — that these things can go out for 7, 8, 9 years. And especially now, if you look at PE — the PE guys are basically like "we don't know what the fuck is going on right" — yet you're still able to go and transact and you're announcing deals at a pace where a lot of the PE folks — so how do you manage this risk? Like it's clearly it's not a risk. You think it's a tailwind for you?

Yeah. I think — you know, private equity is completely different because they keep these companies separate for the most part, to sell them. And so they could never have that technological foundation. Because once you plug it in in a company, what do you do when you sell it to your product competitor? Do you license it to them?

So remove that. They can't have a pooled team of engineers, designers, because if they put them on a business and then they sell it, what do they do? Take the team out and then it's — the team, the business is almost worthless. Or do they sell the team with?

So just the model is completely different. And I believe these structural differences are a big reason why we have been, I'd like to say, successful. So it will never work with the traditional private equity, which has other advantages — you can deploy maybe a lot more capital because it's a little bit more hands off — but you can never achieve the returns I think we have.

结语

I want to say thank you — an incredible business you're building. Congratulations.

Well done everybody.

item.description:
## 一、最反直觉的观察：Bending Spoons 不是"科技公司"，而是"科技界的银行"
大多数人把 Bending Spoons 归类为"连续收购者"或"科技版伯克希尔"，但真正的隐喻其实是**银行**——他们的核心业务不是造产品，而是**把"僵尸资产"的现金流重新定价**。
传统 PE 做的是财务套利：低价买、砍成本、高价卖。Bending Spoons 做的是**技术套利**：他们建了一套 50+ 的专有"操作系统"，把这套 OS "刷"进任何被收购的公司里，就像银行用同一套核心账务系统处理不同储户的钱。**这套 OS 才是真正的产品，被收购的品牌只是"应用层"**。
这解释了一个非常有趣的悖论：Luca 直言几乎不做"客户侧协同"（AOL 卖 Vimeo 广告之类），但疯狂追求"后台协同"。因为**前者是营销幻觉，后者才是复利机器**。这与传统 conglomerate 的思路完全相反——GE、Berkshire 都强调品牌间的看得见的协同，Bending Spoons 恰恰放弃了这一层，反而胜出。
## 二、跨领域连接：他们复制的其实是"米其林三星厨房"的模式，

item.title: [Dwarkesh Clips] Why AI Progress Keeps Surprising Even Its Researchers - Noam Brown
item.dc:creator: Dwarkesh Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽视的"人口方程式"：算力 × 3 的静默复利

Noam Brown 抛出的那个数字——同样的算力每年能跑出 3 倍规模的"有效人口"——远比它听上去更具颠覆性。人们习惯把 AI 进展想象成"模型变聪明"，但他实际上是在讲智能人口的马尔萨斯式爆炸，只不过没有资源上限：因为在这个宇宙里，土地（算力）本身也在指数扩张。

真正意外的地方在于：连他也在保守估计。把 3x/年 的效率提升，与背景中同步指数增长的算力叠加，你得到的不是线性叠加而是指数的指数。这意味着到 2030 年代中期，"每个实验室内部住着好几个地球的人类级智能"不是科幻叙事，而是当前曲线的保守外推。人类历史上从没出现过一个系统，其"公民数量"在同一栋楼里每年翻三倍——这已经不是经济学问题，而是接近相变的物理学问题。

二、预测视界的坍缩：一个来自混沌理论的隐秘信号

最容易被听众滑过、但最应该让人后背发凉的，是那位研究员的一句话："我以前能预测未来 12 个月，现在只敢预测 3 个月。"

这句话的重要性不在字面，而在于它揭示了一个Lyapunov 指数正在上升的动力学系统。在混沌理论中，当一个系统的不稳定性增加，可预测的时间窗口会指数级缩短。研究者的"信心半衰期"从 12 个月压缩到 3 个月——按同样的比率外推，明年可能是 3 周，后年可能是 3 天。

跨领域联想：这与地震前动物的行为异常、心脏病发作前 HRV（心率变异性）的坍塌、金融崩盘前波动率的自相关消失是同一类信号——不是"进展加快"，而是系统正在进入相变前的临界区。Brown 在描述的其实不是速度，而是可预测性本身的解体。

三、下注文化背后的"系统性反向乐观偏差"

那个 Navier-Stokes 的 $1,000 赌局——Frontier Lab 的研究员押 2030 年，Brown 押 2027 年，结果两周后就实现——揭示了一个心理学上少有人命名的现象：

在指数系统内部工作的人，会系统性地低估指数。

这与"人们总是过度乐观"的常识完全相反。原因是：每一次被现实反超，研究者会更新自己的锚点，但更新的幅度总是不足——他们把最近的惊喜当作"异常值"而不是"新趋势线"，然后基于修正过的旧模型再做线性外推。这是贝叶斯更新中的先验刚性（prior stickiness），在指数环境下会累积成灾难性偏差。

最出人意料的推论：这意味着最悲观的 AI 时间线预测者，往往是离得最近的人——不是因为他们看得更清楚，而是因为每天的具体工作让他们看不到复利曲线。就像在飞机内部走动的人感受不到 900 km/h 的速度。真正准确的时间线预测者，可能反而是那些远离前沿、只看积分曲线的外部观察者。

四、隐藏的测量悖论：AI 加速无法被诚实度量

Brown 在讨论"AI 加速研究"时暴露了一个深刻的认识论陷阱： - 问"三年前的任务，今天用 AI 快多少倍"——答案是 100x - 问"今天的任务，没有 AI 会慢多少倍"——答案可能只是 3x

同一个现实，两个数字相差 30 倍。这不是测量误差，而是任务空间本身在被 AI 重塑：你会去做那些 AI 让你能做的事，不做那些它没帮助的事——因此"效率"这个词在指数环境下失去了稳定的分母。

跨领域连接：这正是经济学里困扰了三十年的Solow 悖论（"我们到处都能看到计算机，除了在生产率统计里"）的镜像版。经济学家最终发现，不是计算机没用，而是 GDP 这个度量本身跟不上计算机改造经济结构的速度。今天的 AI 加速也一样——我们没有合适的坐标系去度量一个正在重写自身坐标系的过程。

这或许才是"奇点"最诚实的定义：不是某个具体的时刻，而是我们的测量工具集体失效的那个区域。

📝 转录文本

一、基准情境：即便进展速度不加快，仅仅"维持"就足够眩晕

One thing that's been giving me a bit of singularity vertigo is realizing that even if the current rate of progress simply continues — so it doesn't have to speed up, literally just continues apace — as some of the other headwinds you talked about come up (right? that it's harder to find problems, it's more long-horizon, maybe by the 2030s compute can't keep scaling at this exponential level)… if we simply continue the current rate of progress, I think people are not taking seriously what that implies as we cross over beyond the human horizon.

Here are some of the things that it implies. I think it's really hard to reason about what smarter-than-human intelligences will be like, so let's just think in terms of human population sizes.

The current rate of progress makes it so that a given level of compute allows you to basically run a 3x bigger effective population every single year. And also compute is growing in the background anyway. So you could have a situation where each of the labs — by the end of 2030, probably much sooner, but let's say by the end of 2030 — has enough compute to run, let's say, hundreds of millions of human-level intelligences, based on where the capabilities will be at that point.

And then I think people are not taking seriously: the current level of progress means that a few years down the line, by the mid-2030s or earlier, you would have many Earths' worth of human-level intelligences within each lab — and they'll probably be qualitatively superhuman. But anyway, this is like a base case, I don't know.

Yeah, progress is really fast.

二、研究者自己也在被反复"打脸"：IMO 金牌与 Navier–Stokes 的赌局

And I think that's 100% true. It's worth pointing out: researchers are continually being surprised at the rate of progress.

If you look at what — even among researchers in AI — what were the projections for getting an IMO Gold in 2025? The idea that it could be done with a general-purpose language model, with no tools and no access to the internet — I think even people at OpenAI thought this was outrageous. They thought it was almost impossible.

And then you get to 2026, and literally two weeks before we got Navier–Stokes, I was talking with a researcher at a Frontier Lab about how long it would take to get a Millennium Prize. He was willing to bet me $1,000 that it would take past 2027 — he thought it would take until 2030. And I took that bet. But even I thought it would take longer than how long it's likely to take.

So people have been continuously surprised, even inside the labs.

三、预测窗口的塌缩：从 12 个月到 3 个月

I was literally just talking to somebody yesterday who was working on the Navier–Stokes effort, and he was telling me that he used to say it's really hard to predict where AI would be in 12 months — if somebody asked him, "oh, where are things going?", he would feel comfortable making predictions for the next 12 months, but beyond that, you know, he's just like "I don't know."

And now he's saying he just doesn't feel comfortable making predictions beyond 3 months.

So it is really true that things are going very fast right now.

Yeah.

And you talk about 2030 — like, I don't know what the world looks like in 2030.

That's the truth.

四、AI 劳动的全面自动化？内部加速与 Codex 支出

Yeah. Do you expect the sort of full automation of AI labor — or let's say 95% automation of AI labor — '28, '29, '30, '27?

I don't know. I just said I don't know what the world looks like in 2030.

I mean, we actually released a blog post recently on internal acceleration at OpenAI. We show, for example, that the amount that researchers are spending on Codex is — the top 1%, I think as of early August, were spending like $7,000 or $8,000 a day on Codex for internal use. That's on an exponential. It's going to keep increasing.

五、归因难题：人做的，还是 AI 做的？

And there's a question of: okay, if that keeps going, then how much do you assign to just the AI doing work versus the humans doing work? Is it 95%? Is it 5%?

It's actually really hard to reason about this for a few reasons.

First of all, if it's the human directing the AIs to do the work, then how much do you attribute to the human? How much do you attribute to the AI?

The other thing is that these AIs are jagged — they're exceptionally good at some things. For example, they're exceptionally good at looking over datasets and checking every single data point to see: is this of sufficient quality? You can disproportionately use the AIs for those things compared to previously. So yes, you're using AI way more than before, and it's making some things go 100x faster and 100x better. But there are some things where it doesn't make a huge difference yet.

And of course, if something is suddenly 100x faster and 100x better, you're going to do more of that thing.

六、测量的悖论：两种"加速"是两个完全不同的问题

So, are you comparing to a speed-up of like three years ago — versus, is the question more like: given what we were doing three years ago, how much faster are we able to do it now, versus given what we're doing now, how much slower would it have been three years ago?

These are actually two very different questions. So, anyway, it's really hard to measure.

I do feel confident in saying that things are going faster now than they were even a year ago because of AI progress, and I think that acceleration will continue. A lot of people in the field have very high error bars on this sort of thing.

七、如果非要给一个数字：3x 加速的震撼含义

If you had to put a gun to my head and ask me for a number — I could see things going 3x faster.

Yeah.

And that is huge, right? Already the pace of progress is incredible. Even if we don't get any uplift — like you said, things are going to go much faster by the time we get to 2030. We don't even know what that world looks like.

I think if we get a 3x uplift from internal acceleration, that is massive. Like, right now we're releasing — think about where we were three years ago. If we make that progress in one year, that's huge.

Right.

It'd be like going from not even having o1 — just having non-reasoning models — to Astra.

Yeah. In a single year.

Yeah, yeah.

八、不确定性本身的形状

So I do think things go faster. It could be that things only go 50% faster. It could be — I think it's unlikely, but it's possible — that things go 10x faster. There's a lot of uncertainty around this, and at least from my perspective, I have a lot of uncertainty about it.

If you enjoyed this clip, you can watch the full episode here and subscribe for more clips. Thanks.

观看原视频 →

## 一、被忽视的"人口方程式"：算力 × 3 的静默复利
Noam Brown 抛出的那个数字——**同样的算力每年能跑出 3 倍规模的"有效人口"**——远比它听上去更具颠覆性。人们习惯把 AI 进展想象成"模型变聪明"，但他实际上是在讲**智能人口的马尔萨斯式爆炸，只不过没有资源上限**：因为在这个宇宙里，土地（算力）本身也在指数扩张。
真正意外的地方在于：*连他也在保守估计*。把 3x/年 的效率提升，与背景中同步指数增长的算力叠加，你得到的不是线性叠加而是**指数的指数**。这意味着到 2030 年代中期，"每个实验室内部住着好几个地球的人类级智能"不是科幻叙事，而是当前曲线的**保守外推**。人类历史上从没出现过一个系统，其"公民数量"在**同一栋楼里**每年翻三倍——这已经不是经济学问题，而是接近相变的**物理学**问题。
## 二、预测视界的坍缩：一个来自混沌理论的隐秘信号
最容易被听众滑过、但最应该让人后背发凉的，是那位研究员的一句话：**"我以前能预测未来 12 个月，现在只敢预测 3 个月。"**

item.title: [GoldRepublic Global] Luke Gromen: 53 Countries Defaulted at This Debt Level — We're Next
item.dc:creator: GoldRepublic Global
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、"两个方向都通向同一个悬崖"——货币政策的量子叠加态

Gromen 最反直觉的判断，其实是把美联储放到了一个逻辑陷阱里：加息和降息都是通胀性的。这不是政策失误，而是系统的相变（phase transition）。想想水在 100°C 时的状态——加一点热量它变成蒸汽，减一点热量它凝成液体，但在临界点上，"加"与"减"的方向已经不再决定结果，能量密度本身才是。

美联储现在正站在这个临界点上：降息 → 美元贬值 → 大宗商品飙升 → 通胀回来；加息 → 政府利息支出爆炸 → 财政赤字加剧 → 财政主导地位 → 通胀回来。这不是货币现象，是财政引力场把货币政策吸走了。这就是为什么 Gromen 说"美联储比人们意识到的更被逼入死角"——他描述的其实是一个决策变量已经从系统中消失的状态。

二、意想不到的观察：Bitcoin 是煤矿里的金丝雀，而黄金是煤矿本身

大多数分析师把 Bitcoin 和黄金当作同一交易的两个表达（debasement trade）。但 Gromen 埋了一个非常精妙的层次结构：Bitcoin 是先行指标，黄金是终局资产。

这在信息论上非常优雅。Bitcoin 的流动性更薄、波动性更高、投机成分更浓——正因为如此，它对边际资金流入反应速度最快。而黄金是被央行、主权基金、传统资本压舱的"深水层"，反应慢但代表结构性再定价。

跨领域连接：这跟神经科学中的"预激活神经元"一模一样——大脑决策前 200 毫秒，某些边缘神经元会先放电，虽然这些放电不构成决定本身，但它们的模式提前泄露了决定的方向。Bitcoin 就是宏观系统的预激活神经元。如果你想观察黄金的下一波结构性上涨，不要看黄金——看 Bitcoin 何时脱钩于纳斯达克，重新与实物资产同步。

三、"我宁愿仓库里有铜，也不要银行里有现金"——这句话本身就是历史信号

这句话不是投资建议，是恶性通胀的语言学化石。Gromen 特别提到："每一次世界上的恶性通胀，都是从人们开始说这种话开始的。"

这里藏着一个社会学的相变机制：当足够多的人从"资金 → 资产"的心智模式，切换到"资产 → 资金"的心智模式时，货币的社会契约层就崩塌了。魏玛德国、津巴布韦、委内瑞拉，甚至最近的土耳其，都遵循同样的语言学序列：先是精英开始持有实物（铜、铁、房、金），然后中产模仿，然后普通人恐慌性抢购日用品。

跨领域连接：这跟生态学里的"营养级联崩溃"（trophic cascade）完全同构。当顶级捕食者（在这里是"对法币的信任"）从生态系统消失，整个食物网不是缓慢退化，而是几周内重构。Gromen 说"不是几年，甚至不是几个季度，而是几个月"——他其实是在描述一个营养级联的倒计时。

四、最容易被忽略的隐藏结构：债券市场"挤进"黄金市场的物理不可能性

"You're going to see gold rise because basically the bond market is going to try to fit itself into the gold market."——这句话值得反复咀嚼。

全球债券市场规模约 130 万亿美元，黄金市场（可投资部分）约 15-20 万亿美元。当哪怕 5% 的债券资金试图"迁移"到黄金——那是 6.5 万亿美元冲击一个能吸收几千亿的市场。这在数学上不是"上涨"，是"重估"。

物理类比：这就像把大西洋的水通过一根花园水管排空。水管不会"流得更快"——水管会爆裂。所谓黄金"暴涨到 5000/10000 美元"，不是黄金变贵了，是债券作为财富储存工具的功能性失效被市场瞬间定价。

真正的启示不是买黄金，而是：任何依赖债券作为"无风险抵押品"的金融结构（回购市场、保险公司准备金、养老金匹配、银行资本充足率），都在一个正在消失的地基上运行。这才是 Gromen 说的"53 个国家在这个债务水平违约"的深层意义——违约不是事件，是抵押品消失的必然算术。

📝 转录文本

开场：核心观点速览

Both Fed cuts and Fed rate hikes are inflationary at this point. Doesn't matter what they do. The next recession, we're saying yields are going up in the long end. Maybe they'll go down for like one little second, but they're gonna scream higher.

I would rather have copper in my warehouse than cash in my bank. That's how every hyperinflation in the world has ever started. That's what people say at the beginning of hyperinflation.

You're gonna see gold rise because basically... you're going to see gold rise because basically the bond market is going to try to fit itself into the gold market. And by the way, I think probably one of your early indicators will be Bitcoin.

We're not talking about years. We're probably not talking about quarters. We're probably talking about months until that tipping point is reached. I think the debasement trade is back on, which makes me want to buy gold, Bitcoin, silver.

主持人介绍与欢迎

Welcome to the Macroscopic Podcast. My name is Alex... Welcome to the Macroscopic Podcast. My name is Alexei Joronoff and I'm the host, and this is presented by Gold Republic. And today I have the extreme pleasure and honor to welcome on this podcast Luke Gromen.

Welcome, Luke.

Thanks for having me here, Alexei. It's great to be here. It's great to finally catch up.

It is. As I told you already before, I've been following you since years, and I think you've definitely been one of my top macro analysts out there. Lyn Alden and you... Lyn Alden and you were actually one of the people I followed the most back then five, six years ago, when I started really digging deeper into this journey of trying to understand this very complex monetary system.

第一问：最"异端"的货币观点

And one of the first questions I ask the guests who appear for the first time on my podcast is the following: what is your most heretical view on the monetary system? And this might be a bit of an easy one for you.

I think my most heretical view... well, view on the monetary system is that both Fed cuts and Fed rate hikes are inflationary — on the monetary system, is that at this point, doesn't matter what they do. They are, they are much more cornered than people realize. And I think that is very much a variant perception.

追问：为什么方向已经不再重要

Why does it not matter if the Fed hikes rates or cuts rates — in this case, Warsh, who was supposed to actually cut rates for his president? It's, uh, for his, uh, for his president... um, why does it matter?

Because if you cut rates with inflation above target...

观看原视频 →
