item.title: [a16z] Replit CEO Amjad Masad on What Young People Should Learn in the AI Era
item.dc:creator: a16z
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

三个让人意外的观察

1. "毛刺人"（The Glitch Person）作为文明的免疫系统

Amjad 引用《城市与星辰》的隐喻表面是在说"叛逆青年很珍贵"，但更深的洞察是：一个高度优化的系统必须依赖故障来更新自己。这与生物学中的"体细胞超突变"（somatic hypermutation）惊人相似——免疫系统故意在B细胞的抗体基因区制造错误，以生成能识别未知病原的抗体。也就是说，进化从不奖励精确复制，进化奖励可控的错误。今天的大学是一个"高保真复制系统"——它太擅长把 18 岁的人复印成"合格公民"，因此它正在制造一个没有免疫力的文明。Peter Thiel 奖学金、Replit Academy 这些实验的真正意义不是"造更多创业者"，而是给社会补充"故意的错误率"。

2. Replit CEO 谈教育，却泄露了他对"公司"的秘密判断

注意他中段突然插入的一句："the future of companies is going to change... the company will run itself... a self-driving company." 这句话表面上是跑题，但如果你把它和整段对话叠加看，会发现一个惊人的对称：他对未来"学校"的设想（无年级、无考勤、以兴趣为绳、AI 提供个性化路径）几乎就是他对未来"公司"的设想。也就是说 —— 他不是在设计一所学校，他是在为自己未来的自驾公司训练第一批操作系统兼容的员工。Academy 是 Replit 的用户获取漏斗的最上游，同时也是"新型组织形态"的 alpha 测试。学校即产品原型。跨界连接：这是硅谷版本的"耶稣会学院"——16 世纪耶稣会通过办学校，把自己的世界观装进未来精英的操作系统。

3. "过早优化"这一编程术语被他用来批判 VC，其实指向了一个更黑的真相

他把过早融资比作"premature optimization is the root of all evil"，又把它类比为音乐产业的剥削性合约——这已经很尖锐了。但更深一层的意外是：当资本能够以极低成本"预订"一个年轻人的十年，它本质上在做的是"人生期权的贱卖套利"。就像高频交易之于股票——市场深度不足的地方，越先出手的人赚得越狠。18 岁人生"深度不足"（他还没搞清楚自己是谁），所以任何一个提前锁仓的资本方都在做认知不对称套利。这解释了一个悖论：为什么"YC 给 50 万"和"斯坦福给一门课"其实都是同一种东西的两个变种——两者都在贴现你未成型的自我，只是一个用金钱贴现，一个用学分贴现。真正稀缺、真正未被制度化的，是他反复强调的那个"中间地带"：不承诺、不打分、不锁仓的两年。

一个隐藏的系统性真相

整场对话里 Amjad 从"要做异端"讲到"要respect the elders"，从"disagreeable"讲到"interpersonal skills"，看起来在自我矛盾。但如果把这些放在一个坐标里看——他其实描述的是创业者的"张力管理"：一个人身上必须同时住着两个不兼容的人格（Julian Jaynes 会说这是二分脑的现代版）。这和顶级围棋手、顶级即兴爵士乐手的特征是同构的——在结构里保持自由，在自由里维持结构。真正稀缺的不是叛逆，也不是服从，而是能在两者之间高频切换的"元灵活性"。这也解释了为什么他强调"discernment 只能通过 reps 获得"——因为你不能被教会切换，你只能通过反复失败学会切换的时机。这就是他真正想构建的教育：一个允许你以低代价练习切换的道场。

📝 转录文本

开场：年轻人的真正效用

Ultimately, the utility of young people is to question deeply held beliefs, is to be heretics. And in today's college, it actually the opposite. It kind of beats any outside thought out of them. I just really want to see a world in which it's okay if you want to go on a side quest and go do something that's kind of oddball, but also might end up being super amazing if it works out.

The future of companies is going to change. The whole industry has changed. It's a complete reset on a technology perspective. I'd want to go to a college that's not prescriptive about what I learn. I'm motivated by what skills can it give me in order to achieve what I want to build. One of the core tenants of the academy sidesteps this problem entirely. We don't care if you graduate or not. We don't have grades. We don't have tests. The amount of weight to push against should be a lot less.

When you see a 18-year-old that is really inspiring to you that you're like, I got to spend time with this person. What are they doing that is capturing your interest?

《城市与星辰》：一个关于"毛刺人"的寓言

I think the first thing is that they — as we were talking — uh I remember this sci-fi story that I read once. It's called The City and the Stars, and it's about this future city that's governed by AGI. We sort of invented AGI. It's now governs all of our lives. It solves all all problems, all human problems. There's no wars, there's no disease, everyone lives forever, and people spend their time working on like a thousand-year art projects and doing all sorts of random things to fill up their time.

But they found this problem where they accumulate so much knowledge and memory it becomes like harder to keep it all in their heads. So they invented this technology where they go into some kind of laboratory and they compress their memory — sort of like context compression that we do with AI today. They go through all the memories and they compress them, and then they go through a boot camp to retrain them for their life. So they invented a new way to be born. But it's not — you're not fundamentally a new person. You're still the same person. You're just editing your memory.

But there's a glitch that happens in this system, in this machine, and there's a new person that is fundamentally born new. And he immediately starts causing problems. In the boot camp he starts doing weird things, new things, and everyone's like, "Whoa, that's crazy. You shouldn't be doing that. That's not how we do things." It becomes very disruptive.

And then when they go out into this like city, he starts asking questions like, "What's out there? What's in the stars? What's outside our city borders?" They're like, "We don't talk about outside our city borders."

Sounds like Silo a little bit. "It's probably dangerous out there." Yeah. A little bit like Silo. A little bit like Fallout.

Um, and I don't want to get into the spoilers too much, but eventually — that's what he has — so much drive to change things and go discover the stars. That's why it's called The City and the Stars. The story unfolds in that way and he finds all sorts of interesting things out there.

大学的真问题：它把年轻人变成了什么

And I'm reminded of this because as we're talking about what is college and what is it for, I think a related question is: what is the utility of young people in society? And I think ultimately the utility of young people is to question deeply held beliefs, is to be heretics.

And in today's college it's actually the opposite. It kind of beats any outside thought out of them, right? It tells you you're stupid. We've figured everything out. You need to learn our way, and we need to prepare you for the outside world so you can get a job and be a perfect citizen and go get married, have kids, and get a house and a car and live happily ever after. That world doesn't exist anymore. You can do really well in college and you can still be unemployed with a huge debt.

But not only that, I think the real civilizational missing opportunity is that person in The City and the Stars. It took a glitch to get someone with a clear mind to be able to question deeply held beliefs. And every one of us — we probably have blind spots in society. We have a lot of blind spots in Silicon Valley. There's a lot of ideas that don't come out of Silicon Valley, because there's a monoculture here. There's a certain way of thinking. Every culture is somehow a monoculture. Even the most radical cultures like Silicon Valley.

And so what do you need from young people? You need them to experiment. You need to encourage them to try impossible things. And every now and then they're going to have a breakthrough that once we thought was impossible and now it's suddenly possible because the technology changed, something changed. So college ultimately should be about that. Let's get these people with clear minds, zen mindsets, first-principles mindsets, and encourage them to go question the deeply held beliefs.

如果你 18 岁：理想中的大学

No, I think that's well said. I mean, imagine if you were 18 today and you were able to design your ideal experience — in terms of how much you go to class, to what projects you work on, to what kind of deep study you would engage in, to what you'd want to study. What are some principles that you would add to that, in terms of how you wish, if you could redo 18 to 22, but in 2026, how you'd think about it.

Yeah. I'd want to go to a college that's not prescriptive about what I learn. I want to be in an environment where there's a lot of different paths — like, there's a class about something totally I haven't even thought about, it's outside my world.

乔布斯的书法课

Right. We're talking about the story with Steve Jobs. One of the most inspiring speeches he gave is the Stanford commencement speech, and he talked about connecting things backwards. And so the way Steve Jobs approached college, I think it's the ideal experience of college — where he went to Reed College but he couldn't afford it, so he dropped out but kept dropping into different classes. One of them was calligraphy.

And in the calligraphy class he didn't know why he was interested in it, and he just did it and learned it. Later on when they were inventing the Mac and inventing user interfaces, they're like, "Oh, we should have proportionally spaced fonts, we should have — people should be able to select fonts." And that was a direct callback to his college days learning about fonts and calligraphy.

And so this meandering that I think modern society thinks is sort of useless — I think it's actually the most useful in college. Can you take a class that would change the direction of your life because you discover something totally new and outside of your world? So that's one — I would like to have enough freedom to select the kind of things I want to study.

出勤率与自由

The other thing is: if I am engrossed in building something, give me the space and time to do it. One of the things about my college that was really hard is — we had attendance. Like, they counted attendance. And if you didn't attend for like six classes, you're banned.

And so if I'm going to school, I'm doing all these different things, I'm meeting interesting people, and then I have an idea and I'm manically working really hard — give me the space to do it. Don't expel me from my —

Yeah. Exactly. For sure.

同伴质量

And finally, the quality of people. Like, I think if you're around conventionally minded people, eventually you'll be conventionally minded. If you're in an environment that encourages people to question those deeply held beliefs, I think you will be able to do that.

主持人：伯克利的经验与"侧任务"

Yeah. I went to UC Berkeley — go Bears — and I did enjoy it a lot. But one of the things that I really enjoyed was that there was actually no expectation of attending class for most situations. And so I had many semesters where I had like three jobs in one semester. And often the time that I was expected to be at work overlapped with my class. So I just looked at my midterm schedule in advance and I said, "Okay, these are my two midterms. Hey boss, can I take those two days off?" And otherwise I was working.

But it's interesting because now I look back and I did enjoy that, but oftentimes I look at that experience and say: well, what if the environment was supportive of this? What would happen? Because honestly, I think today when I talk to students — it's been 20 years plus — when I talk to students today, they all do this. This used to be odd behavior, and now it's becoming the norm.

And the thing that's weird though is that it's not encouraged yet. It's still not allowed. And so for me personally, I just really want to see a world in which it's okay if you want to go on a side quest and go do something that's kind of oddball but also might end up being super amazing if it works out.

You should be able to use the college resources. You should be able to use the computer lab, the compute, the bio lab, whatever it is. You shouldn't be going against the grain. It should be actively encouraging you. Actually, they should be bringing resources to you more if you do it. If you have a crazy idea that's taking off, you shouldn't be hiding it from your college. They should be coming, like, "Oh my god, this is amazing. Let's give them more."

Totally. There's this kid, Eric — I think he's Rich's friend — who has to take investor calls from the bathroom because he's hiding in the school. Yeah. They should be [laughter] coaching them through it or enabling it in some way. Bringing in demo day or something.

兴趣即入口：从篮球到统计学

This kind of thing — a couple comments. One is going back to your thing around calligraphy. People get these interests that might seem random and might be random, but in other ways might tie back in other ways. And I think there are ways in which the school can develop — it's hard to force natural interest.

And so for example, I was obsessed with basketball as a kid, but I was also the kid who would ask my math teacher, like, "What's the point of this? Help explain it to me." And if she could have explained it to me, maybe I would have gotten excited. If she would say, "Hey, you're obsessed with basketball — you need to understand the salary cap. Or, actually, basketball is very analytical now, in terms of people using stats and data to evaluate players, and so if you don't understand this, you're not going to be a good student of the game" — that would have gotten me really excited.

And that's why I'm so excited about Alpha School.

Is the way that they take people's natural interests and get them to learn the things they're going to need to know over time out of that.

The thing that's so hard is — we all know the education, the academic industry of education, if you will, the academic canon of education is completely on board with this. They totally understand that it would be great if every student could have a customized curriculum. Joe Lemon of Alpha School talks about this all the time. The problem is that practically it seems impossible. But actually I think now is the moment when it's completely reverted. And it's not just possible — it's actually impossible to imagine why you wouldn't do that.

Specifically, for me, if I think about the academy: if you are going to learn coding, I don't want you just to take a class on Python. No — go build something that you're super excited about in Python. Use it as a tool to learn the language. And the great thing about today, with AI, is every single student can go and do that on their own. And they don't need a customized syllabus or exercise given to them. They just need the freedom and confidence to say: yes, you're allowed to do this. Yes, absolutely. We're super excited about it.

Yeah. I mean, the buzzword for it is like project-based learning. There shouldn't be a buzzword for it — because that should be the standard.

The idea that you're learning something and you don't know the utility of it — I think is a very modern invention. It's very weird to have done in society, that you would go into a statistics class and you would never learn that you could use it for basketball or for some of your other interests.

There was this inversion for a long time of how we learn things — like you would go and you would learn some of the things and you had no idea what the utility is, how you would apply it in the real world. And for someone like me, and I think for a lot of people that are more pragmatically minded, I'm not motivated at all by a pure pursuit of knowledge. I'm motivated by skills. What skills can it give me in order to achieve what I want to build and achieve my dreams? And every now and then, you find a teacher that is able to motivate your learning by telling you what kind of skills you can acquire because of it.

相反的批评：过早职业化

Totally. Well, it's interesting because there is a critique that we're addressing — that we're solving for — which is: there are certain schooling environments where there's very little practical skills gained, or they don't train for the real world afterwards, even though they claim to. But then there's also this opposite critique, and I'm curious how we balance this — which is: some people are sort of professionalizing way too soon and not having childhoods, or not spending time to cultivate intellectually or as a person. Otherwise there's still this sort of ineffable quality that some people think you get at an experience like college, where you're meeting new people, getting new friends, going to parties — I don't know what people are describing exactly — studying the great books, etc. What do you think about the stuff that's gained beyond just the technical skills of building a company or working at a company?

I think there's this huge unfair choice that a lot of young people are provided today. It's either: go get a four-year school where there's a lot of structure around what you should be doing. You're going to have to attend classes, do homework and tests and grades and all of that. And then there's another option — which is you can go and start a startup, and someone will give you $50,000 tomorrow to start it.

And the problem that I see is — look, I think there's lots of people who are still going to go to college and love it. And I think there are lots of young people, even at 16, 17, who should be starting a startup. But I think there's an amazing massive group of people who — I don't know about you guys, but certainly for me, when I was 17 or 18, I knew I wanted to enter business, but it was so nice to have a couple of years to explore and learn, and no pressure. And so personally, I think the investor track should be way underutilized — like only a very small number of teenagers should be raising money instead. And by the way, grants are great, right? Do something temporary. Make it clear it's temporary. That's fine. But the pressure of making a 10-year commitment at 18 isn't for most people. And then the structure of college isn't for everybody either.

And so for me, this middle ground of having two years where you can really explore and you can do whatever you want without the pressure — and Silicon Valley will come to you and provide you with all the information and the resources that you need, and when you have a cool idea, it's just like more, more — that's super exciting to me.

Premature Optimization：把编程原则套到人生上

Yeah. I mean, in programming we have this concept of premature optimization. The idea — I think the saying is premature optimization is the root of all evil. That's how bad people think it is. Where you start optimizing a program that is not eventually relevant or consequential.

And I think a lot of starting startups is premature optimization. And I see in a lot of kids now, where they're part of a group and a lot of their friends are raising a lot of money, and some of them are becoming unicorns, and it just becomes — the motivation is envy. Really negative motivation as opposed to positive. And then they pre-commit to an idea they're not even interested in, and they raise money for it, and they are kind of pre-optimizing for some path that they haven't really reached yet.

And so that's why I always come back to this idea of curiosity. Like — what is actually driving you? Once you find that idea that you want to dedicate your life to, or dedicate the next 10 years to, it's going to have such gravity you're not going to be able to avoid it. For me, I tried not to start Replit — actively not to start it — but it kind of exploded into a startup on its own.

And that's the feeling you should get. It's almost like I guess I have to do it, right? Because there's so much momentum behind it.

I think there's a predatory thing that happens right now — where I've heard that VCs go to Stanford students and they give them a million dollars, not even $50K. $50K is like [laughter] — a million dollars pre-idea. And the moment you start your idea, you already have a cap table.

I think that's sort of like the music industry. Kanye talked a lot about this — where it's how predatory it is. You find a young artist and you lock them into a contract, and they don't even understand that contract. Luckily, I think in Silicon Valley we have the SAFEs — a great contribution by YC and Paul Graham. But it's still somewhat predatory, because you're taking this young person and you're pre-committing them to something they shouldn't have committed to.

既务实又求知：如何两者兼得

Yeah. It's really interesting because you're an interesting person to bring on this podcast — in the academy more broadly — because you're both an entrepreneur and a builder and a hacker and a tinkerer and very pragmatic, but you're also an intellectual. You're very curious, widely read across history and economics and culture and politics, and you spend a lot of time on memes — you sort of pursue your interest there. So going back to this critique: you're neither divorced from the economic real world, but you're not an automaton either. There are some people who are so career focused that really that's just the only thing they think about — how to make more money, or how to make this thing successful.

And so, sometimes people are funneled into either of these paths. And I'm curious how you've thought about — is that something that you've always been just naturally? Or how can people both be very pragmatic in their career as young people and yet also make time or space or interest for following their intellectual curiosity, even if it might seem random or alien from that?

Yeah. I tend to oscillate between having an itch to build something and having an itch to read a lot and explore a lot and see what's out there, what's interesting. And they feed on each other. It's a recursive process where I accumulate enough knowledge and ideas from all the things I explored, that I really want to go build something with it now.

例子：从下棋到训练模型到 Replit 的新产品线

For example, recently I got really into chess — which is very late in life to get into chess. Usually you get into chess when you're six years old. My kid, actually — six years old — is getting into chess. He's pretty soon going to be beating me. [laughter]

But I didn't know why I was interested. I got interested, and then I started writing programs to solve chess, and then I started training models. And I was like, "Why do LLMs like ChatGPT actually suck at chess?"

Oh really? Yeah. And I was like, well, the ARC AGI score is getting up there. These models are almost AGI, but why are they bad at chess? They hallucinate moves and all of that.

So I went into training an LLM to play chess. And I've never trained a model before that. I spent a lot of time exploring how to train models. And I realized — you know, some people now call it RSI or recursive self-improvement, sort of a buzzword for AI being able to do ML — I realized that AI is actually now capable of doing ML.

So the moment we were in like 2024, when Replit Agent came out, before "vibe coding" as a term was coined — suddenly agents were capable of coding, right? And coding fundamentally changed since then. I think we're at a similar moment when it comes to machine learning. You could call it "vibe research," you could call it "auto research" — I think that's Karpathy's term.

I spent a lot of time in that world, and now I'm working on something on Replit to bring that to the world — where anyone can become a machine learning researcher, or any business owner who has data can fine-tune a model to solve a certain problem.

And so when I started playing chess — what are the hops you need to make to understand that, "Oh, that's going to lead me to build a new business line for Replit"? It's just impossible. But I just followed something that I was interested in, and it kind of resulted in something. Invariably it does, at least for me.

But even memes and culture — I get interested in some random subculture on the internet, and I learn something about the world. I learn something about society, about markets, about where the world is headed.

And I have alpha. You have an itch and you listen to the itch. And sometimes the itches build something, they just learn something. And a lot of kids get the itch beaten out of them because over time they learn to ignore it in favor of going through these hoops. And it's helpful to learn how to go through hoops, but it's also helpful to learn how to listen to it.

未来的公司：自驾组织

Not more than people do currently, but I think generally, in order to lead it's also helpful to know how to follow. But I think people spend their entire high school and often college just learning how to follow — just learning how to, someone says something you do it.

My belief is that the future of companies is going to change. In Silicon Valley there's been so many experiments to try to change the nature of firms — how companies work. If you remember: holacracy, Medium did that, GitHub did the "no managers" thing. They all kind of blew up in spectacular ways.

But I think it was a technology problem. I think now you can have agents function as the glue within these organizations, and have the bureaucracy be this invisible thing that's happening by machines in the background — and then people have true autonomy to work on the things that they find most interesting, and AI can sort of judge your impact.

I don't have fully formed thoughts about this, but I see it in our company — where I've changed how I run the company. And we call this idea of like a "self-driving company." Eventually the company will run itself.

Yeah. You know, it's funny because I genuinely don't have an opinion about where it's going to go, but I know it's going to change. I know that everything we're doing now just feels so different.

In starting the academy, I've been spending all this time — I built the pitch deck on Replit. Thank you. And I've been using Claude and ChatGPT — I'm using all of these services as a way to speed up my work, and imagining how that changes an entire organization. The thing I feel very certain about is: it's all going to change. It's going to change a lot faster than you think. And if you're not natively understanding of it, it's going to be hard to make that shift.

Or if you're learning the ways of the past, then you're kind of locked into a way of thinking and way of working that actually will put you at a fundamental disadvantage in the future.

不合群到什么程度才是刚好

Yeah. Back to that following point. I do think learning how to follow is very important. Let me phrase it in a different way: you want to be disagreeable enough such that you have interesting ideas. You're contrarian, you're not just going through the motions, you're following your own curiosity. But we all know people who are so disagreeable they can't work with anybody — they're just so alienating to people.

So maybe another way of following, more broadly, is: you need to learn how to work with people. You need to learn how to navigate systems. You need to learn to get what you want, or to get what is the optimal outcome.

Yeah. I think there is this important thing of respecting the elders in a way, but also fundamentally, truly understanding that they haven't figured everything out. I do think respect is very important. Like, going into a company, you should respect what they've already built, but you should also feel that a lot of things are inadequate — and go change as many things as you can.

So at Replit, I named all the conference rooms after the greats in our industry, in computer science and tech. We have a Marc Andreessen room, obviously — the inventor of the browser. You might know. [laughter] We have Linus Torvalds, Robert Noyce, all these people. And what I try to tell people at the company is: we respect the past, but we're unapologetically going to change it.

And people are going to be mad at us. Like, I don't know if you remember — 2025, I was cancelled for saying you shouldn't learn how to code anymore. And now I talk to [laughter] — Wow. Yeah. That was only a year ago. — This a year ago, and now the same people that were up against me, they're like, "Oh, I don't read code anymore. I just prompt my code."

Yeah. I mean, it's amazing how many things I've been wrong about or right about, five to ten years early. And I think the thing that I love about Silicon Valley is people just move forward. They're okay with it. They accept the takes. You know what I mean?

信任作为基础设施：从奥克兰政治说起

And that's the other thing that I love about the culture of the valley. So I spend a little bit of time — my free time now — volunteering in local politics.

In Oakland. [laughter]

Yeah, it's really interesting. It's a side quest for sure, right? It's a side quest — why would it be relevant at all? And actually I think it's helped me in so many ways in business. The skills are extremely transferable in both directions.

But one of the most interesting things is appreciating how valuable trust is, and if you have a foundation of trust throughout a society, how much it changes the way that you can move forward.

In local politics, as a simple example — let's talk about nonprofits. If you're running a nonprofit and you raise money from someone and you have a conversation with them and they say, "I'll give you $50,000" — the percent likelihood that that $50,000 will land in your bank account is somewhere in the 20 to 50% range after they've committed verbally.

So verbal commitments don't have weight. In Silicon Valley, I think it's probably 75 to 100%, depending on who you're talking to, who you are. And the difference in how you operate — I can confidently continue to move forward on my business if I know that the money's coming. And then by the time you've delivered that check, I've made like six weeks of progress. And now all of a sudden your check is more valuable six weeks later.

And the reverse is also true. If you do not have trust, then all of a sudden you're like, "Well, what if this donor is upset about this thing? Let me do this thing differently, blah blah." And you're not fulfilling your mission. You're worried. You have anxiety and stress about this thing.

And so I think that is something that Silicon Valley offers that can be applied to school.

In what way?

Trusting students to do what they want to do and follow the threads they want to do is something that I think we can uniquely offer. I think Silicon Valley is a place where someone who has a unique idea or a different way of doing things can generally be accepted and allowed to do it. Now, there are some social rules — like you can't just go around being mean to everyone, or lying. It's not that permissive. But if we start trusting young kids and young adults to follow what they want, and then we empower them — even if we think what they're doing is crazy — then they're going to build that future you're talking about. They're going to figure out the next version of holacracy that actually works.

麻烦制造者怎么办？

Let me ask you a question — might be tricky. What are you going to do with the troublemakers? Invariably there's going to be people that are going to be breaking things. Like Zuck famously built Facemash, which was really controversial. "I hacked into someone" might — [laughter] What do you think of that? Obviously there are things that cross some kind of red line on criminality, but —

Oh sure. Yeah. Just to be clear: you have to draw a line somewhere. If you do something like violate our sexual harassment policy, or you're super mean to someone in front of everyone — there are going to be rules, of course. We have to create a culture of trust and positive sum.

At the same time, I think that one of the core tenets of the academy sidesteps this problem entirely. We don't have grades. We don't have tests. The amount of weight to push against should be a lot less. And so therefore, a lot of these challenges — these things that people do — it's like: you want to build Facemash? Go for it. Like, I mean, who cares? I'm willing to defend your right to do that. And I'm also happy, if someone asks me on a podcast, to say, "Yeah, that was a weird idea. I don't know what that kid was thinking. I didn't love it, but you know what? They got to do what they got to do." And that's how people are going to be.

And so I'd say: if you create an environment of trust, and if you allow that to happen, and you design it so that they don't have a sort of anti-authoritarianism mindset — then I think you open up a lot of creativity and opportunity.

Roblox、黑客、抓旗子

Yeah. I also think that there's an opportunity to funnel that drive to test the boundaries in a healthy way. I was reading the story the other day about a kid that hacked into some government thing and is getting like two years in prison. And he was on an interview talking about how he learned to hack on Roblox. And apparently there's a big trend where people learn programming and hacking on Roblox.

I was talking to Dave, the founder-CEO of Roblox. It would be really cool to have some kind of sandbox for these people to play in — and then discover talents, and then funnel them into cybersecurity jobs.

Yeah. Or even the government. Instead of sending these kids to jail, take them to work at the NSA, or work at some — we need cybersecurity talent right now. Why are you putting them in jail?

Yeah, and there's a line — there are kids who are hacking who are probably doing things that I wouldn't be comfortable with. But there's also kids who are doing it for reasons and in ways that are honestly fine. And if we can just have a little bit more permissiveness, I think we can create a lot more opportunity for them and repurpose that talent, as you mentioned.

Yeah. One site I was really into growing up called Hack This Site — hackthissite.org. I don't know if it's still around. It's like a website that has vulnerabilities built in. [laughter] Like — it's like capture the flag, right? Yeah. I mean, we're kind of digging deep into one aspect of it, but — you can have a bounty program in the RC, right? For sure. Absolutely. Or I can encourage the students to do the bounty programs at all the other schools, or all the other companies, because most companies have a bounty program.

分寸感（Discernment）与 Meta-Maxing

Absolutely. Yeah. It's interesting. I mean, going back to your thing around when to trust the elders versus when to disrupt — there's this general trend in terms of what's really important to gain is discernment. Because all rules and heuristics — it really matters the context and case by case. And the way to get discernment is by having reps, and by trusting the students to fail on their own, to make decisions, to learn from it.

You coined "technicism" on this podcast. The thing I'll coin is "meta-maxing." [laughter] When to back versus when to go on pure instinct, versus when that will drive you into trouble. And I think it relates to when there's asymmetric upside versus asymmetric downside. You kind of need reps. And I think that's a lot of what project-based learning, or just giving people more control over their time, is — the idea of giving them more opportunities to choose a path, succeed, fail, learn from it.

成为一个人：价值观、道德与虚拟风气

Yeah. Here's my last question. There are some people who would say: "Hey, remember when Thiel launched his fellowship, and a lot of people were mad — they were like, college, you learn how to be a good person." [laughter] Like, it's something beyond this technical skill set, but even beyond this intellectual — people imagine like Robin Williams, Dead Poets Society, I don't know. There's sort of this like cultivate — you're 18, you're becoming a person. And so I'm curious if you could talk a little bit about how we see it in the Bay Area — in this environment that is both hyper career-oriented but also hyper intellectual — but what is the sort of cultivation of values, or morals, or ethics, or just becoming an adult? What do we say about that?

Yeah, it's actually interesting. So I've traveled all over the world. I've been to refugee camps. I've been to billionaires' houses. I have met people from every — I've been to [laughter] house. I would say that some of the kindest, most thoughtful, most grounded people I've ever met are here in Silicon Valley.

And it's not everyone — I mean, there are some real idiots out there who've made a lot of money. Like, don't get me wrong, I don't have respect for everyone who's made money. That's not the truth. But the positive-sum, high-trust ecosystem, I think, breeds really amazing human beings.

Interpersonal skills is an absolute pillar of the academy. We want our graduates — or attendees, or fellows, or whatever we're going to end up calling them — we want the people who attend the academy to be positive influences on society and the world. And I think that's one of the missions of the academy: to create a positive-sum world.

So I actually think we absolutely believe in a two-year — you know, you're going to spend two years and you're going to grow as a human being. You're going to meet other people, and we're going to create an environment where you can see the benefits of the culture that I think many people don't pay attention to, but is very much here in San Francisco. Having a reputation of being a good person here actually is very valuable — and people trust you with their money, people trust you with governing your company and so on and so forth.

Developing that sense in university is very important. And I think being a well-adjusted person is important. For a while, I think some people played the role of being this "autistic genius" person. And maybe at some point it paid off — I remember the Sequoia blog post about SBF, that's like gold. They deleted it. You can find it on archive.org. I don't think it works anymore.

I think Silicon Valley is no longer this sort of renegade thing. We're kind of — it's an institution. It's part of the establishment anyways. And we also have to interface with the world. People need to understand that we have a responsibility — that we're not just talking amongst ourselves.

And what we're saying — you know, Bernie Sanders read Dwarkesh's blog post. And I criticized Marc Andreessen — kind of the language. It's like people who don't understand the technology — that blog post, in my opinion, did not create more understanding in them. It actually — if you don't understand it, you probably learn the wrong lessons from that thing. And so I think it's important that this academy creates well-adjusted adults that not only can speak the in-group language, which is important, but can eventually be in front of Congress.

关于伦理学：为什么他偏向亚里士多德

Is there anything, I guess lastly, you want to say about cultivation of values, or the idea of being a good person? Is there anything there that you feel school or a school environment contributes to? Or do you think — we spoke about the great books, it'd be good to teach some of these things.

I spent a lot of time studying ethics and morality on my own. I read, for example, a lot of the utilitarian corpus, and I ended up kind of rejecting that. I don't think that's the way of the world. I sort of found my moral compass by reading widely and introspecting, and truly coming to certain conclusions about how I want to act in the world.

Ultimately, the way I would describe myself perhaps is closest to virtue ethics — from Aristotle. And the idea is that I should act in a way that I would be proud of, regardless of who's watching, or who's not watching, or regardless of the impact.

And I think in a weird way, if you're virtuous, and if you have certain principles, the net effect of that is that you are utility-maximizing — I think, if you have the right principles. And you need to also change over time, and you need to figure out where the world is headed and make sure you're fitting into it in the right way.

But all of this to say is that I think there is value in the liberal arts, and reading some of this stuff, and trying to understand how you feel about how you want to act and how you want to present yourself.

One thing that just made me more sympathetic to your argument, in terms of it being axiomatic, is that the world is changing so much that it's hard to have rigid principles in a world that is — a whole philosophy that is rigid — in a world that is changing.

And weirdly, the opposite is true as well: you can't be a consequentialist utilitarian when we're entering the singularity and you can't really predict the future — because that's based on predicting the future.

It is a tough time. I think you need to have principles that are evolving over time. Have some ground-truth principles that you hold dearly, and they should be as axiomatic — as small as possible.

结语：怎样的 18 岁最让他心动

Yeah. In closing, we're grateful for your support of the academy. We're excited to have people building on Replit, potentially interning at Replit, potentially being funded by you. And so maybe as a last question: when you see an 18-year-old, or 20-year-old, or 16-year-old that is really inspiring to you — that you're like, "Oh, I've got to spend time with this person, or be involved with them in some capacity" — what are they doing that is capturing your interest? Or what are you looking for in young talent?

I think the first thing is that they dove really deep in something they can teach me something. I think I can be interested in anything. And I think if you're able to tell a story about some project you've done and you've gone really really deep in it, I think that's always impressive — because that's what most people lack. Most people get bored easily. Most people do the traditional thing.

But did you actually follow a thread all the way through? That's always really impressive. And that shows all sorts of good personality traits — persistence, intrinsic motivation. You might be doing something that is really — you're following your curiosity, and maybe doesn't have an immediate reward.

And I think — like you said — being contrarian, having really important opinions. But it's very easy, if you're smart and young, to think everyone is an idiot. Including me. Like, I'll see young people — they'll talk to me like I don't understand anything. But I think it's important to respect the person that you're talking to — having good interpersonal skills is important, otherwise people don't want to be around you.

Totally. Yeah. I think it's both not being afraid to spike in something — like a lot of people just show up because they're too broad and not really amazing at anything. Follow that to its conclusion, see how good you can get at it. While also having a baseline of interpersonal skills, or just being — the right beable.

Yeah. Be likable — and in a way that's not contrived or fake. Just truly authentic. Because people want to support people who are good people. But the most endearing thing is: you can nerd out on something obscure and interesting.

Totally. Yeah. Awesome job. Thanks for — Thank you so much. Thanks for having me.

## 三个让人意外的观察
**1. "毛刺人"（The Glitch Person）作为文明的免疫系统**
Amjad 引用《城市与星辰》的隐喻表面是在说"叛逆青年很珍贵"，但更深的洞察是：**一个高度优化的系统必须依赖故障来更新自己**。这与生物学中的"体细胞超突变"（somatic hypermutation）惊人相似——免疫系统故意在B细胞的抗体基因区制造错误，以生成能识别未知病原的抗体。也就是说，**进化从不奖励精确复制，进化奖励可控的错误**。今天的大学是一个"高保真复制系统"——它太擅长把 18 岁的人复印成"合格公民"，因此它正在制造一个没有免疫力的文明。Peter Thiel 奖学金、Replit Academy 这些实验的真正意义不是"造更多创业者"，而是**给社会补充"故意的错误率"**。
**2. Replit CEO 谈教育，却泄露了他对"公司"的秘密判断**

item.title: [Latent Space] 🔬Bio-security is an AI Arms Race - Eric Nguyen (CEO, Radical Numerics)
item.dc:creator: Latent Space
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的洞察：进攻方即最佳防守方——"双重使命"背后的深层结构对称性

Eric 提出的最关键的哲学转折不在于"我们要做生物安全"，而在于一句几乎被顺口带过的话："一个擅长生成的模型，也天然擅长判别一个序列是否致病。"

这不是一句公关话术，而是一个深刻的信息论对称性。语言模型的生成 = 概率密度估计，判别 = 同一个密度函数的另一种查询方式。它意味着：在 DNA 空间中，攻防不是两种不同的技术，而是同一个数学对象的两次读取。

这带来一个惊人的推论：Radical Numerics 事实上是把自己变成了 AI 时代的"核武器扩散管制局"的技术底座——因为其他任何试图追赶其防御能力的机构，都必须先追上其进攻能力。这是一种通过技术不对称建立的、隐蔽的准公共治理权。听起来像 OpenAI 的"我们必须走在前面才能保证安全"叙事——但在生物领域，这个叙事第一次拥有了严格数学根据，因为在 NLP 里"更强模型 = 更安全"从未被证明，而在序列空间里生成器与鉴别器共享权重是结构性事实。

二、跨领域连接：这不是"AI + 生物"，这是 压缩理论 × 演化论 × 密码学 的三体缠绕

一个被 Eric 一笔带过、但极具颠覆性的暗线是：DNA 是物理世界压缩进化学空间的"log 文件"。他说 "genome is the imprint of the physical world into DNA"。这句话如果沿着信息论展开：

  • 演化 ≈ 数十亿年的随机梯度下降，损失函数是"能否留下后代"，训练数据是整个物理宇宙。
  • 基因组 = 该 SGD 的模型权重快照。
  • 预训练 GLM 就是在解压这份权重——不是在学 DNA 的语法，而是在学物理世界通过生物筛选后残留的规则。

这解释了 RNA 适配体链式思维那个让 RJ 意外的结果：模型从未见过 RNA 二级结构，为什么能沿着适应度轨迹外推？因为它学的从来不是 RNA，而是"什么样的序列演化会走向更优"这种元规则——一种从 DNA 学到的、跨模态可迁移的演化动力学先验。

更疯狂的类比：这与密码学中的可延展性攻击 (malleability) 惊人相似。Microsoft 的 "paraphrases" 工作证明你可以在保持功能的同时改写序列——这本质上是同态加密的生物学版本：功能不变、密文形式任意。这意味着生物防御体系正在被迫从"字符串匹配"升级为"功能语义匹配"，就像密码学从 MD5 升级到语义等价性验证一样。Radical 正在做的是 DNA 空间的"函数指纹识别"。

三、最容易被忽略但也最重要的一点："专家的悲观主义"是这个领域最大的隐形债务

Eric 在最后回答"想移除什么瓶颈"时，第一个说 GPU（他自己都笑称是套话），第二个说的东西才是真正的信号："越是领域专家，越倾向于对这个领域悲观。"

这句话表面平淡，实则藏着一个跨越所有学科的元规律——我称之为 "熟练度陷阱 (Expertise Trap)"：

  • 每个领域的资深从业者被训练来识别"为什么某件事不可行"，因为这是防止犯错的最优策略。
  • 但颠覆性突破恰好来自"应该不可行"的方向——这也是为什么 CRISPR、AlphaFold、mRNA 疫苗几乎都由领域边缘的人推动。
  • Eric 自己是最好的例子：他花六个月在斯坦福被几乎每一位生物学家告知"生成 DNA 是愚蠢的想法"，然后他做出了 Evo。

这与 Thomas Kuhn 的"科学革命结构"、与硅谷 VC 的"contrarian and right"、与围棋 AlphaGo 走出人类三千年从未考虑过的第 37 手，是同一个现象在不同层面的表达。

一个出人意料的推论：AI 之所以在生物学上突破如此之快，恰恰因为 AI 研究者不具备生物学家的悲观性先验。他们没有被教过"什么不可能"，所以他们做了不可能的事。这也预示着：未来 5 年生物学最大的突破，可能不会来自生物学家，而来自那些"知道足够多以理解问题，但不知道足够多以放弃"的杂交者。

Radical Numerics 的招聘哲学——"领域专家 + 仍是梦想家 (still dreamers)"——本质上是在系统性地筛选具有"反熟练度陷阱"免疫力的人。这是一种极其罕见的组织设计。

四、一个额外的、我忍不住要指出的模式

注意 Eric 反复回避回答的一个技术问题：Omni 是自回归的、扩散的还是别的？他说"我们不把自己绑定在特定训练目标上，我们用工具箱里的每一个工具。"

这句话在 AI 语境下听起来像常规发言，但在生物学语境下是革命性的——因为整个现代生物学的方法论根基就是"控制变量、单一机制、可复现"。Radical 的姿态是："我们不在乎机制的纯洁性，只在乎能力涌现。"

这实际上是把工程学的兼容主义 (methodological pluralism) 移植到生物学——一个被"分子生物学中心法则"训练了 70 年的领域。如果这种方法论真的在生物领域取得压倒性成功，它可能会从根本上重塑生物学作为一门科学的自我认知：从"追求机制理解"转向"追求可预测的操控"。这是库恩式的范式转移前夜的味道。

Can you walk through a few of the tasks you talk about in the blog?

Sometimes can cause a disease, and sometimes it doesn't do anything. Actually many times it doesn't do anything. But there are specific areas in your genome that if you have a different variant or a different letter there, it can cause disease.

And in many cases, because the combinations of these changes in the genome — over 3 billion letters — it's so vast that for clinicians and scientists we actually know only a very small portion of which variants are causal to disease or not.

And so there's these benchmarks from folks who collect variants — different hospital systems and clinics — and some are known and some are still unknown. Folks have created some benchmarks from ClinVar or TraChim to basically: the idea is given a mutation in a DNA, can you tell if it's gonna cause a disease or not?

And so this is a very good setup for DNA models because they're probabilistic. And so when you do make a change, it basically can modify its confidence or their probability of predicting a next letter.

And in this case, we've sort of leveraged that predictability of these models. They've essentially seen and been trained on so much DNA, in particular human DNA. They kind of understand what's common — and usually common or conserved across different other folks usually typically means healthier. And so if it's less common — you can think of it this way — if it's less common, the model can pick it up and sort of predict that it's potentially pathogenic or disease-causing.

Coding vs. non-coding regions

And so we've taken some of these benchmarks. And when you introduce a variant or a mutation, there's different types of mutations and variants. So sometimes you can delete a letter altogether, you can just flip it, you can remove big portions of the DNA — but these are generally single variants.

And in this case, this is where previous DNA models really struggled, especially on humans. And so we showcased that not only is it competitive or capable for humans, but in many cases it's state of the art — and actually most of these cases it's state of the art.

And I think the exciting part is that areas where other models that were currently on the frontier — they still were lagging behind quite a bit in terms of where in the genome. So in the genome, there's coding and non-coding regions — like protein areas, protein regions.

Meaning areas that are actually coding the structure of a protein versus other areas that do other things like regulate what genes are expressed.

Yeah — and so these non-coding regions are largely regulatory. They kind of control how much or when to use a certain gene or turn them on. And in many cases, these non-coding regions — these regulatory regions — variants, their mutations there are much harder to predict if they cause disease or not.

And I think what's exciting about the new generation of models we're building with Omni is that that's where we shine especially. The models are able to pick up mutations and be able to distinguish if it's disease-causing in these non-coding and especially long-range areas.

So I think this is particularly exciting to a lot of geneticists that have struggled to use traditional bioinformatic tools or statistical methods, because they've largely focused on coding regions, which is only about 1.5, 2% of the genome. And turns out many, if not most, of the diseases are in these non-coding regions. And so there's been a real desire to build models that can actually pick up these disease-causing variants in these non-coding regions.

So we have Evo2 — the latest previous genomic model that our team had worked on. And then Borzoi — it's also a DNA model, but a very different kind. Essentially it's a supervised model that predicts, from DNA, functional genomic tracks. So it too is inherently multimodal, but it's not a language model. And these tracks have been annotated extensively by people writing their dissertations and whatever.

Yeah, right. So the big difference there is that it's a supervised task. So it requires labeled outputs. And in our case, these language models — they do not require labeled outputs. So you're doing raw pre-training on unannotated sequences.

So why is that desirable? Well, it's a lot more data — a lot more genomic data that's not annotated. Actually most of it, pretty much in many ways, almost all of it is not annotated. And so being able to learn from an unsupervised manner is hugely desirable.

For us, we wanted to showcase the benefit of pre-training on raw genomic sequences and comparing it to state-of-the-art models in other spaces in DNA.

When you say it's unsupervised, how does the unsupervised property work? How do you convert the output to an actionable ranker or score?

But essentially what we're doing is using the likelihood scores. So the raw outputs of the language model — which basically you can think of it like a probability for predicting what the next letter is. We can essentially showcase the probability score, the likelihood score, for the mutation versus the wild type — so that's seen in the reference genome versus the mutation in this particular case. And then we'll have two scores. And then you can think of it as like using a ratio of the two to showcase basically how different is this mutation from a normal or baseline. And then that's — you could think of it as like a surprise factor that the model is able to use and leverage. And then we can use that to essentially score an actual prediction for disease or not.

But for the specific benchmark, you're going along and you're just using the likelihood distribution of the tokens.

And some tokens are unlikely because of some evolutionary constraint — this doesn't show up often, and because it doesn't show up often across genomes, it is probably going to cause problems and people will not survive, so on. So that's basically your ranking metric.

Yeah, it's one interpretation of how the model is thinking about it. And very similar to natural language — you can describe the same kind of paradigm.

And there's additional cases in mid- and post-training to leverage more than that. Because we can teach it specific structure and benchmarks so that it can build on top of what you just described — which is like what's common in nature — but also because it's a specific task for disease-variant prediction, then the model has additional training introduced during mid-training to showcase, to add additional learning power essentially.

What are some examples of that?

Again, probably secret sauce to some extent — but can give just a gist. We would actually throw in the score itself. That ratio I mentioned — a ratio of wild-type versus mutation — I would say that's more of a zero-shot method where you don't even have to do any mid-training. And that's what Evo2 is doing in particular in this column. So Evo2 is not fine-tuned essentially.

There's an EVE column — where people are basically fine-tuning, using the scores from Evo2. That's from Goodfire. And that's also folks that we greatly respect, and they kind of showcase that these models are able to be state of the art when you can fine-tune them as well — not just zero-shot.

And then our model is introducing sort of a step above that — not just fine-tuning, but also introducing structure (by structure I mean the format of these benchmarks) into the model itself. That Q&A style formatting during mid-training is what gives us an extra boost even.

I see. And extra boost — but I think the other benefit too, that we didn't emphasize too much in the blog, but I think it's really convenient for practical use for scientists: is that you don't — you're doing this without taking the embeddings and then tapping on a head and then doing some regression, which is an extra step, extra hurdle. Can you imagine ChatGPT, if every time you asked a question you had to like fine-tune it for a certain domain?

We've done it so that the model is flexible during mid-training to be trained on many tasks at once. And so the fine-tuning — that last step of training the embeddings — doesn't have to be done. It's out of the box at that point. You just prompt in a certain format and it will — that sort of format tells it which task you're gonna do, and then we'll output the answers in that desired format, basically.

Chain-of-Thought for DNA

I'd be interested to see — there's some discussion of chain of thought. That broke my brain a little bit when I was first hearing about that.

Yeah — I think this is really just a taste of where we think the design capabilities can move toward and way more usable for folks.

You showed the steps of how you came to a conclusion or an argument. And it turns out — even if they were like simple steps — but it just gave the model a chance. Maybe it's sort of like philosophically who knows exactly why it works, but essentially feeding more tokens in and giving it more scratch space to think.

And so people just think this is the beginning of reasoning for these language models — this ability to kind of get to an answer by thinking to itself, by itself. And so it seemed quite successful in language — very successful. And that's why you have a lot of agents that just spend tons of tokens, right? Just showing its work. In many ways it stems from this chain-of-thought paradigm.

And in biology, we saw very little of that. We started to see some of that in protein design a little. And so we wanted to push that and showcase that — well, at first explore it — is that possible in DNA? What does that even mean in genomics? Because you don't really have words that describe its thinking. So how do you take that same paradigm and introduce it to a DNA language model?

The RNA aptamer experiment

And so what we did was a simpler version, in so many ways. We had this dataset of RNA aptamers — so just think of it as these desired sequences with some kind of fitness score associated with them. So we took this large dataset that had RNA input and a fitness score. The fitness score go high, it's good. It's the simplest version. It's a big dataset.

And so what we wanted to showcase was that if we show the model progressively better RNAs in a series of steps with its score — so you have like low scores first and then you gradually move up the chain — can the model continue that trajectory on its own? And then in the final step, does it self-optimize to a point where it's like the best score it can get? That was the experiment.

Can we do that? And so we took a dataset — a large dataset of aptamers. We held out a portion of like the best-performing ones and we showed it only the lower ones, but then we ranked it. So we showcased lower scores with the RNA aptamers, and then progressively got higher, and then asked the model to just like continue with that pattern. And it turns out it was able to recapitulate some of those higher scores that we had not shown it yet.

We were actually in the process of validating this in the wet lab right now. So we didn't get to show it here. But we wanted to know — actually, can it not just do this in silico, which it can (it showcased that it was able to continue this trajectory and create plausible aptamers with higher fitness scores)?

And now we think this is — you know, obviously if this works in the lab — we think this is a hugely, hugely valuable paradigm that can be pretty much applied to every other type of biological sequence. That's usually what you have: you have sequence, you have some kind of fitness score, desired output. And if we can get models to eventually learn that structure and just show a series of progressively stronger sequences — the model can then predict the rest. That's a very powerful paradigm.

Why did RNA work? A surprise

Honestly a bit surprised about this — that specifically this task saw a strong improvement. Maybe my personal bias, but RNA is somewhat notorious for not having good co-evolution data. For viral genomes there is strong evolutionary pressure, but for mammalian, usually RNA does not have evolutionary pressure. The predominant pressure is like RNA will carry coding information. Genomes carry lots of different information. So I'm wondering — where do you think this capability might have emerged in this language model?

That's a good question — and honestly I'm not sure. Like, we're surprised too. One, because the model is pre-trained on DNA and it's really just mid-trained on RNA, very, very in a small way. Yeah, I think what your intuition about DNA having a lot of evolutionary effects or information is probably where. And so I think this is hinting at the idea of why we think it's so important to pre-train on DNA genomes and genomes first, and then sort of add additional modalities on top — because you get a lot of transfer. And you want the modality generalization is the thing that we're working toward.

General biological intelligence

You know, what I didn't talk about as a company as well, is this idea of building toward general biological intelligence, where we are unifying a lot of the different so-called languages or modalities of biology. At the end of the day, they stem from DNA. And I think people have not exploited that fact as much. It's usually really specialized — the domain-specific, modality-specific models — and not leveraging a lot of inherent shared structure from other modalities.

And so one example of that is: you know, when people talk about virtual cells — a little bit of a tangent — but they tend to focus on just RNA and transcripts, and they want to generalize to describing an entire cell. But obviously a cell is a lot more things than that.

In my mind, if you want to learn a system, you want to learn from all the signals or sensors of that world or that system. If it's a cell and you want to fuse — you want to understand the DNA, you want to understand the metabolomics, the epigenomics, proteomics — and that's when you get closer to like, quote-unquote, a virtual cell.

And in our minds we don't even want to stop at just the cell, but we want to fuse all of these sensors across all of biology.

Will it get us to a super intelligence that understands every component and nuance of biology? Who knows? But I am confident that this type of paradigm will get us a hell of a lot further than we are now. That's my bars. Can you make something far more useful than now?

More applications: AMR, rare earths

So another example is for the antimicrobial resistance — I think that's something we're very interested in as well. Context matters — the rare-earths thesis

Rare-earth mineral extraction is interesting. Maybe you wouldn't have a comparative advantage compared to other techniques, because it seems like your strengths are probably in larger-scale design across entire organisms, but focusing on individual proteins — that may be much more of a structural task. And going to talk about ClinVar — the argument is that the model now is a really good statistical representation of what type of mutations are common or not. If you want to do design and understand structure — for disease, that's more natural in a population-genomic way. So where do you think your strongest competitive advantage is? And do you think your model understands structure in addition to function?

Yeah — I'd say what drew us to this particular application — rare earths — and our strengths in general, why we thought it might be suited for it, is two things.

One is I think in areas where context matters. So yeah, you're right — a protein-design task where you're just designing maybe not naturally where we see ourselves competitively advantaged. But in the rare-earths case, our hypothesis is that context matters. And what matters here possibly is certain microorganisms with proteins that have the function that we desire — we can potentially prompt and provide it context for: this is the neighborhood in which — tell Omni, this is the neighborhood of genomes or microorganisms that you should search for new proteins.

So it's really sort of like a mining exercise. And what we can showcase to our models that other folks can — for like protein-structure models — is that we can feed in non-coding regions before that gene of interest or that protein of interest, and then ask for the model to provide variants. So like, mutate this protein — but know that you're in this microorganism — but show me different variants that you've seen in nature, or combine different things that you've seen in nature, given this context.

And I think that is one reason why we can make very evolutionarily diverse sequences and potentially phages. Folks have used Evo models to do this with toxin-antitoxins and a similar technique — they've prompted on things upstream from the proteins of interest, and then asked the model to kind of generate a bunch of plausible other ones.

And I think this case for rare earths — that's super exciting because then we can come up with plausible variants and then test them relatively simply for what they bind to and selectively bind to. Which I think is really interesting for this partner who cares, for example, about securing the supply chain of rare earths for the US strategically. And so we thought that's absolutely something that is worth supporting.

So your point is — not just you're designing a protein, but you're designing an organism which generates a protein, and this protein has an action. Yeah — I'd say in this particular case for rare earths, we're not really interested in the organism, like designing the whole organism. And it helps us narrow and provide additional context.

I guess I think of the genome or DNA broadly as sort of the imprint of the physical world into DNA. And so there's parts of the DNA that we want, but the things around those parts that we want also tells a little bit about the context of where it came from and how it came to be — in its function. And so I just think of it — can we come back to that word — but context. I think context matters in many of these applications, or at least in some of them.

(Laughs) Yeah — I think context matters a lot in biology. The Stanford / Hyena origin story

You and your team, your collaborators, have a long history of these state-space models, doing pushing context. Also — how you go in a first-principles way, diving into the architectures of how GPUs work and designing models which are exploiting the architecture of GPUs.

Yeah, absolutely. If you wanna distract our researchers at Radical Numerics — this is how you nerd-snipe them. You talk about long context and kernels, GPUs — then they're like: wait, did someone say kernels? And they start trying to figure out how to make things fast.

Yeah — long contexts hold a special place in my heart because that's what I focused on in my PhD at Stanford. And that's how we started thinking about DNA. And going back a little bit for fun: we were looking at working on language models in general, and then we noticed our models were good at long context. And so that's the progression of how we started working in the space — it was like: oh, these models seem to be really efficient on long context.

And then with Michael Poli, my lab mate, he worked on the first design of Hyena — this convolutional architecture. And then we started thinking: let's push this further. Let's see what new applications open up if we really lean into long context. And we asked: what's the longest sequence out there? And eventually — unsurprisingly — we landed on DNA. We were like, DNA's gotta be the longest — three billion base pairs.

And we started thinking like: OK, what's being done there? Like what kind of context lengths are people doing there? They're doing super short. They're doing like one or 2000 base pairs or tokens at a time. It's like way smaller than what one would want for DNA. I mean, most human transcripts are like 3K or so — so that's not even what you need to represent like a protein or most of the time.

And so it's clearly a need there, and overlooked. And we saw it as a way to initially — like, let's see if we can do something that we had no idea if it was gonna work, and no idea who would want it. And so we just started tinkering around.

And it turns out out of the box — relatively out of the box — it was doing pretty well at reading DNA. And then it led to: OK, people keep asking about DNA. Pitching Evo — six months of "that's a stupid idea"

And then for some reason we alighted on this idea of: well, no one's writing DNA. Can we get it to write DNA? And that was a really simple question. But in hindsight it almost seems obvious that yeah — you would wanna write DNA and design it. But when I was first pitching the idea of Evo to folks, I spent six months (which I guess in bio-words is not that long, but I spent six months) going around saying: hey, if I generate DNA, would you find that useful? Like, what would you do with it? Would you back us? Would you wanna be a part of this?

And crazy enough, most, almost every scientist at Stanford I talked to thought it was a stupid idea. Like: this would be so cool, generating DNA, how much would we accelerate the field? And then people would say like: what would you do with it? I'm like: I don't know. And then I would get that comment — or comments like "that's not possible." Like: we as humans don't understand the rules — how could you expect an AI to learn it? You can't even tell if it's right or wrong. Like you can't tell the AI yes, that's right or wrong — how can you expect it to learn it? Or there's too many repeat characters, or DNA is too noisy of a distribution — there's no real rules and there's just a bunch of junk in there.

I heard all the reasons. And I was just so stubborn about it. There's gotta be a use case for being able to generate DNA. I just — it just feels right. And I didn't know what it was. So it really was an experiment of: like, what happens.

The first Evo checkpoint

And so when we first trained Evo, I remember we had no idea if it was gonna work. We had no idea. We didn't know what thing was gonna emerge. We just thought: let's just train a big one. Which is kind of ridiculous. But somehow folks were like, sure, why not — let's see what happens. Let's pay some money for the GPUs and let these crazy kids train the model.

And I remember when the first result came back and it kind of like gave us chills — like, oh, maybe there's something going on. Which was: somebody took the model checkpoint, the first one, and threw it at a protein gym — one of the protein benchmarks. And [it] turned out to be competitive with protein-specific models. And we were like: OK, that is pretty surprising because we never told the model what's proteins versus not. And there's actually — you know, there's also protein and DNA. So there was one piece — I think it was just surprising that it was actually competitive with protein-specific models.

And this was like the first experience. And then they just kind of kept on coming, one after another. And it was like: oh, this competitive here, oh, it's state of the art on RNA and our DNA. And we started seeing like: oh, it can learn across different modalities, not just DNA. And then we felt like: OK, there's something there.

And so it kind of went from there. And then folks at NVIDIA were like: let's back Evo2, let's make this even bigger. And then Greg Brockman from OpenAI was like: I'll take a break from OpenAI and take us four months of a sabbatical and help these crazy kids out. And, you know, then we're Slack-messaging Greg Brockman at 3 a.m. trying to debug our code — which is wild.

Yeah — so the trajectory was very surprising in many ways. But at the same time, you still got a lot of feedback like: what are these models good for? What are they useful for in the real world? And so that's really motivated us to start a company.

We thought what we showed was just really just a taste — from like an academic flavor. In a similar way, the language models when they first [came out] — you know, if natural language came out, people asked some of the questions like: what are these things good for? Oh, cool, it can write some jokes for me. Is this gonna lead to an all-composing AGI that can automate everything? They did not think that. They thought it's like a toy — it's got emerging capabilities and they would extrapolate the potential. And in many ways I think what we're seeing here is even more exciting or reminiscent of that trajectory for DNA.

But Evo2 even was showing the bacteriophage — and that wasn't a persuasive — I mean, that's almost a scary example. So the people didn't see that, like — that isn't a light-bulb moment for people.

Yeah — so I mean, and some people — I think either fair or rough critiques, you can even play devil's advocate and say: what it's generating is pretty close to nature, and you're kind of recapitulating just a small variance. And so there's a lot of ways to critique and kind of minimize the potential, which can be fair argument.

Like, so I think at this point, we think what is more important is not just pushing on the science and like — cool, this can be done, and kind of leave it there as a sort of thought experiment. But like: how do we actually use this to improve human understanding of disease, improve treatments, make better rare-earth mineral extractors? How do we actually make this useful is what we care about now as a company, in addition to some of these more scientific questions.

Mechanistic Interpretability for Biology

So maybe that's a good segue. There's — that brings up two things for me. One is the Mech Interp stuff that's in the end of the blog post, and then also the biosafety stuff. Those are both, I think, important applications. So can we — let's do Mech Interp first.

Can you talk a little bit about — and this is actually kind of building on the work that Evo did as well? I remember in the Evo paper there was some Mech Interp work in which they were discussing using — reversing the question and using the model to extract insights about biology. This has actually become a common theme with — I think maybe biology more than any other domain — that people, because it's a scientific question and it's learning patterns about the world, you can actually say: OK, well, what patterns did you learn?

Yeah, so I think Mech Interp is an emerging field in bio that we're extremely excited about. And admittedly we are on the early side, I'd say. So we're building up that team. But so far what we've showcased and been excited about is looking, really analyzing the embeddings and some of the activations in the model.

And so this idea of Mech Interp for bio is borrowing a lot from the natural-language community. Currently, you could think of what the models are doing is compressing a bunch of information it's seen. And so in this compression, it's really basically distilling it down into the key components, key patterns, that helps it understand the data or learns the distribution of the data.

And so what we're trying to do is probe the models to see what did the model distill into its weights and its activations — or sort of like the outputs. And so for us, we started off with a lot of the outputs of the model — so the activations. And we wanted to see: what kind of structure, what kind of visualizations, can we see that help us understand some of the complexities of DNA (which is a ton)?

And so some of these complexities can range around GC content, certain motifs of transcription factors — there's a bunch of regulatory types of patterns and motifs that the model, we believe, has to pick up to be able to do its tasks. To understand whether a disease is caused by a variant. And generally it's going to compress all these different motifs and distill them into the model weights. And so our job is to then find these and see if we can distill a pattern or structure that can be generalized to other cases where we don't understand the patterns. So that's sort of largely the goal.
